senses.d: The first letter of the English and of many other alphabets. The capital A of the alphabets of Middle and Western Europe, as also the small letter (a), besides the forms in Italic, black letter, etc., are all descended from the old Latin A, which was borrowed from the Greek Alpha, of the same form; and this was made from the first letter (�) of the Phœnician alphabet, the equivalent of the Hebrew Aleph, and itself from the Egyptian origin. The Aleph was a consonant letter, with a guttural breath sound that was not an element of Greek articulation; and the Greeks took it to represent their vowel Alpha with the ä sound, the Phœnician alphabet having no vowel symbols.

The name of the sixth tone in the model major scale (that in C), or the first tone of the minor scale, which is named after it the scale in A minor. The second string of the violin is tuned to the A in the treble staff. — A sharp (A♯) is the name of a musical tone intermediate between A and B. — A flat (A♭) is the name of a tone intermediate between A and G.
q: O fair Creseide, the flower and A per se Of Troy and Greece. Chaucer.

senses.d: An adjective, commonly called the indefinite article, and signifying one or any, but less emphatically.
In each; to or for each; as, “twenty leagues a day”, “a hundred pounds a year”, “a dollar a yard”, etc.
In; on; at; by.

In process of; in the act of; into; to; — used with verbal substantives in -ing which begin with a consonant. This is a shortened form of the preposition an (which was used before the vowel sound); as in a hunting, a building, a begging.

A.etym: [Abbreviated form of an (AS. on). See On.]

senses.d: Of.

A.etym: [From AS. of off, from. See Of.]

senses.d: A barbarous corruption of have, of he, and sometimes of it and of they.
An expletive, void of sense, to fill up the meter
q: A merry heart goes all the day, Your sad tires in a mile-a. Shak.

senses.d: The fifth month of the Jewish year according to the ecclesiastical reckoning, the eleventh by the civil computation, coinciding nearly with August.
The destroyer, or angel of the bottomless pit; — the same as Apollyon and Asmodeus.
Hell; the bottomless pit.
q: In all her gates, Abaddon rues Thy bold attempt. Milton.

Abaddon.etym: [Heb. ābaddōn destruction, abyss, fr. ābad to be lost, to perish.]

senses.d: To lower or depress; to throw or cast down; as, to abase the eye.
q: Saying so, he abased his lance. Shelton.

senses.d: To cast down or reduce low or lower, as in rank, office, condition in life, or estimation of worthiness; to depress; to humble; to degrade.
q: Whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased. Luke xiv. ll.

Abase.syn: To Abase, Debase, Degrade. These words agree in the idea of bringing down from a higher to a lower state. Abase has reference to a bringing down in condition or feelings; as, to abase the proud, to abase one's self before God. Debase has reference to the bringing down of a thing in purity, or making it base. It is, therefore, always used in a bad sense, as, to debase the coin of the kingdom, to debase the mind by vicious indulgence, to debase one's style by coarse or vulgar expressions. Abase.etym: [F. abaisser, LL. abassare, abbassare ; ad + bassare, fr. bassus low. See Base, a.]

senses.d: Lowered; humbled.
Borne lower than usual, as a fess; also, having the ends of the wings turned downward towards the point of the shield.
To beat down; to overthrow.
q: The King of Scots . . . sore abated the walls. Edw. Hall.

senses.d: To bring down or reduce from a higher to a lower state, number, or degree; to lessen; to diminish; to contract; to moderate; to cut short; as, to abate a demand; to abate pride, zeal, hope.
q: His eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated. Deut. xxxiv. 7.

senses.d: To deduct; to omit; as, to abate something from a price.
q: Nine thousand parishes, abating the odd hundreds. Fuller.

senses.d: To blunt.
q: To abate the edge of envy. Bacon.

senses.d: To reduce in estimation; to deprive.
q: She hath abated me of half my train. Shak.

senses.d: To bring entirely down or put an end to; to do away with; as, to abate a nuisance, to abate a writ.

Abate.etym: [OF. abatre to beat down, F. abattre, LL. abatere; ab or ad + batere, battere (popular form for L. batuere to beat). Cf. Bate, Batter.]

senses.d: To decrease, or become less in strength or violence; as, pain abates, a storm abates.
q: The fury of Glengarry . . . rapidly abated. Macaulay.

senses.d: To be defeated, or come to naught; to fall through; to fail; as, a writ abates.

Abate.syn: To subside; decrease; intermit; decline; diminish; lessen.

senses.d: Abatement.
Father; religious superior; — in the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic churches, a title given to the bishops, and by the bishops to the patriarch.
In bed, or on the bed.
q: Not to be abed after midnight. Shak.

senses.d: To childbed (in the phrase “brought abed,” that is, delivered of a child).
To shrink back with shuddering from; to regard with horror or detestation; to feel excessive repugnance toward; to detest to extremity; to loathe.
q: Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good. Rom. xii. 9.

senses.d: To fill with horror or disgust.
q: It doth abhor me now I speak the word. Shak.

senses.d: To protest against; to reject solemnly.
q: I utterly abhor, yea, from my soul Refuse you for my judge. Shak.

Abhor.syn: To hate; detest; loathe; abominate. See Hate.
Abhor.etym: [L. abhorrere; ab + horrere to bristle, shiver, shudder: cf. F. abhorrer. See Horrid.]

senses.d: To shrink back with horror, disgust, or dislike; to be contrary or averse; — with
q: Which is utterly abhorring from the end of all law. Milton.

senses.d: Detestation.
Object of abhorrence.
The first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, corresponding nearly to our April. After the Babylonish captivity this month was called Nisan.

Abib.etym: [Heb. abīb, lit. an ear of corn. The month was so called from barley being at that time in ear.]

senses.d: To wait; to pause; to delay.
To stay; to continue in a place; to have one's abode; to dwell; to sojourn; — with with before a person, and commonly with at or in before a place.
q: Let the damsel abide with us a few days. Gen. xxiv. 55.

senses.d: To remain stable or fixed in some state or condition; to continue; to remain.
q: Let every man abide in the same calling. 1 Cor. vii. 20.

Abide.etym: [AS. ābīdan; pref. ā- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + bīdan to bide. See Bide.]

senses.d: To wait for; to be prepared for; to await; to watch for; as, I abide my time.
q: Bonds and afflictions abide me. Acts xx. 23.

senses.d: To endure; to sustain; to submit to.
q: shalt abide her judgment on it. Tennyson.

senses.d: To bear patiently; to tolerate; to put up with.
q: She could not abide Master Shallow. Shak.

senses.d: To stand the consequences of; to answer for; to suffer for.
q: Dearly I abide that boast so vain. Milton.

senses.d: Continuing; lasting.
A lady's waiting-maid.
q: Her abigail reported that Mrs. Gutheridge had a set of night curls for sleeping in. Leslie.

senses.d: The quality or state of being able; power to perform, whether physical, moral, intellectual, conventional, or legal; capacity; skill or competence in doing; sufficiency of strength, skill, resources, etc.; — in the plural, faculty, talent.
q: Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren. Acts xi. 29.
Natural abilities are like natural plants, that need pruning by study. Bacon.
The public men of England, with much of a peculiar kind of ability. Macaulay.

Ability.syn: Capacity; talent; cleverness; faculty; capability; efficiency; aptitude; aptness; address; dexterity; skill.
Ability.etym: [F. habileté, earlier spelling habilité (with silent h), L. habilitas aptitude, ability, fr. habilis apt. See Able.]

senses.d: Cast down; low-lying.
q: From the safe shore their floating carcasses And broken chariot wheels; so thick bestrown Abject and lost lay these, covering the flood. Milton.

senses.d: Sunk to a low condition; down in spirit or hope; degraded; servile; groveling; despicable; as, abject posture, fortune, thoughts.
q: And banish hence these abject, lowly dreams. Shak.

Abject.syn: Mean; groveling; cringing; mean-spirited; slavish; ignoble; worthless; vile; beggarly; contemptible; degraded.
Abject.etym: [L. abjectus, p. p. of abjicere to throw away; ab + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.]

senses.d: To cast off or down; hence, to abase; to degrade; to lower; to debase.
A person in the lowest and most despicable condition; a castaway.
q: Shall these abjects, these victims, these outcasts, know any thing of pleasure? I. Taylor.

senses.d: Fit; adapted; suitable.
q: A many man, to ben an abbot able. Chaucer.

senses.d: Having sufficient power, strength, force, skill, means, or resources of any kind to accomplish the object; possessed of qualifications rendering competent for some end; competent; qualified; capable; as, an able workman, soldier, seaman, a man able to work; a mind able to reason; a person able to be generous; able to endure pain; able to play on a piano.
Specially: Having intellectual qualifications, or strong mental powers; showing ability or skill; talented; clever; powerful; as, the ablest man in the senate; an able speech.
q: No man wrote abler state papers. Macaulay.

senses.d: Legally qualified; possessed of legal competence; as, able to inherit or devise property.

Able.syn: Competent; qualified; fitted; efficient; effective; capable; skillful; clever; vigorous; powerful.
Able.etym: [OF. habile, L. habilis that may be easily held or managed, apt, skillful, fr. habere to have, hold. Cf. Habile and see Habit.]

senses.d: To make able; to enable; to strengthen.
To vouch for.
On board; into or within a ship or boat; hence, into or within a railway car.
Alongside; as, close aboard.
On board of; as, to go aboard a ship.
Across; athwart.
q: Nor iron bands aboard The Pontic Sea by their huge navy cast. Spenser.

senses.d: Act of waiting; delay.
q: And with her fled away without abode. Spenser.

senses.d: Stay or continuance in a place; sojourn.
q: He waxeth at your abode here. Fielding.

senses.d: Place of continuance, or where one dwells; abiding place; residence; a dwelling; a habitation.
q: Come, let me lead you to our poor abode. Wordsworth.

Abode.etym: [OE. abad, abood, fr. abiden to abide. See Abide. For the change of vowel, cf. abode, imp. of abide.]

senses.d: An omen.
q: High-thundering Juno's husband stirs my spirit with true abodes. Chapman.

senses.d: To bode; to foreshow.
To be ominous.
To do away with wholly; to annul; to make void; — said of laws, customs, institutions, governments, etc.; as, to abolish slavery, to abolish folly.
To put an end to, or destroy, as a physical objects; to wipe out.
q: And with thy blood abolish so reproachful blot. Spenser.
His quick instinctive hand Caught at the hilt, as to abolish him. Tennyson.

Abolish.syn: To Abolish, Repeal, Abrogate, Revoke, Annul, Nullify, Cancel.
Abolish.etym: [F. abolir, L. abolere, aboletum; ab + olere to grow. Cf. Finish.]

senses.d: Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loathsome; execrable.
Excessive; large; — used as an intensive.
In an abominable manner; very odiously; detestably.
The feeling of extreme disgust and hatred; abhorrence; detestation; loathing; as, he holds tobacco in abomination.
That which is abominable; anything hateful, wicked, or shamefully vile; an object or state that excites disgust and hatred; a hateful or shameful vice; pollution.
q: Antony, most large in his abominations. Shak.

senses.d: A cause of pollution or wickedness.

Abomination.syn: Detestation; loathing; abhorrence; disgust; aversion; loathsomeness; odiousness.

senses.d: To be in great plenty; to be very prevalent; to be plentiful.
q: The wild boar which abounds in some parts of the continent of Europe. Chambers.
Where sin abounded grace did much more abound. Rom. v. 20.

senses.d: To be copiously supplied; — followed by in or with.
q: Men abounding in natural courage. Macaulay.
A faithful man shall abound with blessings. Prov. xxviii. 20.
It abounds with cabinets of curiosities. Addison.

Abound.etym: [OE. abounden, F. abonder, fr. L. abundare to overflow, abound; ab + unda wave. Cf. Undulate.]

senses.d: Around; all round; on every side of.
In the immediate neighborhood of; in contiguity or proximity to; near, as to place; by or on (one's person).
Over or upon different parts of; through or over in various directions; here and there in; to and fro in; throughout.
q: Lampoons . . . were handed about the coffeehouses. Macaulay.
Roving still about the world. Milton.

senses.d: Near; not far from; — determining approximately time, size, quantity.
q: He went out about the third hour. Matt. xx. 3.

senses.d: In concern with; engaged in; intent on.
q: I must be about my Father's business. Luke ii. 49.

senses.d: On the point or verge of; going; in act of.
q: Paul was now aboutto open his mouth. Acts xviii. 14.

senses.d: Concerning; with regard to; on account of; touching.
q: She must have her way about Sarah. Trollope.

About.etym: [OE. aboute, abouten, abuten; AS. ābutan, onbutan; on + butan, which is from be by + utan outward, from ut out. See But, Out.]

senses.d: On all sides; around.
q: 'Tis time to look about. Shak.

senses.d: In circuit; circularly; by a circuitous way; around the outside; as, a mile about, and a third of a mile across.
Here and there; around; in one place and another.
q: Wandering about from house to house. 1 Tim. v. 13.

senses.d: Nearly; approximately; with close correspondence, in quality, manner, degree, etc.; as, about as cold; about as high; — also of quantity, number, time.
To a reserved position; half round; in the opposite direction; on the opposite tack; as, to face about; to turn one's self about.
In or to a higher place; higher than; on or over the upper surface; over; — opposed to below or beneath.
q: Fowl that may fly above the earth. Gen. i. 20.

senses.d: Figuratively, higher than; superior to in any respect; surpassing; beyond; higher in measure or degree than; as, things above comprehension; above mean actions; conduct above reproach.
q: I saw in the way a light from heaven above the brightness of the sun. Acts xxxvi. 13.

senses.d: Surpassing in number or quantity; more than; as, above a hundred. (Passing into the adverbial sense. See Above, adv., 4.)

Above.etym: [OE. above, aboven, abuffe, AS. abufon; an (or on) on + be by + ufan upward; cf. Goth. uf under. √199. See Over.]

senses.d: In a higher place; overhead; into or from heaven; as, the clouds above.
Earlier in order; higher in the same page; hence, in a foregoing page.
Higher in rank or power; as, he appealed to the court above.
More than; as, above five hundred were present.
At large; widely; broadly; over a wide space; as, a tree spreads its branches abroad.
q: The fox roams far abroad. Prior.

senses.d: Without a certain confine; outside the house; away from one's abode; as, to walk abroad.
q: I went to St. James', where another was preaching in the court abroad. Evelyn.

senses.d: Beyond the bounds of a country; in foreign countries; as, we have broils at home and enemies abroad.
Before the public at large; throughout society or the world; here and there; widely.
q: He went out, and began to publish it much, and to blaze abroad the matter. Mark i. 45.

senses.d: A state of being absent or withdrawn from a place or from companionship; — opposed to presence.
q: Not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence. Phil. ii. 12.

senses.d: Want; destitution; withdrawal.
Inattention to things present; abstraction (of mind); as, absence of mind.
q: To conquer that abstraction which is called absence. Landor.

senses.d: Being away from a place; withdrawn from a place; not present.
Not existing; lacking; as, the part was rudimental or absent.
Inattentive to what is passing; absent-minded; preoccupied; as, an absent air.
q: What is commonly called an absent man is commonly either a very weak or a very affected man. Chesterfield.

Absent.etym: [F., fr. absens, absentis, p. pr. of abesse to be away from; ab + esse to be. Cf. Sooth.]

senses.d: To take or withdraw (one's self) to such a distance as to prevent intercourse; — used with the reflexive pronoun.
q: If after due summons any member absents himself, he is to be fined. Addison.

senses.d: To withhold from being present.
To hold one's self aloof; to forbear or refrain voluntarily, and especially from an indulgence of the passions or appetites; — with from.
q: Not a few abstained from voting. Macaulay.
Who abstains from meat that is not gaunt? Shak.

Abstain.syn: To refrain; forbear; withhold; deny one's self; give up; relinquish.
Abstain.etym: [OE. absteynen, abstenen, OF. astenir, abstenir, F. abstenir, fr. L. abstinere, abstentum, v. t. & v. i., to keep from; ab, abs + tenere to hold. See Tenable.]

senses.d: To hinder; to withhold.
q: Whether he abstain men from marrying. Milton.

senses.d: The act or practice of abstaining; voluntary forbearance of any action, especially the refraining from an indulgence of appetite, or from customary gratifications of animal or sensual propensities. Specifically, the practice of abstaining from intoxicating beverages, — called also total abstinence.
q: The abstinence from a present pleasure that offers itself is a pain, nay, oftentimes, a very great one. Locke.

senses.d: The practice of self-denial by depriving one's self of certain kinds of food or drink, especially of meat.
q: Penance, fasts, and abstinence, To punish bodies for the soul's offense. Dryden.

Abstinence.etym: [F. abstinence, L. abstinentia, fr. abstinere. See Abstain.]

senses.d: An overflowing fullness; ample sufficiency; great plenty; profusion; copious supply; superfluity; wealth: — strictly applicable to quantity only, but sometimes used of number.
q: It is lamentable to remember what abundance of noble blood hath been shed with small benefit to the Christian state. Raleigh.

Abundance.syn: Exuberance; plenteousness; plenty; copiousness; overflow; riches; affluence; wealth.
Abundance.etym: [OE. (h)abundaunce, abundance, F. abondance, L. abundantia, fr. abundare. See Abound.]

senses.d: Fully sufficient; plentiful; in copious supply; — followed by in, rarely by with.

Abundant.syn: Ample; plentiful; copious; plenteous; exuberant; overflowing; rich; teeming; profuse; bountiful; liberal. See Ample.
Abundant.etym: [OE. (h)abundant, aboundant, F. abondant, fr. L. abudans, p. pr. of abundare. See Abound.]

senses.d: In a sufficient degree; fully; amply; plentifully; in large measure.

To put to a wrong use; to misapply; to misuse; to put to a bad use; to use for a wrong purpose or end; to pervert; as, to abuse inherited gold; to make an excessive use of; as, to abuse one's authority.
q: This principle (if one may so abuse the word) shoots rapidly into popularity. Froude.

senses.d: To use ill; to maltreat; to act injuriously to; to punish or to tax excessively; to hurt; as, to abuse prisoners, to abuse one's powers, one's patience.
To revile; to reproach coarsely; to disparage.
q: The . . . tellers of news abused the general. Macaulay.

senses.d: To dishonor.
To violate; to ravish.
To deceive; to impose on.
q: Their eyes red and staring, cozened with a moist cloud, and abused by a double object. Jer. Taylor.

Abuse.syn: To maltreat; injure; revile; reproach; vilify; vituperate; asperse; traduce; malign.
Abuse.etym: [F. abuser; L. abusus, p. p. of abuti to abuse, misuse; ab + uti to use. See Use.]

senses.d: Improper treatment or use; application to a wrong or bad purpose; misuse; as, an abuse of our natural powers; an abuse of civil rights, or of privileges or advantages; an abuse of language.
q: Liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty, as well as by the abuses of power. Madison.

senses.d: Physical ill treatment; injury.
A corrupt practice or custom; offense; crime; fault; as, the abuses in the civil service.
q: Abuse after disappeared without a struggle.. Macaulay.

senses.d: Vituperative words; coarse, insulting speech; abusive language; virulent condemnation; reviling.
q: The two parties, after exchanging a good deal of abuse, came to blows. Macaulay.

senses.d: Violation; rape; as, abuse of a female child.
q: Or is it some abuse, and no such thing? Shak.

Abuse.syn: Invective; contumely; reproach; scurrility; insult; opprobrium.
Abuse.etym: [F. abus, L. abusus, fr. abuti. See Abuse, v. t.]

senses.d: One who abuses .
To receive with a consenting mind (something offered); as, to accept a gift; — often followed by of.
q: If you accept them, then their worth is great. Shak.
To accept of ransom for my son. Milton.
She accepted of a treat. Addison.

senses.d: To receive with favor; to approve.
q: The Lord accept thy burnt sacrifice. Ps. xx. 3.
Peradventure he will accept of me. Gen. xxxii. 20.

senses.d: To receive or admit and agree to; to assent to; as, I accept your proposal, amendment, or excuse.
To take by the mind; to understand; as, How are these words to be accepted?
To receive as obligatory and promise to pay; as, to accept a bill of exchange.
In a deliberate body, to receive in acquittance of a duty imposed; as, to accept the report of a committee.

Accept.syn: To receive; take; admit. See Receive.
Accept.etym: [F. accepter, L. acceptare, freq. of accipere; ad + capere to take; akin to E. heave.]

senses.d: Accepted.
Capable, worthy, or sure of being accepted or received with pleasure; pleasing to a receiver; gratifying; agreeable; welcome; as, an acceptable present, one acceptable to us.
In an acceptable manner; in a manner to please or give satisfaction.
The act of accepting; a receiving what is offered, with approbation, satisfaction, or acquiescence; esp., favorable reception; approval; as, the acceptance of a gift, office, doctrine, etc.
q: They shall come up with acceptance on mine altar. Isa. lx. 7.

senses.d: State of being accepted; acceptableness.
An assent and engagement by the person on whom a bill of exchange is drawn, to pay it when due according to the terms of the acceptance.

An agreeing to terms or proposals by which a bargain is concluded and the parties are bound; the reception or taking of a thing bought as that for which it was bought, or as that agreed to be delivered, or the taking possession as owner.
An agreeing to the action of another, by some act which binds the person in law.
Meaning; acceptation.
Acceptance; reception; favorable reception or regard; state of being acceptable.
q: This is saying worthy of all acceptation. 1 Tim. i. 15.
Some things . . . are notwithstanding of so great dignity and acceptation with God. Hooker.

senses.d: The meaning in which a word or expression is understood, or generally received; as, term is to be used according to its usual acceptation.
q: My words, in common acceptation, Could never give this provocation. Gay.

senses.d: A coming to, or near approach; admittance; admission; accessibility; as, to gain access to a prince.
q: I did repel his letters, and denied His access to me. Shak.

senses.d: The means, place, or way by which a thing may be approached; passage way; as, the access is by a neck of land.
Admission to sexual intercourse.
q: During coverture, access of the husband shall be presumed, unless the contrary be shown. Blackstone.

senses.d: Increase by something added; addition; as, an access of territory. [In this sense accession is more generally used.]
q: I, from the influence of thy looks, receive Access in every virtue. Milton.

senses.d: An onset, attack, or fit of disease.
q: The first access looked like an apoplexy. Burnet.

senses.d: A paroxysm; a fit of passion; an outburst; as, an access of fury.

Access.etym: [F. accès, L. accessus, fr. accedere. See Accede.]

senses.d: To go with or attend as a companion or associate; to keep company with; to go along with; — followed by with or by; as, he accompanied his speech with a bow.
q: The Persian dames, . . . In sumptuous cars, accompanied his march. Glover.
They are never alone that are accompanied with noble thoughts. Sir P. Sidney.
He was accompanied by two carts filled with wounded rebels. Macaulay.

senses.d: To cohabit with.

Accompany.etym: [OF. aacompaignier, F. accompagner, to associate with, fr. OF. compaign, compain, companion. See Company.]

senses.d: To associate in a company; to keep company.
q: Men say that they will drive away one another, . . . and not accompany together. Holland.

senses.d: To cohabit (with).
To perform an accompanying part or parts in a composition.
To complete, as time or distance.
q: That He would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem. Dan. ix. 2.
He had accomplished half a league or more. Prescott.

senses.d: To bring to an issue of full success; to effect; to perform; to execute fully; to fulfill; as, to accomplish a design, an object, a promise.
q: This that is written must yet be accomplished in me. Luke xxii. 37.

senses.d: To equip or furnish thoroughly; hence, to complete in acquirements; to render accomplished; to polish.
q: The armorers accomplishing the knights. Shak.
It is fully accomplished for all those ends to which Providence did appoint it. Wilkins.
These qualities . . . go to accomplish a perfect woman. Cowden Clarke.

senses.d: To gain; to obtain.

Accomplish.syn: To do; perform; fulfill; realize; effect; effectuate; complete; consummate; execute; achieve; perfect; equip; furnish.
Accomplish.etym: [OE. acomplissen, OF. accomplir, F. accomplir; L. ad + complere to fill up, complete. See Complete, Finish.]

senses.d: Completed; effected; established; as, an accomplished fact.
Complete in acquirements as the result usually of training; — commonly in a good sense; as, an accomplished scholar, an accomplished villain.
q: They . . . show themselves accomplished bees. Holland.
Daughter of God and man, accomplished Eve. Milton.

senses.d: The act of accomplishing; entire performance; completion; fulfillment; as, the accomplishment of an enterprise, of a prophecy, etc.
That which completes, perfects, or equips thoroughly; acquirement; attainment; that which constitutes excellence of mind, or elegance of manners, acquired by education or training.
q: Accomplishments have taken virtue's place, And wisdom falls before exterior grace. Cowper.

senses.d: Agreement or concurrence of opinion, will, or action; harmony of mind; consent; assent.
q: A mediator of an accord and peace between them. Bacon.
These all continued with one accord in prayer. Acts i. 14.

senses.d: Harmony of sounds; agreement in pitch and tone; concord; as, the accord of tones.
q: Those sweet accords are even the angels' lays. Sir J. Davies.

senses.d: Agreement, harmony, or just correspondence of things; as, the accord of light and shade in painting.
Voluntary or spontaneous motion or impulse to act; — preceded by own; as, of one's own accord.
q: That which groweth of its own accord of thy harvest thou shalt not reap. Lev. xxv. 5.
Of his own accord he went unto you. 2 Cor. vii. 17.

senses.d: An agreement between parties in controversy, by which satisfaction for an injury is stipulated, and which, when executed, bars a suit.
q: They rushed with one accord into the theater. Acts xix. 29.

Accord.etym: [OE. acord, accord, OF. acort, acorde, F. accord, fr. OF. acorder, F. accorder. See Accord, v. t.]

senses.d: To make to agree or correspond; to suit one thing to another; to adjust; — followed by to.
q: Her hands accorded the lute's music to the voice. Sidney.

senses.d: To bring to an agreement, as persons; to reconcile; to settle, adjust, harmonize, or compose, as things; as, to accord suits or controversies.
q: When they were accorded from the fray. Spenser.
All which particulars, being confessedly knotty and difficult can never be accorded but by a competent stock of critical learning. South.

senses.d: To grant as suitable or proper; to concede; to award; as, to accord to one due praise.

Accord.etym: [OE. acorden, accorden, OF. acorder, F. accorder, fr. LL. accordare; L. ad + cor, cordis, heart. Cf. Concord, Discord, and see Heart.]

senses.d: To agree; to correspond; to be in harmony; — followed by with, formerly also by to; as, his disposition accords with his looks.
q: My heart accordeth with my tongue. Shak.
Thy actions to thy words accord. Milton.

senses.d: To agree in pitch and tone.
Agreeing; in agreement or harmony; harmonious.
q: According to him, every person was to be bought. Macaulay.
Our zeal should be according to knowledge. Sprat.
Is all things well, According as I gave directions? Shak.
The land which the Lord will give you according as he hath promised. Ex. xii. 25.

senses.d: Accordingly; correspondingly.
Agreeably; correspondingly; suitably; in a manner conformable.
q: Behold, and so proceed accordingly. Shak.

senses.d: In natural sequence; consequently; so.
A reckoning; computation; calculation; enumeration; a record of some reckoning; as, the Julian account of time.
q: A beggarly account of empty boxes. Shak.

senses.d: A registry of pecuniary transactions; a written or printed statement of business dealings or debts and credits, and also of other things subjected to a reckoning or review; as, to keep one's account at the bank.

A statement in general of reasons, causes, grounds, etc., explanatory of some event; as, no satisfactory account has been given of these phenomena. Hence, the word is often used simply for reason, ground, consideration, motive, etc.; as, on no account, on every account, on all accounts.
A statement of facts or occurrences; recital of transactions; a relation or narrative; a report; a description; as, an account of a battle.
A statement and explanation or vindication of one's conduct with reference to judgment thereon.
q: Give an account of thy stewardship. Luke xvi. 2.

senses.d: An estimate or estimation; valuation; judgment.
Importance; worth; value; advantage; profit.

Account.syn: Narrative; narration; relation; recital; description; explanation; rehearsal.
Account.etym: [OE. acount, account, accompt, OF. acont, fr. aconter. See Account, v. t., Count, n., 1.]

senses.d: To reckon; to compute; to count.
q: The motion of . . . the sun whereby years are accounted. Sir T. Browne.

senses.d: To place to one's account; to put to the credit of; to assign; — with to.
To value, estimate, or hold in opinion; to judge or consider; to deem.
q: Accounting that God was able to raise him up. Heb. xi. 19.

senses.d: To recount; to relate.

Account.etym: [OE. acounten, accompten, OF. aconter, à (L. ad) + conter to count. F. conter to tell, compter to count, L. computare. See Count, v. t.]

senses.d: To render or receive an account or relation of particulars; as, an officer must account with or to the treasurer for money received.
To render an account; to answer in judgment; — with for; as, we must account for the use of our opportunities.
To give a satisfactory reason; to tell the cause of; to explain; — with for; as, idleness accounts for poverty.
q: Newer was preaching more accounted of than in the sixteenth century. Canon Robinson.

senses.d: To devote to destruction; to imprecate misery or evil upon; to curse; to execrate; to anathematize.
q: And the city shall be accursed. Josh. vi. 17.
Thro' you, my life will be accurst. Tennyson.

Accurse.etym: [OE. acursien, acorsien; pref. a + cursien to curse. See Curse.]

senses.d: Doomed to destruction or misery; cursed; hence, bad enough to be under the curse; execrable; detestable; exceedingly hateful; — as, an accursed deed.
The act of accusing or charging with a crime or with a lighter offense.
q: We come not by the way of accusation To taint that honor every good tongue blesses. Shak.

senses.d: That of which one is accused; the charge of an offense or crime, or the declaration containing the charge.
q: set up over his head his accusation. Matt. xxvii. 37.

Accusation.etym: [OF. acusation, F. accusation, L. accusatio, fr. accusare. See Accuse.]

senses.d: Accusation.
To charge with, or declare to have committed, a crime or offense
q: Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me. Acts xxiv. 13.
We are accused of having persuaded Austria and Sardinia to lay down their arms. Macaulay.

senses.d: To charge with a fault; to blame; to censure.
q: Their thoughts the meanwhile accusing or else excusing one another. Rom. ii. 15.

senses.d: To betray; to show.

Accuse.syn: To charge; blame; censure; reproach; criminate; indict; impeach; arraign.
Accuse.etym: [OF. acuser, F. accuser, L. accusare, to call to account, accuse; ad + causa cause, lawsuit. Cf. Cause.]

senses.d: Charged with offense; as, an accused person.
One who accuses; one who brings a charge of crime or fault.

Accuser.etym: [OE. acuser, accusour; cf. OF. acuseor, fr. L. accusator, fr. accusare.]

senses.d: To make familiar by use; to habituate, familiarize, or inure; — with to.
q: I shall always fear that he who accustoms himself to fraud in little things, wants only opportunity to practice it in greater. Adventurer.

Accustom.etym: [OF. acostumer, acustumer, F. accoutumer; à (L. ad) + OF. costume, F. coutume, custom. See Custom.]

senses.d: To be wont.
To cohabit.
q: We with the best men accustom openly; you with the basest commit private adulteries. Milton.

senses.d: Custom.
Familiar through use; usual; customary.
Frequented by customers.
The potter's field, said to have lain south of Jerusalem, purchased with the bribe which Judas took for betraying his Master, and therefore called the field of blood. Fig.: A field of bloodshed.
q: The system of warfare . . . which had already converted immense tracts into one universal aceldama. De Quincey.

Aceldama.etym: [Gr. �, fr. Syr. ōkēl damō the field of blood.]

senses.d: To own or admit the knowledge of; to recognize as a fact or truth; to declare one's belief in; as, to acknowledge the being of a God.
q: I acknowledge my transgressions. Ps. li. 3.
For ends generally acknowledged to be good. Macaulay.

senses.d: To own or recognize in a particular character or relationship; to admit the claims or authority of; to give recognition to.
q: In all thy ways acknowledge Him. Prov. iii. 6.
By my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee. Shak.

senses.d: To own with gratitude or as a benefit or an obligation; as, to acknowledge a favor, the receipt of a letter.
q: They his gifts acknowledged none. Milton.

senses.d: To own as genuine; to assent to, as a legal instrument, to give it validity; to avow or admit in legal form; as, to acknowledge a deed.

Acknowledge.syn: To avow; proclaim; recognize; own; admit; allow; concede; confess.
Acknowledge.etym: [Prob. fr. pref. a- + the verb knowledge. See Knowledge, and cf. Acknow.]

senses.d: Acquainted.
To furnish or give experimental knowledge of; to make (one) to know; to make familiar; — followed by with.
q: Before a man can speak on any subject, it is necessary to be acquainted with it. Locke.
A man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. Isa. liii. 3.

senses.d: To communicate notice to; to inform; to make cognizant; — followed by with (formerly, also, by of), or by that, introducing the intelligence; as, to acquaint a friend with the particulars of an act.
q: Acquaint her here of my son Paris' love. Shak.
I must acquaint you that I have received New dated letters from Northumberland. Shak.

senses.d: To familiarize; to accustom.

Acquaint.etym: [OE. aqueinten, acointen, OF. acointier, LL. adcognitare, fr. L. ad + cognitus, p. p. of cognoscere to know; con- + noscere to know. See Quaint, Know.]

senses.d: A state of being acquainted, or of having intimate, or more than slight or superficial, knowledge; personal knowledge gained by intercourse short of that of friendship or intimacy; as, I know the man; but have no acquaintance with him.
q: Contract no friendship, or even acquaintance, with a guileful man. Sir W. Jones.

senses.d: A person or persons with whom one is acquainted.
q: Montgomery was an old acquaintance of Ferguson. Macaulay.
Our admiration of a famous man lessens upon our nearer acquaintance with him. Addison.
We contract at last such a familiarity with them as makes it difficult and irksome for us to call off our minds. Atterbury.
It is in our power to confine our friendships and intimacies to men of virtue. Rogers.

Acquaintance.etym: [OE. aqueintance, OF. acointance, fr. acointier. See Acquaint.]

senses.d: Personally known; familiar. See To be acquainted with, under Acquaint, v. t.
Acquitted; set free; rid of.
To discharge, as a claim or debt; to clear off; to pay off; to requite.
q: A responsibility that can never be absolutely acquitted. I. Taylor.

senses.d: To pay for; to atone for.

To set free, release or discharge from an obligation, duty, liability, burden, or from an accusation or charge; — now followed by of before the charge, formerly by from; as, the jury acquitted the prisoner; we acquit a man of evil intentions.
To clear one's self.

Acquit.syn: To absolve; clear; exonerate; exonerate; exculpate; release; discharge. See Absolve.
Acquit.etym: [OE. aquiten, OF. aquiter, F. acquitter; � (L. ad) + OF. quiter, F. quitter, to quit. See Quit, and cf. Acquiet.]

senses.d: Any field of arable or pasture land.

A piece of land, containing 160 square rods, or 4,840 square yards, or 43,560 square feet. This is the English statute acre. That of the United States is the same. The Scotch acre was about 1.26 of the English, and the Irish 1.62 of the English.
q: I like that ancient Saxon phrase, which calls The burial ground, God's acre. Longfellow.

Acre.etym: [OE. aker, AS. æcer; akin to OS. accar, OHG. achar, Ger. acker, Icel. akr, Sw. åker, Dan. ager, Goth. akrs, L. ager, Gr. �, Skr. ajra. √2, 206.]

senses.d: That which is done or doing; the exercise of power, or the effect, of which power exerted is the cause; a performance; a deed.
q: That best portion of a good man's life, His little, nameless, unremembered acts Of kindness and of love. Wordsworth.

senses.d: The result of public deliberation; the decision or determination of a legislative body, council, court of justice, etc.; a decree, edit, law, judgment, resolve, award; as, an act of Parliament, or of Congress.
A formal solemn writing, expressing that something has been done.
A performance of part of a play; one of the principal divisions of a play or dramatic work in which a certain definite part of the action is completed.
A thesis maintained in public, in some English universities, by a candidate for a degree, or to show the proficiency of a student.
A state of reality or real existence as opposed to a possibility or possible existence.
q: The seeds of plants are not at first in act, but in possibility, what they afterward grow to be. Hooker.

senses.d: Process of doing; action. In act, in the very doing; on the point of (doing).
q: This woman was taken . . . in the very act. John viii. 4.

Act.etym: [L. actus, fr. agere to drive, do: cf. F. acte. See Agent.]

senses.d: To move to action; to actuate; to animate.
q: Self-love, the spring of motion, acts the soul. Pope.

senses.d: To perform; to execute; to do.
q: That we act our temporal affairs with a desire no greater than our necessity. Jer. Taylor.
Industry doth beget by producing good habits, and facility of acting things expedient for us to do. Barrow.
Uplifted hands that at convenient times Could act extortion and the worst of crimes. Cowper.

senses.d: To perform, as an actor; to represent dramatically on the stage.
To assume the office or character of; to play; to personate; as, to act the hero.
To feign or counterfeit; to simulate.
q: With acted fear the villain thus pursued. Dryden.

Act.etym: [L. actus, p. p. of agere to drive, lead, do; but influenced by E. act, n.]

senses.d: To exert power; to produce an effect; as, the stomach acts upon food.
To perform actions; to fulfill functions; to put forth energy; to move, as opposed to remaining at rest; to carry into effect a determination of the will.
q: He hangs between, in doubt to act or rest. Pope.

senses.d: To behave or conduct, as in morals, private duties, or public offices; to bear or deport one's self; as, we know not why he has acted so.
To perform on the stage; to represent a character.
q: To show the world how Garrick did not act. Cowper.

senses.d: A process or condition of acting or moving, as opposed to rest; the doing of something; exertion of power or force, as when one body acts on another; the effect of power exerted on one body by another; agency; activity; operation; as, the action of heat; a man of action.
q: One wise in council, one in action brave. Pope.

senses.d: An act; a thing done; a deed; an enterprise. (pl.): Habitual deeds; hence, conduct; behavior; demeanor.
q: The Lord is a Good of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed. 1 Sam. ii. 3.

senses.d: The event or connected series of events, either real or imaginary, forming the subject of a play, poem, or other composition; the unfolding of the drama of events.
Movement; as, the horse has a spirited action.
Effective motion; also, mechanism; as, the breech action of a gun.
Any one of the active processes going on in an organism; the performance of a function; as, the action of the heart, the muscles, or the gastric juice.
Gesticulation; the external deportment of the speaker, or the suiting of his attitude, voice, gestures, and countenance, to the subject, or to the feelings.
The attitude or position of the several parts of the body as expressive of the sentiment or passion depicted.

A suit or process, by which a demand is made of a right in a court of justice; in a broad sense, a judicial proceeding for the enforcement or protection of a right, the redress or prevention of a wrong, or the punishment of a public offense.
A share in the capital stock of a joint-stock company, or in the public funds; hence, in the plural, equivalent to stocks.
q: The Euripus of funds and actions. Burke.

senses.d: An engagement between troops in war, whether on land or water; a battle; a fight; as, a general action, a partial action.
The mechanical contrivance by means of which the impulse of the player's finger is transmitted to the strings of a pianoforte or to the valve of an organ pipe.

Action.etym: [OF. action, L. actio, fr. agere to do. See Act.]

senses.d: The state or quality of being active; nimbleness; agility; vigorous action or operation; energy; active force; as, an increasing variety of human activities.
The name given in the Bible to the first man, the progenitor of the human race.
“Original sin;” human frailty.
q: And whipped the offending Adam out of him. Shak.

senses.d: A stone imagined by some to be of impenetrable hardness; a name given to the diamond and other substances of extreme hardness; but in modern mineralogy it has no technical signification. It is now a rhetorical or poetical name for the embodiment of impenetrable hardness.
q: Opposed the rocky orb Of tenfold adamant, his ample shield. Milton.

senses.d: Lodestone; magnet.
q: As true to thee as steel to adamant. Greene.

Adamant.etym: [OE. adamaunt, adamant, diamond, magnet, OF. adamant, L. adamas, adamantis, the hardest metal, fr. Gr. αδἄμασ, -αντοσ; ἀ priv. + δαμᾳ̑ν to tame, subdue. In OE., from confusion with L. adamare to love, be attached to, the word meant also magnet, as in OF. and LL. See Diamond, Tame.]

senses.d: The twelfth month of the Hebrew ecclesiastical year, and the sixth of the civil. It corresponded nearly with March.
To give by way of increased possession (to any one); to bestow (on).
q: The Lord shall add to me another son. Gen. xxx. 24.

senses.d: To join or unite, as one thing to another, or as several particulars, so as to increase the number, augment the quantity, enlarge the magnitude, or so as to form into one aggregate. Hence: To sum up; to put together mentally; as, to add numbers; to add up a column.
q: Back to thy punishment, False fugitive, and to thy speed add wings. Milton.
As easily as he can add together the ideas of two days or two years. Locke.

senses.d: To append, as a statement; to say further.
q: He added that he would willingly consent to the entire abolition of the tax. Macaulay.

Add.syn: To Add, Join, Annex, Unite, Coalesce.
Add.etym: [L. addere; ad + dare to give, put. Cf. Date, Do.]

senses.d: To make an addition. To add to, to augment; to increase; as, it adds to our anxiety.
To perform the arithmetical operation of addition; as, he adds rapidly.
One who, or that which, adds; esp., a machine for adding numbers.
A serpent.
A small venomous serpent of the genus Vipera. The common European adder is the Vipera (or Pelias) berus. The puff adders of Africa are species of Clotho.

Adder.etym: [OE. addere, naddere, eddre, AS. nædre, adder, snake; akin to OS. nadra, OHG. natra, natara, Ger. natter, Goth. nadrs, Icel. naðr, masc., naðra, fem.: cf. W. neidr, Gorn. naddyr, Ir. nathair, L. natrix, water snake. An adder is for a nadder.]

senses.d: Addicted; devoted.
To apply habitually; to devote; to habituate; — with to.
q: He is addicted to his study. Beau. & Fl.
That part of mankind that addict their minds to speculations. Adventurer.
His genius addicted him to the study of antiquity. Fuller.
A man gross . . . and addicted to low company. Macaulay.

senses.d: To adapt; to make suitable; to fit.
q: The land about is exceedingly addicted to wood, but the coldness of the place hinders the growth. Evelyn.

Addict.syn: Addict, Devote, Consecrate, Dedicate. Addict was formerly used in a good sense; as, addicted to letters; but is now mostly employed in a bad sense or an indifferent one; as, addicted to vice; addicted to sensual indulgence. “Addicted to staying at home.” J. S. Mill. Devote is always taken in a good sense, expressing habitual earnestness in the pursuit of some favorite object; as, devoted to science. Consecrate and dedicate express devotion of a higher kind, involving religious sentiment; as, consecrated to the service of the church; dedicated to God.
Addict.etym: [L. addictus, p. p. of addicere to adjudge, devote; ad + dicere to say. See Diction.]

senses.d: The act of adding two or more things together; — opposed to subtraction or diminution.
Anything added; increase; augmentation; as, a piazza is an addition to a building.
That part of arithmetic which treats of adding numbers.
A dot at the right side of a note as an indication that its sound is to be lengthened one half.
A title annexed to a man's name, to identify him more precisely; as, John Doe, Esq.; Richard Roe, Gent.; Robert Dale, Mason; Thomas Way, of New York; a mark of distinction; a title.
Something added to a coat of arms, as a mark of honor; — opposed to abatement.

Addition.etym: [F. addition, L. additio, fr. addere to add.]

senses.d: To charge, bind, or command, solemnly, as if under oath, or under the penalty of a curse; to appeal to in the most solemn or impressive manner; to entreat earnestly.
q: Joshua adjured them at that time, saying, Cursed be the man before the Lord, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho. Josh. vi. 26.
The high priest . . . said . . . I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ. Matt. xxvi. 63.
The commissioners adjured them not to let pass so favorable an opportunity of securing their liberties. Marshall.

Adjure.etym: [L. adjurare, adjurdium, to swear to; later, to adjure: cf. F. adjurer. See Jury.]

senses.d: To manage or conduct, as public affairs; to direct or superintend the execution, application, or conduct of; as, to administer the government or the state.
q: For forms of government let fools contest: Whate'er is best administered is best. Pope.

senses.d: To dispense; to serve out; to supply; execute; as, to administer relief, to administer the sacrament.
q: administer their tepid, genial airs. Philips.
Justice was administered with an exactness and purity not before known. Macaulay.

senses.d: To apply, as medicine or a remedy; to give, as a dose or something beneficial or suitable. Extended to a blow, a reproof, etc.
q: A noxious drug had been administered to him. Macaulay.

senses.d: To tender, as an oath.
q: Swear . . . to keep the oath that we administer. Shak.

senses.d: To settle, as the estate of one who dies without a will, or whose will fails of an executor.

Administer.syn: To manage; conduct; minister; supply; dispense; give out; distribute; furnish.
Administer.etym: [OE. aministren, OF. aministrer, F. administer, fr. L. administrare; ad + ministrare to serve. See Minister.]

senses.d: To contribute; to bring aid or supplies; to conduce; to minister.
q: A fountain . . . administers to the pleasure as well as the plenty of the place. Spectator.

senses.d: To perform the office of administrator; to act officially; as, A administers upon the estate of B.
Administrator.
The act of administering; government of public affairs; the service rendered, or duties assumed, in conducting affairs; the conducting of any office or employment; direction; management.
q: His financial administration was of a piece with his military administration. Macaulay.

senses.d: The executive part of government; the persons collectively who are intrusted with the execution of laws and the superintendence of public affairs; the chief magistrate and his cabinet or council; or the council, or ministry, alone, as in Great Britain.
q: A mild and popular administration. Macaulay.
The administration has been opposed in parliament. Johnson.

senses.d: The act of administering, or tendering something to another; dispensation; as, the administration of a medicine, of an oath, of justice, or of the sacrament.
The management and disposal, under legal authority, of the estate of an intestate, or of a testator having no competent executor.

Administration.syn: Conduct; management; direction; regulation; execution; dispensation; distribution.
Administration.etym: [OE. administracioun, L. administratio: cf. F. administration.]

senses.d: Wonder; astonishment.
q: Season your admiration for a while. Shak.

senses.d: Wonder mingled with approbation or delight; an emotion excited by a person or thing possessed of wonderful or high excellence; as, admiration of a beautiful woman, of a landscape, of virtue.
Cause of admiration; something to excite wonder, or pleased surprise; a prodigy.
q: Now, good Lafeu, bring in the admiration. Shak.

Admiration.syn: Wonder; approval; appreciation; adoration; reverence; worship.

senses.d: To regard with wonder or astonishment; to view with surprise; to marvel at.
q: Examples rather to be admired than imitated. Fuller.

senses.d: To regard with wonder and delight; to look upon with an elevated feeling of pleasure, as something which calls out approbation, esteem, love, or reverence; to estimate or prize highly; as, to admire a person of high moral worth, to admire a landscape.
q: Admired as heroes and as gods obeyed. Pope.

Admire.etym: [F. admirer, fr. L. admirari; ad + mirari to wonder, for smirari, akin to Gr. � to smile, Skr. smi, and E. smile.]

senses.d: To wonder; to marvel; to be affected with surprise; — sometimes with at.
q: To wonder at Pharaoh, and even admire at myself. Fuller.

senses.d: Regarded with wonder and delight; highly prized; as, an admired poem.
Wonderful; also, admirable.
To warn or notify of a fault; to reprove gently or kindly, but seriously; to exhort.
To counsel against wrong practices; to cation or advise; to warn against danger or an offense; — followed by of, against, or a subordinate clause.
q: Admonishing one another in psalms and hymns. Col. iii. 16.
I warned thee, I admonished thee, foretold The danger, and the lurking enemy. Milton.

senses.d: To instruct or direct; to inform; to notify.
q: Moses was admonished of God, when he was about to make the tabernacle. Heb. viii. 5.

Admonish.etym: [OE. amonesten, OF. amonester, F. admonester, fr. a supposed LL. admonesstrare, fr. L. admonere to remind, warn; ad + monere to warn. See Monition.]

senses.d: Gentle or friendly reproof; counseling against a fault or error; expression of authoritative advice; friendly caution or warning.

Admonition.etym: [OE. amonicioun, OF. amonition, F. admonition, fr. L. admonitio, fr. admonere. See Admonish.]

senses.d: To do; in doing; as, there is nothing ado.
Doing; trouble; difficulty; troublesome business; fuss; bustle; as, to make a great ado about trifles.
q: With much ado, he partly kept awake. Dryden.
Let's follow to see the end of this ado. Shak.

Ado.etym: [OE. at do, northern form for to do. Cf. Affair.]

senses.d: The act of adopting, or state of being adopted; voluntary acceptance of a child of other parents to be the same as one's own child.
Admission to a more intimate relation; reception; as, the adoption of persons into hospitals or monasteries, or of one society into another.
The choosing and making that to be one's own which originally was not so; acceptance; as, the adoption of opinions.

Adoption.etym: [L. adoptio, allied to adoptare to adopt: cf. F. adoption.]

senses.d: To deck or dress with ornaments; to embellish; to set off to advantage; to render pleasing or attractive.
q: As a bride adorneth herself with her jewels. Isa. lxi. 10.
At church, with meek and unaffected grace, His looks adorned the venerable place. Goldsmith.

Adorn.syn: To deck; decorate; embellish; ornament; beautify; grace; dignify; exalt; honor.
Adorn.etym: [OE. aournen, anournen, adornen, OF. aorner, fr. L. aaornare; ad + ornare to furnish, embellish. See Adore, Ornate.]

senses.d: Adornment.
Adorned; decorated.
To commit adultery; to pollute.
A man who commits adultery; a married man who has sexual intercourse with a woman not his wife.
A man who violates his religious covenant.

Adulterer.etym: [Formed fr. the verb adulter, with the E. ending -er. See Advoutrer.]

senses.d: A woman who commits adultery.
A woman who violates her religious engagements.
Guilty of, or given to, adultery; pertaining to adultery; illicit.
Characterized by adulteration; spurious.

The unfaithfulness of a married person to the marriage bed; sexual intercourse by a married man with another than his wife, or voluntary sexual intercourse by a married woman with another than her husband.
Adulteration; corruption.
Lewdness or unchastity of thought as well as act, as forbidden by the seventh commandment.
The fine and penalty imposed for the offense of adultery.
The intrusion of a person into a bishopric during the life of the bishop.
Injury; degradation; ruin.
q: You might wrest the caduceus out of my hand to the adultery and spoil of nature. B. Jonson.

senses.d: To bring forward; to move towards the van or front; to make to go on.
To raise; to elevate.
q: They . . . advanced their eyelids. Shak.

senses.d: To raise to a higher rank; to promote.
q: Ahasueres . . . advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes. Esther iii. 1.

senses.d: To accelerate the growth or progress; to further; to forward; to help on; to aid; to heighten; as, to advance the ripening of fruit; to advance one's interests.
To bring to view or notice; to offer or propose; to show; as, to advance an argument.
q: Some ne'er advance a judgment of their own. Pope.

senses.d: To make earlier, as an event or date; to hasten.
To furnish, as money or other value, before it becomes due, or in aid of an enterprise; to supply beforehand; as, a merchant advances money on a contract or on goods consigned to him.
To raise to a higher point; to enhance; to raise in rate; as, to advance the price of goods.
To extol; to laud.
q: Greatly advancing his gay chivalry. Spenser.

Advance.syn: To raise; elevate; exalt; aggrandize; improve; heighten; accelerate; allege; adduce; assign.
Advance.etym: [OE. avancen, avauncen, F. avancer, fr. a supposed LL. abantiare; ab + ante (F. avant) before. The spelling with d was a mistake, a- being supposed to be fr. L. ad. See Avaunt.]

senses.d: To move or go forward; to proceed; as, he advanced to greet me.
To increase or make progress in any respect; as, to advance in knowledge, in stature, in years, in price.
To rise in rank, office, or consequence; to be preferred or promoted.
q: Advanced to a level with ancient peers. Prescott.

senses.d: The act of advancing or moving forward or upward; progress.
Improvement or progression, physically, mentally, morally, or socially; as, an advance in health, knowledge, or religion; an advance in rank or office.
An addition to the price; rise in price or value; as, an advance on the prime cost of goods.
The first step towards the attainment of a result; approach made to gain favor, to form an acquaintance, to adjust a difference, etc.; an overture; a tender; an offer; — usually in the plural.
q: made the like advances to the dissenters. Swift.

senses.d: A furnishing of something before an equivalent is received (as money or goods), towards a capital or stock, or on loan; payment beforehand; the money or goods thus furnished; money or value supplied beforehand.
q: I shall, with pleasure, make the necessary advances. Jay.
The account was made up with intent to show what advances had been made. Kent.

Advance.etym: [Cf. F. avance, fr. avancer. See Advance, v.]

senses.d: Before in place, or beforehand in time; — used for advanced; as, an advance guard, or that before the main guard or body of an army; advance payment, or that made before it is due; advance proofs, advance sheets, pages of a forthcoming volume, received in advance of the time of publication.
In the van or front.
In the front or before others, as regards progress or ideas; as, advanced opinions, advanced thinkers.
Far on in life or time.
q: A gentleman advanced in years, with a hard experience written in his wrinkles. Hawthorne.

senses.d: Any condition, circumstance, opportunity, or means, particularly favorable to success, or to any desired end; benefit; as, the enemy had the advantage of a more elevated position.
q: Give me advantage of some brief discourse. Shak.
The advantages of a close alliance. Macaulay.

senses.d: Superiority; mastery; — with of or over.
q: Lest Satan should get an advantage of us. 2 Cor. ii. 11.

senses.d: Superiority of state, or that which gives it; benefit; gain; profit; as, the advantage of a good constitution.
Interest of money; increase; overplus (as the thirteenth in the baker's dozen).
q: And with advantage means to pay thy love. Shak.

Advantage.etym: [OE. avantage, avauntage, F. avantage, fr. avant before. See Advance, and cf. Vantage.]

senses.d: To give an advantage to; to further; to promote; to benefit; to profit.
q: The truth is, the archbishop's own stiffness and averseness to comply with the court designs, advantaged his adversaries against him. Fuller.
What is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself, or be cast away? Luke ix. 25.

senses.d: That which happens without design; chance; hazard; hap; hence, chance of danger or loss.
q: Nay, a far less good to man it will be found, if she must, at all adventures, be fastened upon him individually. Milton.

senses.d: Risk; danger; peril.
q: He was in great adventure of his life. Berners.

senses.d: The encountering of risks; hazardous and striking enterprise; a bold undertaking, in which hazards are to be encountered, and the issue is staked upon unforeseen events; a daring feat.
q: He loved excitement and adventure. Macaulay.

senses.d: A remarkable occurrence; a striking event; a stirring incident; as, the adventures of one's life.
A mercantile or speculative enterprise of hazard; a venture; a shipment by a merchant on his own account.

Adventure.etym: [OE. aventure, aunter, anter, F. aventure, fr. LL. adventura, fr. L. advenire, adventum, to arrive, which in the Romance languages took the sense of “to happen, befall.” See Advene.]

senses.d: To risk, or hazard; jeopard; to venture.
q: He would not adventure himself into the theater. Acts xix. 31.

senses.d: To venture upon; to run the risk of; to dare.
q: Yet they adventured to go back. Bunyan.
Discriminations might be adventured. J. Taylor.

Adventure.etym: [OE. aventuren, auntren, F. aventurer, fr. aventure. See Adventure, n.]

senses.d: To try the chance; to take the risk.
q: I would adventure for such merchandise. Shak.

senses.d: One who is turned against another or others with a design to oppose or resist them; a member of an opposing or hostile party; an opponent; an antagonist; an enemy; a foe.
q: His ancient knot of dangerous adversaries. Shak.
Agree with thine adversary quickly. Matt. v. 25.
It may be thought that to vindicate the permanency of truth is to dispute without an adversary. Beattie.

Adversary.etym: [OE. adversarie, direct fr. the Latin, and adversaire, fr. OF. adversier, aversier, fr. L. adversarius (a.) turned toward, (n.) an adversary. See Adverse.]

senses.d: Opposed; opposite; adverse; antagonistic.
Having an opposing party; not unopposed; as, an adversary suit.
Opposition; contrariety.
q: Adversity is not without comforts and hopes. Bacon.

Adversity.syn: Affliction; distress; misery; disaster; trouble; suffering; trial.
Adversity.etym: [OE. adversite, F. adversité, fr. L. adversitas.]

senses.d: To give notice to; to inform or apprise; to notify; to make known; hence, to warn; — often followed by of before the subject of information; as, to advertise a man of his loss.
q: I will advertise thee what this people shall do. Num. xxiv. 14.

senses.d: To give public notice of; to announce publicly, esp. by a printed notice; as, to advertise goods for sale, a lost article, the sailing day of a vessel, a political meeting.

Advertise.syn: To apprise; inform; make known; notify; announce; proclaim; promulgate; publish.
Advertise.etym: [F. avertir, formerly also spelt advertir, to warn, give notice to, L. advertere to turn to. The ending was probably influenced by the noun advertisement. See Advert.]

senses.d: An opinion recommended or offered, as worthy to be followed; counsel.
q: We may give advice, but we can not give conduct. Franklin.

senses.d: Deliberate consideration; knowledge.
q: How shall I dote on her with more advice, That thus without advice begin to love her? Shak.

senses.d: Information or notice given; intelligence; as, late advices from France; — commonly in the plural.
Counseling to perform a specific illegal act.

Advice.syn: Counsel; suggestion; recommendation; admonition; exhortation; information; notice.
Advice.etym: [OE. avis, F. avis; � + OF. vis, fr. L. visum seemed, seen; really p. p. of videre to see, so that vis meant that which has seemed best. See Vision, and cf. Avise, Advise.]

senses.d: To give advice to; to offer an opinion, as worthy or expedient to be followed; to counsel; to warn.
To give information or notice to; to inform; — with of before the thing communicated; as, we were advised of the risk.
q: Bid thy master well advise himself. Shak.

Advise.etym: [OE. avisen to perceive, consider, inform, F. aviser, fr. LL. advisare. advisare; ad + visare, fr. L. videre, visum, to see. See Advice, and cf. Avise.]

senses.d: To consider; to deliberate.
q: Advise if this be worth attempting. Milton.

senses.d: To take counsel; to consult; — followed by with; as, to advise with friends.
Counsel; advice; information.
q: And mused awhile, waking advisement takes of what had passed in sleep. Daniel.

senses.d: Consideration; deliberation; consultation.
q: Tempering the passion with advisement slow. Spenser.

Advisement.etym: [OE. avisement, F. avisement, fr. aviser. See Advise, and cf. Avisement.]

senses.d: One who pleads the cause of another. Specifically: One who pleads the cause of another before a tribunal or judicial court; a counselor.
One who defends, vindicates, or espouses any cause by argument; a pleader; as, an advocate of free trade, an advocate of truth.
Christ, considered as an intercessor.
q: We have an Advocate with the Father. 1 John ii. 1.

Advocate.etym: [OE. avocat, avocet, OF. avocat, fr. L. advocatus, one summoned or called to another; properly the p. p. of advocare to call to, call to one's aid; ad + vocare to call. See Advowee, Avowee, Vocal.]

senses.d: To plead in favor of; to defend by argument, before a tribunal or the public; to support, vindicate, or recommend publicly.
q: To advocate the cause of thy client. Bp. Sanderson (1624).
This is the only thing distinct and sensible, that has been advocated. Burke.
Eminent orators were engaged to advocate his cause. Mitford.

senses.d: To act as advocate.
At, to, or from a great distance; far away; — often used with from preceding, or off following; as, he was seen from afar; I saw him afar off.
q: The steep where Fame's proud temple shines afar. Beattie.

senses.d: That which is done or is to be done; matter; concern; as, a difficult affair to manage; business of any kind, commercial, professional, or public; — often in the plural. “At the head of affairs.” Junius.
Any proceeding or action which it is wished to refer to or characterize vaguely; as, an affair of honor, i.e., a duel; an affair of love, i.e., an intrigue.
An action or engagement not of sufficient magnitude to be called a battle.
Action; endeavor.
q: And with his best affair Obeyed the pleasure of the Sun. Chapman.

senses.d: A material object (vaguely designated).
q: A certain affair of fine red cloth much worn and faded. Hawthorne.

Affair.etym: [OE. afere, affere, OF. afaire, F. affaire, fr. a faire to do; L.. ad + facere to do. See Fact, and cf. Ado.]

senses.d: To act upon; to produce an effect or change upon.
q: As might affect the earth with cold heat. Milton.
The climate affected their health and spirits. Macaulay.

senses.d: To influence or move, as the feelings or passions; to touch.
q: A consideration of the rationale of our passions seems to me very necessary for all who would affect them upon solid and pure principles.

senses.d: To love; to regard with affection.
q: As for Queen Katharine, he rather respected than affected, rather honored than loved, her. Fuller.

senses.d: To show a fondness for; to like to use or practice; to choose; hence, to frequent habitually.
q: For he does neither affect company, nor is he fit for it, indeed. Shak.
Do not affect the society of your inferiors in rank, nor court that of the great. Hazlitt.

senses.d: To dispose or incline.
q: Men whom they thought best affected to religion and their country's liberty. Milton.

senses.d: To aim at; to aspire; to covet.
q: This proud man affects imperial �way. Dryden.

senses.d: To tend to by affinity or disposition.
q: The drops of every fluid affect a round figure. Newton.

senses.d: To make a show of; to put on a pretense of; to feign; to assume; as, to affect ignorance.
q: Careless she is with artful care, Affecting to seem unaffected. Congreve.
Thou dost affect my manners. Shak.

senses.d: To assign; to appoint.
q: One of the domestics was affected to his special service. Thackeray.

Affect.syn: To influence; operate; act on; concern; move; melt; soften; subdue; overcome; pretend; assume.
Affect.etym: [L. affectus, p. p. of afficere to affect by active agency; ad + facere to make: cf. F. affectere, L. affectare, freq. of afficere. See Fact.]

senses.d: Affection; inclination; passion; feeling; disposition.
The emotional complex associated with an idea or mental state. In hysteria, the affect is sometimes entirely dissociated, sometimes transferred to another than the original idea.
Regarded with affection; beloved.
q: His affected Hercules. Chapman.

senses.d: Inclined; disposed; attached.
q: How stand you affected to his wish? Shak.

senses.d: Given to false show; assuming or pretending to possess what is not natural or real.
q: He is . . . too spruce, too affected, too odd. Shak.

senses.d: Assumed artificially; not natural.
q: Affected coldness and indifference. Addison.

senses.d: Made up of terms involving different powers of the unknown quantity; adfected; as, an affected equation.
The act of affecting or acting upon; the state of being affected.
An attribute; a quality or property; a condition; a bodily state; as, figure, weight, etc. , are affections of bodies.
q: And, truly, waking dreams were, more or less, An old and strange affection of the house. Tennyson.

senses.d: Bent of mind; a feeling or natural impulse or natural impulse acting upon and swaying the mind; any emotion; as, the benevolent affections, esteem, gratitude, etc.; the malevolent affections, hatred, envy, etc.; inclination; disposition; propensity; tendency.
q: Affection is applicable to an unpleasant as well as a pleasant state of the mind, when impressed by any object or quality. Cogan.

senses.d: A settled good will; kind feeling; love; zealous or tender attachment; — often in the pl. Formerly followed by to, but now more generally by for or towards; as, filial, social, or conjugal affections; to have an affection for or towards children.
q: All his affections are set on his own country. Macaulay.

senses.d: Prejudice; bias.
Disease; morbid symptom; malady; as, a pulmonary affection.
The lively representation of any emotion.
Affectation.
Passion; violent emotion.
q: Most wretched man, That to affections does the bridle lend. Spenser.

Affection.syn: Attachment; passion; tenderness; fondness; kindness; love; good will. See Attachment; Disease.
Affection.etym: [F. affection, L. affectio, fr. afficere. See Affect.]

senses.d: Having affection or warm regard; loving; fond; as, an affectionate brother.
Kindly inclined; zealous.
q: Man, in his love God, and desire to please him, can never be too affectionate. Sprat.

senses.d: Proceeding from affection; indicating love; tender; as, the affectionate care of a parent; affectionate countenance, message, language.
Strongly inclined; — with to.

Affectionate.syn: Tender; attached; loving; devoted; warm; fond; earnest; ardent.

senses.d: With affection; lovingly; fondly; tenderly; kindly.
Disposed.
q: Be kindly affectioned one to another. Rom. xii. 10.

senses.d: Affected; conceited.

Relationship by marriage (as between a husband and his wife's blood relations, or between a wife and her husband's blood relations); — in contradistinction to consanguinity, or relationship by blood; — followed by with, to, or between.
q: Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh. 1 Kings iii. 1.

senses.d: Kinship generally; close agreement; relation; conformity; resemblance; connection; as, the affinity of sounds, of colors, or of languages.
q: There is a close affinity between imposture and credulity. Sir G. C. Lewis.

senses.d: Companionship; acquaintance.
q: About forty years past, I began a happy affinity with William Cranmer. Burton.

senses.d: That attraction which takes place, at an insensible distance, between the heterogeneous particles of bodies, and unites them to form chemical compounds; chemism; chemical or elective affinity or attraction.
A relation between species or highe� groups dependent on resemblance in the whole plan of structure, and indicating community of origin.
A superior spiritual relationship or attraction held to exist sometimes between persons, esp. persons of the opposite sex; also, the man or woman who exerts such psychical or spiritual attraction.

Affinity.etym: [OF. afinité, F. affinité, L. affinites, fr. affinis. See Affined.]

senses.d: to assert or confirm, as a judgment, decree, or order, brought before an appellate court for review.
To assert positively; to tell with confidence; to aver; to maintain as true; — opposed to deny.
q: Jesus, . . . whom Paul affirmed to be alive. Acts xxv. 19.

senses.d: To declare, as a fact, solemnly, under judicial sanction. See Affirmation, 4.

Affirm.syn: To assert; aver; declare; asseverate; assure; pronounce; protest; avouch; confirm; establish; ratify.
Affirm.etym: [OE. affermen, OF. afermer, F. affirmer, affermir, fr. L. affirmare; ad + firmare to make firm, firmus firm. See Firm.]

senses.d: To declare or assert positively.
q: Not that I so affirm, though so it seem To thee, who hast thy dwelling here on earth. Milton.

senses.d: To make a solemn declaration, before an authorized magistrate or tribunal, under the penalties of perjury; to testify by affirmation.
To strike or cast down; to overthrow.
To inflict some great injury or hurt upon, causing continued pain or mental distress; to trouble grievously; to torment.
q: They did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. Exod. i. 11.
That which was the worst now least afflicts me. Milton.

senses.d: To make low or humble.
q: Men are apt to prefer a prosperous error before an afflicted truth. Jer. Taylor.

Afflict.syn: To trouble; grieve; pain; distress; harass; torment; wound; hurt.
Afflict.etym: [L. afflictus, p. p. of affigere to cast down, deject; ad + fligere to strike: cf. OF. aflit, afflict, p. p. Cf. Flagellate.]

senses.d: Afflicted.
The cause of continued pain of body or mind, as sickness, losses, etc.; an instance of grievous distress; a pain or grief.
q: To repay that money will be a biting affliction. Shak.

senses.d: The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress, or grief.
q: Some virtues are seen only in affliction. Addison.

Affliction.syn: Calamity; sorrow; distress; grief; pain; adversity; misery; wretchedness; misfortune; trouble; hardship.

senses.d: To give forth; to supply, yield, or produce as the natural result, fruit, or issue; as, grapes afford wine; olives afford oil; the earth affords fruit; the sea affords an abundant supply of fish.
To give, grant, or confer, with a remoter reference to its being the natural result; to provide; to furnish; as, a good life affords consolation in old age.
q: His tuneful Muse affords the sweetest numbers. Addison.
The quiet lanes . . . afford calmer retreats. Gilpin.

senses.d: To offer, provide, or supply, as in selling, granting, expending, with profit, or without loss or too great injury; as, A affords his goods cheaper than B; a man can afford a sum yearly in charity.
To incur, stand, or bear without serious detriment, as an act which might under other circumstances be injurious; — with an auxiliary, as can, could, might, etc.; to be able or rich enough.
q: The merchant can afford to trade for smaller profits. Hamilton.
He could afford to suffer With those whom he saw suffer. Wordsworth.

Afford.etym: [OE. aforthen, AS. geforðian, forðian, to further, accomplish, afford, fr. forð forth, forward. The prefix ge- has no well defined sense. See Forth.]

senses.d: To impress with sudden fear; to frighten; to alarm.
q: Dreams affright our souls. Shak.
A drear and dying sound Affrights the flamens at their service quaint. Milton.

Affright.syn: To terrify; frighten; alarm; dismay; appall; scare; startle; daunt; intimidate.
Affright.etym: [Orig. p. p.; OE. afright, AS. āfyrhtan to terrify; ā- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + fyrhto fright. See Fright.]

senses.d: Affrighted.
Sudden and great fear; terror. It expresses a stronger impression than fear, or apprehension, perhaps less than terror.
q: He looks behind him with affright, and forward with despair. Goldsmith.

senses.d: The act of frightening; also, a cause of terror; an object of dread.
On foot.
q: We 'll walk afoot a while. Shak.

senses.d: Fig.: In motion; in action; astir; in progress.
q: The matter being afoot. Shak.

senses.d: Before.
q: If he have never drunk wine afore. Shak.

senses.d: In the fore part of a vessel.

Afore.etym: [OE. afore, aforn, AS. onforan or ætforan; pref. a- + fore.]

senses.d: Before (in all its senses).
Before; in front of; farther forward than; as, afore the windlass.
Beforehand; in anticipation.
q: She is come aforehand to anoint my body. Mark xiv. 8.

senses.d: Prepared; previously provided; — opposed to behindhand.
q: Aforehand in all matters of power. Bacon.

senses.d: In time past; formerly.
Impressed with fear or apprehension; in fear; apprehensive.

Afraid.etym: [OE. afrayed, affraide, p. p. of afraien to affray. See Affray, and cf. Afeard.]

senses.d: Anew; again; once more; newly.
q: They crucify . . . the Son of God afresh. Heb. vi. 6.

senses.d: Near or towards the stern of a vessel; astern; abaft.

Aft.etym: [AS. æftan behind; orig. superl. of of, off. See After.]

senses.d: Next; later in time; subsequent; succeeding; as, an after period of life.
Hinder; nearer the rear.

After.etym: [AS. æfter after, behind; akin to Goth. aftaro, aftra, backwards, Icel. aptr, Sw. and Dan. efter, OHG. aftar behind, Dutch and LG. achter, Gr. απωτἔρω further off. The ending -ter is an old comparative suffix, in E. generally -ther (as in other), and after is a compar. of of, off. √194. See Of; cf.

senses.d: Behind in place; as, men in line one after another.
Below in rank; next to in order.
q: Codrus after Ph�bus sings the best. Dryden.

senses.d: Later in time; subsequent; as, after supper, after three days. It often precedes a clause. Formerly that was interposed between it and the clause.
q: After I am risen again, I will go before you into Galilee. Matt. xxvi. 32.

senses.d: Subsequent to and in consequence of; as, after what you have said, I shall be careful.
Subsequent to and notwithstanding; as, after all our advice, you took that course.
Moving toward from behind; following, in search of; in pursuit of.
q: Ye shall not go after other gods. Deut. vi. 14.
After whom is the king of Israel come out? 1 Sam. xxiv. 14.

senses.d: Denoting the aim or object; concerning; in relation to; as, to look after workmen; to inquire after a friend; to thirst after righteousness.
In imitation of; in conformity with; after the manner of; as, to make a thing after a model; a picture after Rubens; the boy takes after his father.
q: Our eldest son was named George after his uncle. Goldsmith.

senses.d: According to; in accordance with; in conformity with the nature of; as, he acted after his kind.
q: He shall not judge after the sight of his eyes. Isa. xi. 3.
They that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh. Rom. viii. 5.

senses.d: According to the direction and influence of; in proportion to; befitting.
q: He takes greatness of kingdoms according to bulk and currency, and not after their intrinsic value. Bacon.

senses.d: Subsequently in time or place; behind; afterward; as, he follows after.
q: It was about the space of three hours after. Acts. v. 7.

senses.d: The part of the day which follows noon, between noon and evening.
At a later or succeeding time.

Afterwards.etym: [AS. æfteweard, a., behind. See Aft, and -ward (suffix). The final s in afterwards is adverbial, orig. a genitive ending.]

senses.d: In return, back; as, bring us word again.
Another time; once more; anew.
q: If a man die, shall he live again? Job xiv. 14.

senses.d: Once repeated; — of quantity; as, as large again, half as much again.
In any other place.
On the other hand.
Moreover; besides; further.
q: Again, it is of great consequence to avoid, etc. Hersche�.

Again.etym: [OE. agein, agayn, AS. ongegn, ongeán, against, again; on + geán, akin to Ger. gegewn against, Icel. gegn. Cf. Gainsay.]

senses.d: Against; also, towards (in order to meet).
q: Albeit that it is again his kind. Chaucer.

senses.d: Abreast; opposite to; facing; towards; as, against the mouth of a river; — in this sense often preceded by over.
q: Jacob saw the angels of God come against him. Tyndale.

senses.d: From an opposite direction so as to strike or come in contact with; in contact with; upon; as, hail beats against the roof.

In opposition to, whether the opposition is of sentiment or of action; on the other side; counter to; in contrariety to; hence, adverse to; as, against reason; against law; to run a race against time.
q: The gate would have been shut against her. Fielding.
An argument against the use of steam. Tyndale.

senses.d: By of before the time that; in preparation for; so as to be ready for the time when.
