q: Urijah the priest made it, against King Ahaz came from Damascus. 2 Kings xvi. 11.

Against.etym: [OE. agens, ageynes, AS. ongegn. The s is adverbial, orig. a genitive ending. See Again.]

senses.d: On the way; agoing; as, to be agate; to set the bells agate.
A semipellucid, uncrystallized variety of quartz, presenting various tints in the same specimen. Its colors are delicately arranged in stripes or bands, or blended in clouds.
A kind of type, larger than pearl and smaller than nonpareil; in England called ruby.
A diminutive person; so called in allusion to the small figures cut in agate for rings and seals.
A tool used by gold-wire drawers, bookbinders, etc.; — so called from the agate fixed in it for burnishing.

Agate.etym: [F. agate, It. agata, L. achates, fr. Gr. �.]

senses.d: The whole duration of a being, whether animal, vegetable, or other kind; lifetime.
q: Mine age is as nothing before thee. Ps. xxxix. 5.

senses.d: That part of the duration of a being or a thing which is between its beginning and any given time; as, what is the present age of a man, or of the earth?
The latter part of life; an advanced period of life; seniority; state of being old.
q: Nor wrong mine age with this indignity. Shak.

senses.d: One of the stages of life; as, the age of infancy, of youth, etc.
Mature age; especially, the time of life at which one attains full personal rights and capacities; as, to come of age; he (or she) is of age.
The time of life at which some particular power or capacity is understood to become vested; as, the age of consent; the age of discretion.
A particular period of time in history, as distinguished from others; as, the golden age, the age of Pericles.
q: Truth, in some age or other, will find her witness. Milton.

senses.d: A great period in the history of the Earth.
A century; the period of one hundred years.
q: Fleury . . . apologizes for these five ages. Hallam.

senses.d: The people who live at a particular period; hence, a generation.
q: The way which the age follows. J. H. Newman.
Lo! where the stage, the poor, degraded stage, Holds its warped mirror to a gaping age. C. Sprague.

senses.d: A long time.

Age.syn: Time; period; generation; date; era; epoch.
Age.etym: [OF. aage, eage, F. âge, fr. L. aetas through a supposed LL. aetaticum. L. aetas is contracted fr. aevitas, fr. aevum lifetime, age; akin to E. aye ever. Cf. Each.]

senses.d: To grow aged; to become old; to show marks of age; as, he grew fat as he aged.
q: They live one hundred and thirty years, and never age for all that. Holland.
I am aging; that is, I have a whitish, or rather a light-colored, hair here and there. Landor.

senses.d: To cause to grow old; to impart the characteristics of age to; as, grief ages us.

In poker, the right belonging to the player to the left of the dealer to pass the first round in betting, and then to come in last or stay out; also, the player holding this position; the eldest hand.
Old; having lived long; having lived almost to or beyond the usual time allotted to that species of being; as, an aged man; an aged oak.
Belonging to old age.
Having a certain age; at the age of; having lived; as, a man aged forty years.
Past; gone by; since; as, ten years ago; gone long ago.

Ago.etym: [OE. ago, agon, p. p. of agon to go away, pass by, AS. āgān to pass away; ā- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + gān to go. See Go.]

senses.d: Ago.
q: Three days agone I fell sick. 1 Sam. xxx. 13.

senses.d: Agonic line.
Violent contest or striving.
q: The world is convulsed by the agonies of great nations. Macaulay.

senses.d: Pain so extreme as to cause writhing or contortions of the body, similar to those made in the athletic contests in Greece; and hence, extreme pain of mind or body; anguish; paroxysm of grief; specifically, the sufferings of Christ in the garden of Gethsemane.
q: Being in an agony he prayed more earnestly. Luke xxii. 44.

senses.d: Paroxysm of joy; keen emotion.
q: With cries and agonies of wild delight. Pope.

senses.d: The last struggle of life; death struggle.

Agony.syn: Anguish; torment; throe; distress; pangs; suffering.
Agony.etym: [L. agonia, Gr. �, orig. a contest, fr. �: cf. F. agonie. See Agon.]

senses.d: In good part; kindly.
To harmonize in opinion, statement, or action; to be in unison or concord; to be or become united or consistent; to concur; as, all parties agree in the expediency of the law.
q: If music and sweet poetry agree. Shak.
Their witness agreed not together. Mark xiv. 56.
The more you agree together, the less hurt can your enemies do you. Sir T. Browne.

senses.d: To yield assent; to accede; — followed by to; as, to agree to an offer, or to opinion.
To make a stipulation by way of settling differences or determining a price; to exchange promises; to come to terms or to a common resolve; to promise.
q: Agree with thine adversary quickly. Matt. v. 25.
Didst not thou agree with me for a penny ? Matt. xx. 13.

senses.d: To be conformable; to resemble; to coincide; to correspond; as, the picture does not agree with the original; the two scales agree exactly.
To suit or be adapted in its effects; to do well; as, the same food does not agree with every constitution.
To correspond in gender, number, case, or person.

Agree.syn: To assent; concur; consent; acquiesce; accede; engage; promise; stipulate; contract; bargain; correspond; harmonize; fit; tally; coincide; comport.
Agree.etym: [F. agréer to accept or receive kindly, fr. à gré; à (L. ad) + gré good will, consent, liking, fr. L. gratus pleasing, agreeable. See Grateful.]

senses.d: To make harmonious; to reconcile or make friends.
To admit, or come to one mind concerning; to settle; to arrange; as, to agree the fact; to agree differences.
State of agreeing; harmony of opinion, statement, action, or character; concurrence; concord; conformity; as, a good agreement subsists among the members of the council.
q: What agreement hath the temple of God with idols ? 2 Cor. vi. 16.
Expansion and duration have this further agreement. Locke.

senses.d: Concord or correspondence of one word with another in gender, number, case, or person.
A concurrence in an engagement that something shall be done or omitted; an exchange of promises; mutual understanding, arrangement, or stipulation; a contract.
On the ground; stranded; — a nautical term applied to a ship when its bottom lodges on the ground.
An acute fever.
An intermittent fever, attended by alternate cold and hot fits.
The cold fit or rigor of the intermittent fever; as, fever and ague.
A chill, or state of shaking, as with cold.

Ague.etym: [OE. agu, ague, OF. agu, F. aigu, sharp, OF. fem. ague, LL. (febris) acuta, a sharp, acute fever, fr. L. acutus sharp. See Acute.]

senses.d: To strike with an ague, or with a cold fit.
An exclamation, expressive of surprise, pity, complaint, entreaty, contempt, threatening, delight, triumph, etc., according to the manner of utterance.

Ah.etym: [OE. a: cf. OF. a, F. ah, L. ah, Gr. �, Sk. ā, Icel. æ, OHG. ā, Lith. á, áá.]

senses.d: An exclamation expressing, by different intonations, triumph, mixed with derision or irony, or simple surprise.
A sunk fence. See Ha-ha.
The three-toed sloth (Bradypus tridactylus) of South America. See Sloth.

Ai.etym: [Braz. aï, haï, from the animal's cry: cf. F. aï.]

senses.d: To support, either by furnishing strength or means in coöperation to effect a purpose, or to prevent or to remove evil; to help; to assist.
q: You speedy helpers . . . Appear and aid me in this enterprise. Shak.

Aid.syn: To help; assist; support; sustain; succor; relieve; befriend; coöperate; promote. See Help.
Aid.etym: [F. aider, OF. aidier, fr. L. adjutare to help, freq. of adjuvare to help; ad + juvare to help. Cf. Adjutant.]

senses.d: Help; succor; assistance; relief.
q: An unconstitutional mode of obtaining aid. Hallam.

senses.d: The person or thing that promotes or helps in something done; a helper; an assistant.
q: It is not good that man should be alone; let us make unto him an aid like unto himself. Tobit viii. 6.

senses.d: A subsidy granted to the king by Parliament; also, an exchequer loan.
A pecuniary tribute paid by a vassal to his lord on special occasions.
An aid-de-camp, so called by abbreviation; as, a general's aid.

Aid.etym: [F. aide, OF. aïde, aïe, fr. the verb. See Aid, v. t.]

senses.d: To affect with pain or uneasiness, either physical or mental; to trouble; to be the matter with; — used to express some uneasiness or affection, whose cause is unknown; as, what ails the man? I know not what ails him.
q: What aileth thee, Hagar? Gen. xxi. 17.

Ail.etym: [OE. eilen, ailen, AS. eglan to trouble, pain; akin to Goth. us-agljan to distress, agls troublesome, irksome, aglo, aglitha, pain, and prob. to E. awe. √3.]

senses.d: To be affected with pain or uneasiness of any sort; to be ill or indisposed or in trouble.
q: When he ails ever so little . . . he is so peevish. Richardson.

senses.d: Indisposition or morbid affection.
The fluid which we breathe, and which surrounds the earth; the atmosphere. It is invisible, inodorous, insipid, transparent, compressible, elastic, and ponderable.
Symbolically: Something unsubstantial, light, or volatile.
q: He was still all air and fire.

senses.d: A particular state of the atmosphere, as respects heat, cold, moisture, etc., or as affecting the sensations; as, a smoky air, a damp air, the morning air, etc.
Any aëriform body; a gas; as, oxygen was formerly called vital air.
Air in motion; a light breeze; a gentle wind.
q: Let vernal airs through trembling osiers play. Pope.

senses.d: Odoriferous or contaminated air.
That which surrounds and influences.
q: The keen, the wholesome air of poverty. Wordsworth.

senses.d: Utterance abroad; publicity; vent.
q: You gave it air before me. Dryden.

senses.d: Intelligence; information.

A musical idea, or motive, rhythmically developed in consecutive single tones, so as to form a symmetrical and balanced whole, which may be sung by a single voice to the stanzas of a hymn or song, or even to plain prose, or played upon an instrument; a melody; a tune; an aria.
The peculiar look, appearance, and bearing of a person; mien; demeanor; as, the air of a youth; a heavy air; a lofty air.
Peculiar appearance; apparent character; semblance; manner; style.
q: It was communicated with the air of a secret. Pope.

Air.etym: [OE. air, eir, F. air, L. aër, fr. Gr. αἤρ, air, mist, for αϝηῤ, fr. root αϝ̓ to blow, breathe, probably akin to E. wind. In sense 10 the French has taking a meaning fr. It. aria atmosphere, air, fr. the same Latin word; and in senses 11, 12, 13 the French meaning is either fr. L. aria, or due to co

senses.d: To expose to the air for the purpose of cooling, refreshing, or purifying; to ventilate; as, to air a room.
q: It were good wisdom . . . that the jail were aired. Bacon.
Were you but riding forth to air yourself. Shak.

senses.d: To expose for the sake of public notice; to display ostentatiously; as, to air one's opinion.
q: Airing a snowy hand and signet gem. Tennyson.

senses.d: To expose to heat, for the purpose of expelling dampness, or of warming; as, to air linen; to air liquors.
A winglike organ, or part.
A compact variety or sulphate of lime, or gypsum, of fine texture, and usually white and translucent, but sometimes yellow, red, or gray. It is carved into vases, mantel ornaments, etc.
A box or vessel for holding odoriferous ointments, etc.; — so called from the stone of which it was originally made.

Alabaster.etym: [L. alabaster, Gr. αλἄβαστροσ, said to be derived fr. Alabastron, the name of a town in Egypt, near which it was common: cf. OF. alabastre, F. albâtre.]

senses.d: A summons to arms, as on the approach of an enemy.
q: Arming to answer in a night alarm. Shak.

senses.d: Any sound or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a warning sound to arouse attention; a warning of danger.
q: Sound an alarm in my holy mountain. Joel ii. 1.

senses.d: A sudden attack; disturbance; broil.
q: Thy palace fill with insults and alarms. Pope.

senses.d: Sudden surprise with fear or terror excited by apprehension of danger; in the military use, commonly, sudden apprehension of being attacked by surprise.
q: Alarm and resentment spread throughout the camp. Macaulay.

senses.d: A mechanical contrivance for awaking persons from sleep, or rousing their attention; an alarum.

Alarm.syn: Fright; affright; terror; trepidation; apprehension; consternation; dismay; agitation; disquiet; disquietude.
Alarm.etym: [F. alarme, It. all' arme to arms ! fr. L. arma, pl., arms. See Arms, and cf. Alarum.]

senses.d: To call to arms for defense; to give notice to (any one) of approaching danger; to rouse to vigilance and action; to put on the alert.
To keep in excitement; to disturb.
To surprise with apprehension of danger; to fill with anxiety in regard to threatening evil; to excite with sudden fear.
q: Alarmed by rumors of military preparation. Macaulay.

senses.d: An exclamation expressive of sorrow, pity, or apprehension of evil; — in old writers, sometimes followed by day or white; alas the day, like alack a day, or alas the white.

Alas.etym: [OE. alas, allas, OF. alas, F. hélas; a interj. (L. ah.) + las wretched (that I am), L. lassus weary, akin to E. late. See Late.]

senses.d: Even though; although; notwithstanding.
q: Albeit so masked, Madam, I love the truth. Tennyson.

Albeit.etym: [OE. al be although it be, where al is our all. Cf. Although.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Alexandria in Egypt; as, the Alexandrian library.
Applied to a kind of heroic verse. See Alexandrine, n.
Same as Almug (and etymologically preferable).
Not belonging to the same country, land, or government, or to the citizens or subjects thereof; foreign; as, alien subjects, enemies, property, shores.
Wholly different in nature; foreign; adverse; inconsistent (with); incongruous; — followed by from or sometimes by to; as, principles alien from our religion.
q: An alien sound of melancholy. Wordsworth.

Alien.etym: [OF. alien, L. alienus, fr. alius another; properly, therefore, belonging to another. See Else.]

senses.d: A foreigner; one owing allegiance, or belonging, to another country; a foreign-born resident of a country in which he does not possess the privileges of a citizen. Hence, a stranger. See Alienage.
One excluded from certain privileges; one alienated or estranged; as, aliens from God's mercies.
q: Aliens from the common wealth of Israel. Ephes. ii. 12.

senses.d: To alienate; to estrange; to transfer, as property or ownership.
q: The prince was totally aliened from all thoughts of . . . the marriage. Clarendon.

senses.d: Estranged; withdrawn in affection; foreign; — with from.
q: O alienate from God. Milton.

Alienate.etym: [L. alienatus, p. p. of alienare, fr. alienus. See Alien, and cf. Aliene.]

senses.d: To convey or transfer to another, as title, property, or right; to part voluntarily with ownership of.
To withdraw, as the affections; to make indifferent of averse, where love or friendship before subsisted; to estrange; to wean; — with from.
q: The errors which . . . alienated a loyal gentry and priesthood from the House of Stuart. Macaulay.
The recollection of his former life is a dream that only the more alienates him from the realities of the present. I. Taylor.

senses.d: A stranger; an alien.
Having resemblance or similitude; similar; without difference.
q: The darkness and the light are both alike to thee. Ps. cxxxix. 12.

senses.d: In the same manner, form, or degree; in common; equally; as, we are all alike concerned in religion.
Having life, in opposition to dead; living; being in a state in which the organs perform their functions; as, an animal or a plant which is alive.
In a state of action; in force or operation; unextinguished; unexpired; existent; as, to keep the fire alive; to keep the affections alive.
Exhibiting the activity and motion of many living beings; swarming; thronged.
q: The Boyne, for a quarter of a mile, was alive with muskets and green boughs. Macaulay.

senses.d: Sprightly; lively; brisk.
Having susceptibility; easily impressed; having lively feelings, as opposed to apathy; sensitive.
q: Tremblingly alive to nature's laws. Falconer.

senses.d: Of all living (by way of emphasis).
q: Northumberland was the proudest man alive. Clarendon.

Alive.etym: [OE. on live, AS. on līfe in life; līfe being dat. of līf life. See Life, and cf. Live, a.]

senses.d: The whole quantity, extent, duration, amount, quality, or degree of; the whole; the whole number of; any whatever; every; as, all the wheat; all the land; all the year; all the strength; all happiness; all abundance; loss of all power; beyond all doubt; you will see us all (or all of us).
q: Prove all things: hold fast that which is good. 1 Thess. v. 21.

senses.d: Any.
Only; alone; nothing but.
q: I was born to speak all mirth and no matter. Shak.

All.etym: [OE. al, pl. alle, AS. eal, pl. ealle, Northumbrian alle, akin to D. & OHG. al, Ger. all, Icel. allr. Dan. al, Sw. all, Goth. alls; and perh. to Ir. and Gael. uile, W. oll.]

senses.d: Wholly; completely; altogether; entirely; quite; very; as, all bedewed; my friend is all for amusement.
Even; just. (Often a mere intensive adjunct.)
q: All as his straying flock he fed. Spenser.
A damsel lay deploring All on a rock reclined. Gay.

senses.d: The whole number, quantity, or amount; the entire thing; everything included or concerned; the aggregate; the whole; totality; everything or every person; as, our all is at stake.
q: Death, as the Psalmist saith, is certain to all. Shak.
All that thou seest is mine. Gen. xxxi. 43.

senses.d: Although; albeit.
q: All they were wondrous loth. Spenser.

All.etym: [Orig. all, adv., wholly: used with though or if, which being dropped before the subjunctive left all as if in the sense although.]

senses.d: To bring forward with positiveness; to declare; to affirm; to assert; as, to allege a fact.
To cite or quote; as, to allege the authority of a judge.
To produce or urge as a reason, plea, or excuse; as, he refused to lend, alleging a resolution against lending.

Allege.syn: To bring forward; adduce; advance; assign; produce; declare; affirm; assert; aver; predicate.
Allege.etym: [OE. aleggen to bring forward as evidence, OF. esligier to buy, prop. to free from legal difficulties, fr. an assumed LL. exlitigare; L. ex + litigare to quarrel, sue (see Litigate). The word was confused with L. allegare (see Allegation), and lex law. Cf. Allay.]

senses.d: To alleviate; to lighten, as a burden or a trouble.

A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it in its properties and circumstances. The real subject is thus kept out of view, and we are left to collect the intentions of the writer or speaker by the resemblance of the secondary to the primary subject.
Anything which represents by suggestive resemblance; an emblem.
A figure representation which has a meaning beyond notion directly conveyed by the object painted or sculptured.

Allegory.etym: [L. allegoria, Gr. �, description of one thing under the image of another; � other + � to speak in the assembly, harangue, � place of assembly, fr. � to assemble: cf. F. allégorie.]

senses.d: An exclamation signifying Praise ye Jehovah. Hence: A song of praise to God. See Hallelujah, the commoner form.
q: I heard a great voice of much people in heaven, saying, Alleluia. Rev. xix. 1.

Alleluia.etym: [L. alleluia, Gr. �, fr. Heb. hallēlū-yāh. See Hallelujah.]

senses.d: United; joined; leagued; akin; related. See Ally.
To praise; to approve of; hence, to sanction.
q: Ye allow the deeds of your fathers. Luke xi. 48.
We commend his pains, condemn his pride, allow his life, approve his learning. Fuller.

senses.d: To like; to be suited or pleased with.
q: How allow you the model of these clothes? Massinger.

senses.d: To sanction; to invest; to intrust.
q: Thou shalt be . . . allowed with absolute power. Shak.

senses.d: To grant, give, admit, accord, afford, or yield; to let one have; as, to allow a servant his liberty; to allow a free passage; to allow one day for rest.
q: He was allowed about three hundred pounds a year. Macaulay.

senses.d: To own or acknowledge; to accept as true; to concede; to accede to an opinion; as, to allow a right; to allow a claim; to allow the truth of a proposition.
q: I allow, with Mrs. Grundy and most moralists, that Miss Newcome's conduct . . . was highly reprehensible. Thackeray.

senses.d: To grant (something) as a deduction or an addition; esp. to abate or deduct; as, to allow a sum for leakage.
To grant license to; to permit; to consent to; as, to allow a son to be absent.

Allow.syn: To allot; assign; bestow; concede; admit; permit; suffer; tolerate. See Permit.
Allow.etym: [OE. alouen, OF. alouer, aloer, aluer, F. allouer, fr. LL. allocare to admit as proved, to place, use; confused with OF. aloer, fr. L. allaudare to extol; ad + laudare to praise. See Local, and cf. Allocate, Laud.]

senses.d: To admit; to concede; to make allowance or abatement.
q: Allowing still for the different ways of making it. Addison.

senses.d: Approval; approbation.
The act of allowing, granting, conceding, or admitting; authorization; permission; sanction; tolerance.
q: Without the king's will or the state's allowance. Shak.

senses.d: Acknowledgment.
q: The censure of the which one must in your allowance o'erweigh a whole theater of others. Shak.

senses.d: License; indulgence.

That which is allowed; a share or portion allotted or granted; a sum granted as a reimbursement, a bounty, or as appropriate for any purpose; a stated quantity, as of food or drink; hence, a limited quantity of meat and drink, when provisions fall short.
q: I can give the boy a handsome allowance. Thackeray.

senses.d: Abatement; deduction; the taking into account of mitigating circumstances; as, to make allowance for the inexperience of youth.
q: After making the largest allowance for fraud. Macaulay.

senses.d: A customary deduction from the gross weight of goods, different in different countries, such as tare and tret.
To put upon a fixed allowance (esp. of provisions and drink); to supply in a fixed and limited quantity; as, the captain was obliged to allowance his crew; our provisions were allowanced.
To attempt to draw; to tempt by a lure or bait, that is, by the offer of some good, real or apparent; to invite by something flattering or acceptable; to entice; to attract.
q: With promised joys allured them on. Falconer.
The golden sun in splendor likest Heaven Allured his eye. Milton.

Allure.syn: To attract; entice; tempt; decoy; seduce.
Allure.etym: [OF. aleurrer, alurer, fr. a (L. ad) + leurre lure. See Lure.]

senses.d: Allurement.
Gait; bearing.
q: The swing, the gait, the pose, the allure of these men. Harper's Mag.

senses.d: To unite, or form a connection between, as between families by marriage, or between princes and states by treaty, league, or confederacy; — often followed by to or with.
q: O chief! in blood, and now in arms allied. Pope.

senses.d: To connect or form a relation between by similitude, resemblance, friendship, or love.
q: These three did love each other dearly well, And with so firm affection were allied. Spenser.
The virtue nearest to our vice allied. Pope.

Ally.etym: [OE. alien, OF. alier, F. alier, fr. L. alligare to bind to; ad + ligare to bind. Cf. Alligate, Alloy, Allay, Ligament.]

senses.d: A relative; a kinsman.
One united to another by treaty or league; — usually applied to sovereigns or states; a confederate.
q: The English soldiers and their French allies. Macaulay.

senses.d: Anything associated with another as a helper; an auxiliary.
q: Science, instead of being the enemy of religion, becomes its ally. Buckle.

senses.d: Anything akin to another by structure, etc.
Unlimited in might; omnipotent; all-powerful; irresistible.
q: I am the Almighty God. Gen. xvii. 1.

senses.d: Great; extreme; terrible.
q: Poor Aroar can not live, and can not die, — so that he is in an almighty fix. De Quincey.

Almighty.etym: [AS. ealmihtig, ælmihtig; eal (OE. al) all + mihtig mighty.]

senses.d: The fruit of the almond tree.
The tree that bears the fruit; almond tree.
Anything shaped like an almond.

Almond.etym: [OE. almande, almaunde, alemaunde, F. amande, L. amygdala, fr. Gr. αμυγδἄλη: cf. Sp. almendra. Cf. Amygdalate.]

senses.d: Nearly; well nigh; all but; for the greatest part.
q: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. Acts xxvi. 28.

Almost.etym: [AS. ealmæst, ælmæst, quite the most, almost all; eal (OE. al) all + m�st most.]

senses.d: Anything given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing; a gift of charity.
q: A devout man . . . which gave much alms to the people. Acts x. 2.
Alms are but the vehicles of prayer. Dryden.

Alms.etym: [OE. almes, almesse, AS. ælmysse, fr. L. eleemosyna, Gr. ελεημοσὔνη mercy, charity, alms, fr. ελεεἰ̑ν to pity. Cf. Almonry, Eleemosynary.]

senses.d: An act of charity.
A tree or wood of the Bible (2 Chron. ii. 8; 1 K. x. 11).

Almug.etym: [Heb., perh. borrowed fr. Skr. valguka sandalwood.]

senses.d: The wood of the agalloch.

A genus of succulent plants, some classed as trees, others as shrubs, but the greater number having the habit and appearance of evergreen herbaceous plants; from some of which are prepared articles for medicine and the arts. They are natives of warm countries.
The inspissated juice of several species of aloe, used as a purgative.

Aloe.etym: [L. aloë, Gr. αλὄη, aloe: cf. OF. aloe, F. aloès.]

senses.d: Quite by one's self; apart from, or exclusive of, others; single; solitary; — applied to a person or thing.
q: Alone on a wide, wide sea. Coleridge.
It is not good that the man should be alone. Gen. ii. 18.

senses.d: Of or by itself; by themselves; without any thing more or any one else; without a sharer; only.
q: Man shall not live by bread alone. Luke iv. 4.
The citizens alone should be at the expense. Franklin.

senses.d: Sole; only; exclusive.
q: God, by whose alone power and conversation we all live, and move, and have our being. Bentley.

senses.d: Hence; Unique; rare; matchless.

Alone.etym: [All + one. OE. al one all allone, AS. ān one, alone. See All, One, Lone.]

senses.d: Solely; simply; exclusively.
By the length; in a line with the length; lengthwise.
q: Some laid along . . . on spokes of wheels are hung. Dryden.

senses.d: In a line, or with a progressive motion; onward; forward.
q: We will go along by the king's highway. Numb. xxi. 22.
He struck with his o'ertaking wings, And chased us south along. Coleridge.

senses.d: In company; together.
q: He to England shall along with you. Shak.

Along.etym: [OE. along, anlong, AS. andlang, along; pref. and- (akin to OFris. ond-, OHG. ant-, Ger. ent-, Goth. and-, anda-, L. ante, Gr. �, Skr. anti, over against) + lang long. See Long.]

senses.d: By the length of, as distinguished from across.
q: The kine . . . went along the highway. 1 Sam. vi. 12.

senses.d: (Now heard only in the prep. phrase along of.)
Same as Alewife.
At or from a distance, but within view, or at a small distance; apart; away.
q: Our palace stood aloof from streets. Dryden.

senses.d: Without sympathy; unfavorably.
q: To make the Bible as from the hand of God, and then to look at it aloof and with caution, is the worst of all impieties. I. Taylor.

Aloof.etym: [Pref. a- + loof, fr. D. loef luff, and so meaning, as a nautical word, to the windward. See Loof, Luff.]

senses.d: Away from; clear from.
q: Rivetus . . . would fain work himself aloof these rocks and quicksands. Milton.

senses.d: With a loud voice, or great noise; loudly; audibly.
q: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice. Isa. lviii. 1.

senses.d: The first letter in the Greek alphabet, answering to A, and hence used to denote the beginning.
q: In am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last. Rev. xxii. 13.

Alpha.etym: [L. alpha, Gr. ἄλφα, from Heb. āleph, name of the first letter in the alphabet, also meaning ox.]

senses.d: Prior to some specified time, either past, present, or future; by this time; previously.
q: I say unto you, that Elias is come already. Matt. xvii. 12.

senses.d: In like manner; likewise.
In addition; besides; as well; further; too.
q: Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven . . . for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. Matt. vi. 20.

senses.d: Even as; as; so.

Also.etym: [All + so. OE. al so, AS. ealswā, alsw�, ælswæ; eal, al, æl, all + swā so. See All, So, As.]

senses.d: The higher part of the scale. See Alto.
A raised structure (as a square or oblong erection of stone or wood) on which sacrifices are offered or incense burned to a deity.
q: Noah builded an altar unto the Lord. Gen. viii. 20.

senses.d: In the Christian church, a construction of stone, wood, or other material for the celebration of the Holy Eucharist; the communion table.

Altar.etym: [OE. alter, auter, autier, fr. L. altare, pl. altaria, altar, prob. fr. altus high: cf. OF. alter, autier, F. autel. Cf. Altitude.]

senses.d: To make otherwise; to change in some respect, either partially or wholly; to vary; to modify.
q: It gilds all objects, but it alters none. Pope.
My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. Ps. lxxxix. 34.

senses.d: To agitate; to affect mentally.
To geld.

Alter.etym: [F. altérer, LL. alterare, fr. L. alter other, alius other. Cf. Else, Other.]

senses.d: To become, in some respects, different; to vary; to change; as, the weather alters almost daily; rocks or minerals alter by exposure.
Grant all this; be it that; supposing that; notwithstanding; though.
q: Although all shall be offended, yet will not I. Mark xiv. 29.

senses.d: All together; conjointly.
q: Altogether they went at once. Chaucer.

senses.d: Without exception; wholly; completely.
q: Every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Ps. xxxix. 5.

Altogether.etym: [OE. altogedere; al all + togedere together. See Together.]

senses.d: Always.
q: I would not live alway. Job vii. 16.

senses.d: At all times; ever; perpetually; throughout all time; continually; as, God is always the same.
q: Even in Heaven his looks and thoughts. Milton.

senses.d: Constancy during a certain period, or regularly at stated intervals; invariably; uniformly; — opposed to sometimes or occasionally.
q: He always rides a black galloway. Bulwer.

Always.etym: [All + way. The s is an adverbial (orig. a genitive) ending.]

senses.d: The first person singular of the verb be, in the indicative mode, present tense. See Be.
q: God said unto Moses, I am that am. Exod. iii. 14.

Am.etym: [AS. am, eom, akin to Gothic im, Icel. em, Olr. am, Lith. esmi, L. sum., Gr. �, Zend ahmi, Skr. asmi, fr. a root as to be. �. See Are, and cf. Be, Was.]

senses.d: To bewilder; to stupefy; to bring into a maze.
q: A labyrinth to amaze his foes. Shak.

senses.d: To confound, as by fear, wonder, extreme surprise; to overwhelm with wonder; to astound; to astonish greatly.
q: And all the people were amazed, and said, Is not this the son of David? Matt. xii. 23.

Amaze.syn: To astonish; astound; confound; bewilder; perplex; surprise.

senses.d: To be astounded.
Bewilderment, arising from fear, surprise, or wonder; amazement.
q: The wild, bewildered Of one to stone converted by amaze. Byron.

senses.d: The condition of being amazed; bewilderment ; overwhelming wonder, as from surprise, sudden fear, horror, or admiration.
q: His words impression left Of much amazement. Milton.

senses.d: Frenzy; madness.
A minister of the highest rank sent to a foreign court to represent there his sovereign or country.
An official messenger and representative.
Same as Embassage.

A yellowish translucent resin resembling copal, found as a fossil in alluvial soils, with beds of lignite, or on the seashore in many places. It takes a fine polish, and is used for pipe mouthpieces, beads, etc., and as a basis for a fine varnish. By friction, it becomes strongly electric.
Amber color, or anything amber-colored; a clear light yellow; as, the amber of the sky.
Ambergris.
q: You that smell of amber at my charge. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: The balsam, liquidambar.

Amber.etym: [OE. aumbre, F. ambre, Sp. ámbar, and with the Ar. article, alámbar, fr. Ar. 'anbar ambergris.]

senses.d: Consisting of amber; made of amber.
Resembling amber, especially in color; amber-colored.
To scent or flavor with ambergris; as, ambered wine.
To preserve in amber; as, an ambered fly.
A disposition or arrangement of troops for attacking an enemy unexpectedly from a concealed station. Hence: Unseen peril; a device to entrap; a snare.
q: Heaven, whose high walls fear no assault or siege Or ambush from the deep. Milton.

senses.d: A concealed station, where troops or enemies lie in wait to attack by surprise.
q: Bold in close ambush, base in open field. Dryden.

senses.d: The troops posted in a concealed place, for attacking by surprise; liers in wait.
q: The ambush arose quickly out of their place. Josh. viii. 19.

Ambush.etym: [F. embûche, fr. the verb. See Ambush, v. t.]

senses.d: To station in ambush with a view to surprise an enemy.
q: By ambushed men behind their temple laid, We have the king of Mexico betrayed. Dryden.

senses.d: To attack by ambush; to waylay.

Ambush.etym: [OE. enbussen, enbushen, OF. embushier, embuissier, F. embûcher, embusquer, fr. LL. imboscare; in + LL. boscus, buscus, a wood; akin to G. bush, E. bush. See Ambuscade, Bush.]

senses.d: To lie in wait, for the purpose of attacking by surprise; to lurk.
q: Nor saw the snake that ambushed for his prey. Trumbull.

senses.d: An ambush.
An expression used at the end of prayers, and meaning, So be it. At the end of a creed, it is a solemn asseveration of belief. When it introduces a declaration, it is equivalent to truly, verily.
q: And let all the people say, Amen. Ps. cvi. 48.
Amen, amen, I say to thee, except a man be born again, he can not see the kingdom of God. John ii. 3. Rhemish Trans.

Amen.etym: [L. amen, Gr. αμἤν, Heb. āmēn certainly, truly.]

senses.d: To say Amen to; to sanction fully.
To change or modify in any way for the better
by simply removing what is erroneous, corrupt, superfluous, faulty, and the like;
by supplying deficiencies;
by substituting something else in the place of what is removed; to rectify.
q: Mar not the thing that can not be amended. Shak.
An instant emergency, granting no possibility for revision, or opening for amended thought. De Quincey.
We shall cheer her sorrows, and amend her blood, by wedding her to a Norman. Sir W. Scott.

Amend.syn: To Amend, Emend, Correct, Reform, Rectify.
Amend.etym: [F. amender, L. emendare; e (ex) + mendum, menda, fault, akin to Skr. minda personal defect. Cf. Emend, Mend.]

senses.d: To grow better by rectifying something wrong in manners or morals; to improve.
Compensation for a loss or injury; recompense; reparation.
q: Yet thus far fortune maketh us amends. Shak.

Amends.etym: [F. amendes, pl. of amende. Cf. Amende.]

senses.d: To punish by a pecuniary penalty, the amount of which is not fixed by law, but left to the discretion of the court; as, the court amerced the criminal in the sum of one hundred dollars.
To punish, in general; to mulct.
q: Millions of spirits for his fault amerced Of Heaven. Milton.
Shall by him be amerced with penance due. Spenser.

Amerce.etym: [OF. amercier, fr. a merci at the mercy of, liable to a punishment. See Mercy.]

senses.d: A variety of crystallized quartz, of a purple or bluish violet color, of different shades. It is much used as a jeweler's stone.
A purple color in a nobleman's escutcheon, or coat of arms.

Amethyst.etym: [F. ametiste, amatiste, F. améthyste, L. amethystus, fr. Gr. � without drunkenness; as a noun, a remedy for drunkenness, the amethyst, supposed to have this power; ἀ priv. + � to be drunken, � strong drink, wine. See Mead.]

senses.d: Lovable; lovely; pleasing.
q: So amiable a prospect. Sir T. Herbert.

senses.d: Friendly; kindly; sweet; gracious; as, an amiable temper or mood; amiable ideas.
Possessing sweetness of disposition; having sweetness of temper, kind-heartedness, etc., which causes one to be liked; as, an amiable woman.
Done out of love.
q: Lay an amiable siege to the honesty of this Ford's wife. Shak.

Amiable.etym: [F. amiable, L. amicabilis friendly, fr. amicus friend, fr. amare to love. The meaning has been influenced by F. aimable, L. amabilis lovable, fr. amare to love. Cf. Amicable, Amorous, Amability.]

senses.d: Astray; faultily; improperly; wrongly; ill.
q: What error drives our eyes and ears amiss? Shak.
Ye ask and receive not, because ye ask amiss. James iv. 3.

senses.d: Wrong; faulty; out of order; improper; as, it may not be amiss to ask advice.
q: His wisdom and virtue can not always rectify that which is amiss in himself or his circumstances. Wollaston.

senses.d: A fault, wrong, or mistake.
q: Each toy seems prologue to some great amiss. Shak.

senses.d: A fossil cephalopod shell related to the nautilus. There are many genera and species, and all are extinct, the typical forms having existed only in the Mesozoic age, when they were exceedingly numerous. They differ from the nautili in having the margins of the septa very much lobed or plaited, and the siphuncle dorsal. Also called serpent stone, snake stone, and cornu Ammonis.

Ammonite.etym: [L. cornu Ammonis born of Ammon; L. Ammon, Gr. � an appellation of Jupiter, as represented with the horns of a ram. It was originally the name of an. Egyptian god, Amun.]

senses.d: Mixed or mingled; surrounded by.
q: They heard, And from his presence hid themselves among The thickest trees. Milton.

senses.d: Conjoined, or associated with, or making part of the number of; in the number or class of.
q: Blessed art thou among women. Luke i. 28.

senses.d: Expressing a relation of dispersion, distribution, etc.; also, a relation of reciprocal action.
q: What news among the merchants? Shak.
Human sacrifices were practiced among them. Hume.
Divide that gold amongst you. Marlowe.
Whether they quarreled among themselves, or with their neighbors. Addison.

Among.etym: [OE. amongist, amonges, amonge, among, AS. onmang, ongemang, gemang, in a crowd or mixture. For the ending -st see Amidst. See Mingle.]

senses.d: To go up; to ascend.
q: So up he rose, and thence amounted straight. Spenser.

senses.d: To rise or reach by an accumulation of particular sums or quantities; to come (to) in the aggregate or whole; — with to or unto.
To rise, reach, or extend in effect, substance, or influence; to be equivalent; to come practically (to); as, the testimony amounts to very little.

Amount.etym: [OF. amonter to increase, advance, ascend, fr. amont (equiv. to L. ad montem to the mountain) upward, F. amont up the river. See Mount, n.]

senses.d: To signify; to amount to.
The sum total of two or more sums or quantities; the aggregate; the whole quantity; a totality; as, the amount of 7 and 9 is 16; the amount of a bill; the amount of this year's revenue.
The effect, substance, value, significance, or result; the sum; as, the amount of the testimony is this.
q: The whole amount of that enormous fame. Pope.

senses.d: This word is properly an adjective, but is commonly called the indefinite article. It is used before nouns of the singular number only, and signifies one, or any, but somewhat less emphatically. In such expressions as “twice an hour,” “once an age,” a shilling an ounce (see 2d A, 2), it has a distributive force, and is equivalent to each, every.

An.etym: [AS. ān one, the same word as the numeral. See One, and cf. A.]

senses.d: If; — a word used by old English authors.
q: Nay, an thou dalliest, then I am thy foe. B. Jonson.

An.etym: [Shortened fr. and, OE. an., and, sometimes and if, in introducing conditional clauses, like Icel. enda if, the same word as and. Prob. and was originally pleonastic before the conditional clause.]

senses.d: Of each; an equal quantity; as, wine and honey, ana (or, contracted, aa), � ij., that is, of wine and honey, each, two ounces.
q: An apothecary with a . . . long bill of anas. Dryden.

senses.d: A race of giants living in Palestine.
An expression equivalent to What did you say? Sir? Eh?
A ban or curse pronounced with religious solemnity by ecclesiastical authority, and accompanied by excommunication. Hence: Denunciation of anything as accursed.
q: denounce anathemas against unbelievers. Priestley.

senses.d: An imprecation; a curse; a malediction.
q: Finally she fled to London followed by the anathemas of both . Thackeray.

senses.d: Any person or thing anathematized, or cursed by ecclesiastical authority.
q: The Jewish nation were an anathema destined to destruction. St. Paul . . . says he could wish, to save them from it, to become an anathema, and be destroyed himself. Locke.

Anathema.etym: [L. anath�ma, fr. Gr. � anything devoted, esp. to evil, a curse; also L. anath�ma, fr. Gr. � a votive offering; all fr. � to set up as a votive gift, dedicate; � up + � to set. See Thesis.]

senses.d: One from whom a person is descended, whether on the father's or mother's side, at any distance of time; a progenitor; a fore father.
An earlier type; a progenitor; as, this fossil animal is regarded as the ancestor of the horse.
One from whom an estate has descended; — the correlative of heir.

Ancestor.etym: [OE. ancestre, auncestre, also ancessour; the first forms fr. OF. ancestre, F. ancêtre, fr. the L. nom. antessor one who goes before; the last form fr. OF. ancessor, fr. L. acc. antecessorem, fr. antecedere to go before; ante before + cedere to go. See Cede, and cf. Antecessor.]

senses.d: A iron instrument which is attached to a ship by a cable (rope or chain), and which, being cast overboard, lays hold of the earth by a fluke or hook and thus retains the ship in a particular station.

Any instrument or contrivance serving a purpose like that of a ship's anchor, as an arrangement of timber to hold a dam fast; a contrivance to hold the end of a bridge cable, or other similar part; a contrivance used by founders to hold the core of a mold in place.
Fig.: That which gives stability or security; that on which we place dependence for safety.
q: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul. Heb. vi. 19.

senses.d: An emblem of hope.
A metal tie holding adjoining parts of a building together.
One of the anchor-shaped spicules of certain sponges; also, one of the calcareous spinules of certain Holothurians, as in species of Synapta.

Anchor.etym: [OE. anker, AS. ancor, oncer, L. ancora, sometimes spelt anchora, fr. Gr. ἄγκυρα, akin to E. angle: cf. F. ancre. See Angle, n.]

senses.d: To place at anchor; to secure by an anchor; as, to anchor a ship.
To fix or fasten; to fix in a stable condition; as, to anchor the cables of a suspension bridge.
q: Till that my nails were anchored in thine eyes. Shak.

senses.d: To cast anchor; to come to anchor; as, our ship (or the captain) anchored in the stream.
To stop; to fix or rest.
q: My invention . . . anchors on Isabel. Shak.

senses.d: An anchoret.

Anchor.etym: [OE. anker, ancre, AS. ancra, fr. L. anachoreta. See Anchoret.]

senses.d: Old; that happened or existed in former times, usually at a great distance of time; belonging to times long past; specifically applied to the times before the fall of the Roman empire; — opposed to modern; as, ancient authors, literature, history; ancient days.
q: Witness those ancient empires of the earth. Milton.
Gildas Albanius . . . much ancienter than his namesake surnamed the Wise. Fuller.

senses.d: Old; that has been of long duration; of long standing; of great age; as, an ancient forest; an ancient castle.
q: Remove not the ancient landmarks, which thy fathers have set. Prov. xxii. 28.
An ancient man, strangely habited, asked for quarters. Scott.

senses.d: Known for a long time, or from early times; — opposed to recent or new; as, the ancient continent.
q: A friend, perhaps, or an ancient acquaintance. Barrow.

senses.d: Dignified, like an aged man; magisterial; venerable.
q: He wrought but some few hours of the day, and then would he seem very grave and ancient. Holland.

senses.d: Experienced; versed.
q: Though was the youngest brother, yet he was the most ancient in the business of the realm. Berners.

senses.d: Former; sometime.
q: They mourned their ancient leader lost. Pope.

Ancient.syn: Old; primitive; pristine; antique; antiquated; old-fashioned; obsolete.
Ancient.etym: [OE. auncien, F. ancien, LL. antianus, fr. L. ante before. See Ante-, pref.]

senses.d: Those who lived in former ages, as opposed to the moderns.
An aged man; a patriarch. Hence: A governor; a ruler; a person of influence.
q: The Lord will enter into judgment with the ancients of his people, and the princes thereof. Isa. iii. 14.

senses.d: A senior; an elder; a predecessor.
q: Junius and Andronicus . . . in Christianity . . . were his ancients. Hooker.

senses.d: One of the senior members of the Inns of Court or of Chancery.
An ensign or flag.
q: More dishonorable ragged than an old-faced ancient. Shak.

senses.d: The bearer of a flag; an ensign.
q: This is Othello's ancient, as I take it. Shak.

senses.d: A particle which expresses the relation of connection or addition. It is used to conjoin a word with a word, a clause with a clause, or a sentence with a sentence.
In order to; — used instead of the infinitival to, especially after try, come, go.
q: At least to try and teach the erring soul. Milton.

senses.d: It is sometimes, in old songs, a mere expletive.
q: When that I was and a little tiny boy. Shak.

senses.d: If; though. See An, conj.
q: As they will set an house on fire, and it were but to roast their eggs. Bacon.

And.etym: [AS. and; akin to OS. endi, Icel. enda, OHG. anti, enti, inti, unti, G. und, D. en, OD. ende. Cf, An if, Ante-.]

senses.d: A messenger.
q: The dear good angel of the Spring, The nightingale. B. Jonson.

senses.d: A spiritual, celestial being, superior to man in power and intelligence. In the Scriptures the angels appear as God's messengers.
q: O, welcome, pure-eyed Faith, white-handed Hope, Thou hovering angel, girt with golden wings. Milton.

senses.d: One of a class of “fallen angels;” an evil spirit; as, the devil and his angels.
A minister or pastor of a church, as in the Seven Asiatic churches.
q: Unto the angel of the church of Ephesus write. Rev. ii. 1.

senses.d: Attendant spirit; genius; demon.
An appellation given to a person supposed to be of angelic goodness or loveliness; a darling.
q: When pain and anguish wring the brow, A ministering angel thou. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: An ancient gold coin of England, bearing the figure of the archangel Michael. It varied in value from 6s. 8d. to 10s.

Angel.etym: [AS. ængel, engel, influenced by OF. angele, angle, F. ange. Both the AS. and the OF. words are from L. angelus, Gr. ἄγγελοσ messenger, a messenger of God, an angel.]

senses.d: Trouble; vexation; also, physical pain or smart of a sore, etc.
q: I made the experiment, setting the moxa where . . . the greatest anger and soreness still continued. Temple.

senses.d: A strong passion or emotion of displeasure or antagonism, excited by a real or supposed injury or insult to one's self or others, or by the intent to do such injury.
q: Anger is like A full hot horse, who being allowed his way, Self-mettle tires him. Shak.

Anger.syn: Resentment; wrath; rage; fury; passion; ire gall; choler; indignation; displeasure; vexation; grudge; spleen.
Anger.etym: [OE. anger, angre, affliction, anger, fr. Icel. angr affliction, sorrow; akin to Dan. anger regret, Swed. ånger regret, AS. ange oppressed, sad, L. angor a strangling, anguish, angere to strangle, Gr. ἄγχειν to strangle, Skr. aṁhas pain, and to E. anguish, anxious, quinsy, and perh. awe, ugly. The w

senses.d: To make painful; to cause to smart; to inflame.
q: He . . . angereth malign ulcers. Bacon.

senses.d: To excite to anger; to enrage; to provoke.
q: Taxes and impositions . . . which rather angered than grieved the people. Clarendon.

senses.d: The inclosed space near the point where two lines meet; a corner; a nook.
q: Into the utmost angle of the world. Spenser.
To search the tenderest angles of the heart. Milton.

senses.d: The figure made by. two lines which meet.
A projecting or sharp corner; an angular fragment.
q: Though but an angle reached him of the stone. Dryden.

senses.d: A name given to four of the twelve astrological “houses.”
A fishhook; tackle for catching fish, consisting of a line, hook, and bait, with or without a rod.
q: Give me mine angle: we 'll to the river there. Shak.
A fisher next his trembling angle bears. Pope.

Angle.etym: [F. angle, L. angulus angle, corner; akin to uncus hook, Gr. αγκὔλοσ bent, crooked, angular, ἄγκοσ a bend or hollow, AS. angel hook, fish-hook, G. angel, and F. anchor.]

senses.d: To fish with an angle (fishhook), or with hook and line.
To use some bait or artifice; to intrigue; to scheme; as, to angle for praise.
q: The hearts of all that he did angle for. Shak.

senses.d: To try to gain by some insinuating artifice; to allure.
Troublesome; vexatious; rigorous.
q: God had provided a severe and angry education to chastise the forwardness of a young spirit. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: Inflamed and painful, as a sore.
Touched with anger; under the emotion of anger; feeling resentment; enraged; — followed generally by with before a person, and at before a thing.
q: Be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves. Gen. xlv. 5.
Wherefore should God be angry at thy voice? Eccles. v. 6.

senses.d: Showing anger; proceeding from anger; acting as if moved by anger; wearing the marks of anger; as, angry words or tones; an angry sky; angry waves.
Red.
q: Sweet rose, whose hue, angry and brave. Herbert.

senses.d: Sharp; keen; stimulated.
q: I never ate with angrier appetite. Tennyson.

Angry.syn: Passionate; resentful; irritated; irascible; indignant; provoked; enraged; incensed; exasperated; irate; hot; raging; furious; wrathful; wroth; choleric; inflamed; infuriated.

senses.d: Extreme pain, either of body or mind; excruciating distress.
q: But they hearkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit, and for cruel bondage. Ex. vi. 9.
Anguish as of her that bringeth forth her first child. Jer. iv. 31.

Anguish.syn: Agony; pang; torture; torment. See Agony.
Anguish.etym: [OE. anguishe, anguise, angoise, F. angoisse, fr. L. angustia narrowness, difficulty, distress, fr. angustus narrow, difficult, fr. angere to press together. See Anger.]

senses.d: To distress with extreme pain or grief.
An umbelliferous plant (Pimpinella anisum) growing naturally in Egypt, and cultivated in Spain, Malta, etc., for its carminative and aromatic seeds.
The fruit or seeds of this plant.

Anise.etym: [OE. anys, F. anis, L. anisum, anethum, fr. Gr. ἄνισον, ἄνηθον.]

senses.d: The joint which connects the foot with the leg; the tarsus.

Ankle.etym: [OE. ancle, anclow, AS. ancleow; akin to Icel. ökkla, ökli, Dan. and Sw. ankel, D. enklaauw, enkel, G. enkel, and perh. OHG. encha, ancha thigh, shin: cf. Skr. anga limb, anguri finger. Cf. Haunch.]

senses.d: An East Indian money of account, the sixteenth of a rupee, or about 2� cents.
To smear or rub over with oil or an unctuous substance; also, to spread over, as oil.
q: And fragrant oils the stiffened limbs anoint. Dryden.
He anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay. John ix. 6.

senses.d: To apply oil to or to pour oil upon, etc., as a sacred rite, especially for consecration.
q: Then shalt thou take the anointing oil, and pour it upon his head and anoint him. Exod. xxix. 7.
Anoint Hazael to be king over Syria. 1 Kings xix. 15.

Anoint.etym: [OF. enoint, p. p. of enoindre, fr. L. inungere; in + ungere, unguere, to smear, anoint. See Ointment, Unguent.]

senses.d: Anointed.
Straightway; at once.
q: The same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it. Matt. xiii. 20.

senses.d: Soon; in a little while.
q: As it shall better appear anon. Stow.

senses.d: At another time; then; again.
q: Sometimes he trots, . . . anon he rears upright. Shak.
A pouncet box, which ever and anon He gave his nose. Shak.

Anon.etym: [OE. anoon, anon, anan, lit., in one (moment), fr. AS. on in + ān one. See On and One.]

senses.d: One more, in addition to a former number; a second or additional one, similar in likeness or in effect.
q: Another yet! — a seventh! I 'll see no more. Shak.
Would serve to scale another Hero's tower. Shak.

senses.d: Not the same; different.
q: He winks, and turns his lips another way. Shak.

senses.d: Any or some; any different person, indefinitely; any one else; some one else.
q: Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth. Prov. xxvii. 2.
While I am coming, another steppeth down before me. John v. 7.

senses.d: To speak in defense against; to reply to in defense; as, to answer a charge; to answer an accusation.
To speak or write in return to, as in return to a call or question, or to a speech, declaration, argument, or the like; to reply to (a question, remark, etc.); to respond to.
q: She answers him as if she knew his mind. Shak.
So spake the apostate angel, though in pain: . . . And him thus answered soon his bold compeer. Milton.

senses.d: To respond to satisfactorily; to meet successfully by way of explanation, argument, or justification, and the like; to refute.
q: No man was able to answer him a word. Matt. xxii. 46.
These shifts refuted, answer thine appellant. Milton.
The reasoning was not and could not be answered. Macaulay.

senses.d: To be or act in return or response to.
q: This proud king . . . studies day and night To answer all the debts he owes unto you. Shak.

senses.d: To render account to or for.
q: I will . . . send him to answer thee. Shak.

senses.d: To atone; to be punished for.
q: And grievously hath Cæzar answered it. Shak.

senses.d: To be opposite to; to face.
q: The windows answering each other, we could just discern the glowing horizon them. Gilpin.

senses.d: To be or act an equivalent to, or as adequate or sufficient for; to serve for; to repay.
q: Money answereth all things. Eccles. x. 19.

senses.d: To be or act in accommodation, conformity, relation, or proportion to; to correspond to; to suit.
q: Weapons must needs be dangerous things, if they answered the bulk of so prodigious a person. Swift.

Answer.etym: [OE. andswerien, AS. andswerian, andswarian, to answer, fr. andswaru, n., answer. See Answer, n.]

senses.d: To speak or write by way of return (originally, to a charge), or in reply; to make response.
q: There was no voice, nor any that answered. 1 Kings xviii. 26.

senses.d: To make a satisfactory response or return.
q: Let his neck answer for it, if there is any martial law. Shak.

senses.d: To be or act in return.
q: Do the strings answer to thy noble hand? Dryden.

senses.d: To be opposite, or to act in opposition.
To be or act as an equivalent, or as adequate or sufficient; as, a very few will answer.
To be or act in conformity, or by way of accommodation, correspondence, relation, or proportion; to conform; to correspond; to suit; — usually with to.
q: That the time may have all shadow and silence in it, and the place answer to convenience. Shak.
If this but answer to my just belief, I 'll remember you. Shak.
As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man. Pro�. xxvii. 19.

senses.d: A reply to a change; a defense.
q: At my first answer no man stood with me. 2 Tim. iv. 16.

senses.d: Something said or written in reply to a question, a call, an argument, an address, or the like; a reply.
q: A soft answer turneth away wrath. Prov. xv. 1.
I called him, but he gave me no answer. Cant. v. 6.

senses.d: Something done in return for, or in consequence of, something else; a responsive action.
q: Great the slaughter is Here made by the Roman; great the answer be Britons must take. Shak.

senses.d: A solution, the result of a mathematical operation; as, the answer to a problem.

A counter-statement of facts in a course of pleadings; a confutation of what the other party has alleged; a responsive declaration by a witness in reply to a question. In Equity, it is the usual form of defense to the complainant's charges in his bill.

Answer.etym: [OE. andsware, AS. andswaru; and against + swerian to swear. �, �. See Anti-, and Swear, and cf. 1st un-.]

senses.d: Obliged to answer; liable to be called to account; liable to pay, indemnify, or make good; accountable; amenable; responsible; as, an agent is answerable to his principal; to be answerable for a debt, or for damages.
q: Will any man argue that . . . he can not be justly punished, but is answerable only to God? Swift.

senses.d: Capable of being answered or refuted; admitting a satisfactory answer.
q: The argument, though subtle, is yet answerable. Johnson.

senses.d: Correspondent; conformable; hence, comparable.
q: What wit and policy of man is answerable to their discreet and orderly course? Holland.
This revelation . . . was answerable to that of the apostle to the Thessalonians. Milton.

senses.d: Proportionate; commensurate; suitable; as, an achievement answerable to the preparation for it.
Equal; equivalent; adequate.
q: Had the valor of his soldiers been answerable, he had reached that year, as was thought, the utmost bounds of Britain. Milton.

senses.d: A hymenopterous insect of the Linnæan genus Formica, which is now made a family of several genera; an emmet; a pismire.

Ant.etym: [OE. ante, amete, emete, AS. æmete akin to G. ameise. Cf. Emmet.]

senses.d: A denier or opponent of Christ. Specif.: A great antagonist, person or power, expected to precede Christ's second coming.
The quality of being ancient; ancientness; great age; as, a statue of remarkable antiquity; a family of great antiquity.
Old age.
q: It not your voice broken? . . . and every part about you blasted with antiquity? Shak.

senses.d: Ancient times; former ages; times long since past; as, Cicero was an eloquent orator of antiquity.
The ancients; the people of ancient times.
q: That such pillars were raised by Seth all antiquity has �vowed. Sir W. Raleigh.

senses.d: An old gentleman.
q: You are a shrewd antiquity, neighbor Clench. B. Jonson.

senses.d: A relic or monument of ancient times; as, a coin, a statue, etc.; an ancient institution.

Antiquity.etym: [L. antiquitas, fr. antiquus: cf. F. antiquité. See Antique.]

senses.d: An iron block, usually with a steel face, upon which metals are hammered and shaped.
Anything resembling an anvil in shape or use.

Anvil.etym: [OE. anvelt, anfelt, anefelt, AS. anfilt, onfilt; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. anafalz, D. aanbeld.]

senses.d: To form or shape on an anvil; to hammer out; as, anviled armor.
One indifferently, out of an indefinite number; one indefinitely, whosoever or whatsoever it may be.
q: No man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son. Matt. xi. 27.

senses.d: Some, of whatever kind, quantity, or number; as, are there any witnesses present? are there any other houses like it?
q: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, . . . and it shall be given him. Jas. i. 5.
That if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem. Acts ix. 2.

Any.etym: [OE. æni”, æni, eni, ani, oni, AS. ǣnig, fr. ān one. It is akin to OS. ēnig, OHG. einic, G. einig, D. eenig. See One.]

senses.d: To any extent; in any degree; at all.
q: You are not to go loose any longer. Shak.
Before you go any farther. Steele.

senses.d: With a quick pace; quick; fast; speedily.
q: His dewy locks did drop with brine apace. Spenser.
A visible triumph of the gospel draws on apace. I. Taylor.

Apace.etym: [Pref. a- + pace. OE. a pas at a walk, in which a is the article. See Pace.]

senses.d: Separately, in regard to space or company; in a state of separation as to place; aside.
q: Others apart sat on a hill retired. Milton.
The Lord hath set apart him that is godly for himself. Ps. iv. 3.

senses.d: In a state of separation, of exclusion, or of distinction, as to purpose, use, or character, or as a matter of thought; separately; independently; as, consider the two propositions apart.
Aside; away.
q: Let Pleasure go, put Care apart. Keble.

senses.d: In two or more parts; asunder; to piece; as, to take a piece of machinery apart.

Apart.etym: [F. à part; (L. ad) + part part. See Part.]

senses.d: A quadrumanous mammal, esp. of the family Simiadæ, having teeth of the same number and form as in man, and possessing neither a tail nor cheek pouches. The name is applied esp. to species of the genus Hylobates, and is sometimes used as a general term for all Quadrumana. The higher forms, the gorilla, chimpanzee, and ourang, are often called anthropoid apes or man apes.
One who imitates servilely (in allusion to the manners of the ape); a mimic.
A dupe.

Ape.etym: [AS. apa; akin to D. aap, OHG. affo, G. affe, Icel. api, Sw. apa, Dan. abe, W. epa.]

senses.d: To mimic, as an ape imitates human actions; to imitate or follow servilely or irrationally.
q: The people of England will not ape the fashions they have never tried. Burke.

senses.d: Each by itself; by the single one; to each; as the share of each; as, these melons cost a shilling apiece.

A deity among the Greeks and Romans. He was the god of light and day (the “sun god”), of archery, prophecy, medicine, poetry, and music, etc., and was represented as the model of manly grace and beauty; — called also Phébus.
The Destroyer; — a name used (Rev. ix. 11) for the angel of the bottomless pit, answering to the Hebrew Abaddon.
Literally: One sent forth; a messenger. Specifically: One of the twelve disciples of Christ, specially chosen as his companions and witnesses, and sent forth to preach the gospel.
q: He called unto him his disciples, and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles. Luke vi. 13.

senses.d: The missionary who first plants the Christian faith in any part of the world; also, one who initiates any great moral reform, or first advocates any important belief; one who has extraordinary success as a missionary or reformer; as, Dionysius of Corinth is called the apostle of France, John Eliot the apostle to the Indians, Theobald Mathew the apostle of temperance.
A brief letter dimissory sent by a court appealed from to the superior court, stating the case, etc.; a paper sent up on appeals in the admiralty courts.

Apostle.etym: [OE. apostle, apostel, postle, AS. apostol, L. apostolus, fr. Gr. � messenger, one sent forth or away, fr. � to send off or away; � from + � to send; akin to G. stellen to set, E. stall: cf. F. apôtre, Of. apostre, apostle, apostele, apostole.]

senses.d: The office or dignity of an apostle.
One who prepares and sells drugs or compounds for medicinal purposes.

Apothecary.etym: [OE. apotecarie, fr. LL. apothecarius, fr. L. apotheca storehouse, Gr. απο, fr. � to put away; � from + � to put: cf. F. apothicaire, OF. apotecaire. See Thesis.]

senses.d: External clothing; vesture; garments; dress; garb; external habiliments or array.
q: Fresh in his new apparel, proud and young. Denham.
At public devotion his resigned carriage made religion appear in the natural apparel of simplicity. Tatler.

senses.d: A small ornamental piece of embroidery worn on albs and some other ecclesiastical vestments.
The furniture of a ship, as masts, sails, rigging, anchors, guns, etc.

Apparel.syn: Dress; clothing; vesture; garments; raiment; garb; costume; attire; habiliments.
Apparel.etym: [OE. apparel, apareil, OF. apareil, appareil, preparation, provision, furniture, OF. apareiller to match, prepare, F. appareiller; OF. a (L. ad) + pareil like, similar, fr. LL. pariculus, dim. of L. par equal. See Pair.]

senses.d: To make or get (something) ready; to prepare.
To furnish with apparatus; to equip; to fit out.
q: Ships . . . appareled to fight. Hayward.

senses.d: To dress or clothe; to attire.
q: They which are gorgeously appareled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts. Luke vii. 25.

senses.d: To dress with external ornaments; to cover with something ornamental; to deck; to embellish; as, trees appareled with flowers, or a garden with verdure.
q: Appareled in celestial light. Wordsworth.

senses.d: Capable of being seen, or easily seen; open to view; visible to the eye; within sight or view.
q: The moon . . . apparent queen. Milton.

senses.d: Clear or manifest to the understanding; plain; evident; obvious; known; palpable; indubitable.
q: It is apparent foul play. Shak.

senses.d: Appearing to the eye or mind (distinguished from, but not necessarily opposed to, true or real); seeming; as the apparent motion or diameter of the sun.
q: To live on terms of civility, and even of apparent friendship. Macaulay.
What Berkeley calls visible magnitude was by astronomers called apparent magnitude. Reid.

Apparent.syn: Visible; distinct; plain; obvious; clear; certain; evident; manifest; indubitable; notorious.
Apparent.etym: [F. apparent, L. apparens, -entis, p. pr. of apparere. See Appear.]

senses.d: An heir apparent.
q: I'll draw it as apparent to the crown. Shak.

senses.d: Visibly.
Plainly; clearly; manifestly; evidently.
q: If he should scorn me so apparently. Shak.

senses.d: Seemingly; in appearance; as, a man may be apparently friendly, yet malicious in heart.

To make application for the removal of (a cause) from an inferior to a superior judge or court for a rehearing or review on account of alleged injustice or illegality in the trial below. We say, the cause was appealed from an inferior court.
To summon; to challenge.
q: Man to man will I appeal the Norman to the lists. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: To invoke.

Appeal.etym: [OE. appelen, apelen, to appeal, accuse, OF. appeler, fr. L. appellare to approach, address, invoke, summon, call, name; akin to appellere to drive to; ad + pellere to drive. See Pulse, and cf. Peal.]

senses.d: To apply for the removal of a cause from an inferior to a superior judge or court for the purpose of reëxamination of for decision.
q: I appeal unto Cæsar. Acts xxv. 11.

senses.d: To call upon another to decide a question controverted, to corroborate a statement, to vindicate one's rights, etc.; as, I appeal to all mankind for the truth of what is alleged. Hence: To call on one for aid; to make earnest request.
q: I appeal to the Scriptures in the original. Horsley.
They appealed to the sword. Macaulay.

senses.d: An application for the removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior judge or court for reëxamination or review.
A summons to answer to a charge.
A call upon a person or an authority for proof or decision, in one's favor; reference to another as witness; a call for help or a favor; entreaty.
q: A kind of appeal to the Deity, the author of wonders. Bacon.

senses.d: Resort to physical means; recourse.
q: Every milder method is to be tried, before a nation makes an appeal to arms. Kent.

Appeal.etym: [OE. appel, apel, OF. apel, F. appel, fr. appeler. See Appeal, v. t.]

senses.d: To come or be in sight; to be in view; to become visible.
q: And God . . . said, Let . . . the dry land appear. Gen. i. 9.

senses.d: To come before the public; as, a great writer appeared at that time.

To stand in presence of some authority, tribunal, or superior person, to answer a charge, plead a cause, or the like; to present one's self as a party or advocate before a court, or as a person to be tried.
q: We must all appear before the judgment seat. 2 Cor. v. 10.
One ruffian escaped because no prosecutor dared to appear. Macaulay.

senses.d: To become visible to the apprehension of the mind; to be known as a subject of observation or comprehension, or as a thing proved; to be obvious or manifest.
q: It doth not yet appear what we shall be. 1 John iii. 2.
Of their vain contest appeared no end. Milton.

senses.d: To seem; to have a certain semblance; to look.
q: They disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Matt. vi. 16.

Appear.etym: [OE. apperen, aperen, OF. aparoir, F. apparoir, fr. L. appar�re to appear + par�reto come forth, to be visible; prob. from the same root as par�re to produce. Cf. Apparent, Parent, Peer, v. i.]

senses.d: Appearance.
The act of appearing or coming into sight; the act of becoming visible to the eye; as, his sudden appearance surprised me.
A thing seed; a phenomenon; a phase; an apparition; as, an appearance in the sky.
Personal presence; exhibition of the person; look; aspect; mien.
q: And now am come to see . . . It thy appearance answer loud report. Milton.

senses.d: Semblance, or apparent likeness; external show. pl. Outward signs, or circumstances, fitted to make a particular impression or to determine the judgment as to the character of a person or a thing, an act or a state; as, appearances are against him.
q: There was upon the tabernacle, as it were, the appearance of fire. Num. ix. 15.
For man looketh on the outward appearance. 1 Sam. xvi. 7.
Judge not according to the appearance. John. vii. 24.

senses.d: The act of appearing in a particular place, or in society, a company, or any proceedings; a coming before the public in a particular character; as, a person makes his appearance as an historian, an artist, or an orator.
q: Will he now retire, After appearance, and again prolong Our expectation? Milton.

senses.d: Probability; likelihood.
q: There is that which hath no appearance. Bacon.

senses.d: The coming into court of either of the parties; the being present in court; the coming into court of a party summoned in an action, either by himself or by his attorney, expressed by a formal entry by the proper officer to that effect; the act or proceeding by which a party proceeded against places himself before the court, and submits to its jurisdiction.

Appearance.syn: Coming; arrival; presence; semblance; pretense; air; look; manner; mien; figure; aspect.
Appearance.etym: [F. apparence, L. apparentia, fr. apparere. See Appear.]

senses.d: To make quiet; to calm; to reduce to a state of peace; to still; to pacify; to dispel (anger or hatred); as, to appease the tumult of the ocean, or of the passions; to appease hunger or thirst.

Appease.syn: To pacify; quiet; conciliate; propitiate; assuage; compose; calm; allay; hush; soothe; tranquilize.
Appease.etym: [OE. apesen, apaisen, OF. apaisier, apaissier, F. apaiser, fr. a (L. ad) + OF. pais peace, F. paix, fr. L. pax, pacis. See Peace.]

senses.d: To belong or pertain, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom; to relate.
q: Things appertaining to this life. Hooker.
Give it unto him to whom it appertaineth. Lev. vi. 5.

Appertain.etym: [OE. apperteinen, apertenen, OF. apartenir, F. appartenir, fr. L. appertinere; ad + pertinere to reach to, belong. See Pertain.]

senses.d: The desire for some personal gratification, either of the body or of the mind.
q: The object of appetite it whatsoever sensible good may be wished for; the object of will is that good which reason does lead us to seek. Hooker.

senses.d: Desire for, or relish of, food or drink; hunger.
q: Men must have appetite before they will eat. Buckle.

senses.d: Any strong desire; an eagerness or longing.
q: It God had given to eagles an appetite to swim. Jer. Taylor.
To gratify the vulgar appetite for the marvelous. Macaulay.

senses.d: Tendency; appetency.
q: In all bodies there as an appetite of union. Bacon.

senses.d: The thing desired.
q: Power being the natural appetite of princes. Swift.

Appetite.etym: [OE. appetit, F. appétit, fr. L. appetitus, fr. appetere to strive after, long for; ad + petere to seek. See Petition, and cf. Appetence.]

senses.d: The fleshy pome or fruit of a rosaceous tree (Pyrus malus) cultivated in numberless varieties in the temperate zones.
Any tree genus Pyrus which has the stalk sunken into the base of the fruit; an apple tree.
Any fruit or other vegetable production resembling, or supposed to resemble, the apple; as, apple of love, or love apple (a tomato), balsam apple, egg apple, oak apple.
Anything round like an apple; as, an apple of gold.

Apple.etym: [OE. appel, eppel, AS. æppel, æpl; akin to Fries. & D. appel, OHG, aphul, aphol, G. apfel, Icel. epli, Sw. äple, Dan. æble, Gael. ubhall, W. afal, Arm. aval, Lith. obůlys, Russ. iabloko; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To grow like an apple; to bear apples.
To lay or place; to put or adjust (one thing to another); — with to; as, to apply the hand to the breast; to apply medicaments to a diseased part of the body.
q: He said, and the sword his throat applied. Dryden.

senses.d: To put to use; to use or employ for a particular purpose, or in a particular case; to appropriate; to devote; as, to apply money to the payment of a debt.
To make use of, declare, or pronounce, as suitable, fitting, or relative; as, to apply the testimony to the case; to apply an epithet to a person.
q: Yet God at last To Satan, first in sin, his doom applied. Milton.

senses.d: To fix closely; to engage and employ diligently, or with attention; to attach; to incline.
q: Apply thine heart unto instruction. Prov. xxiii. 12.

senses.d: To direct or address.
q: Sacred vows . . . applied to grisly Pluto. Pope.

senses.d: To betake; to address; to refer; — used reflexively.
q: I applied myself to him for help. Johnson.

senses.d: To busy; to keep at work; to ply.
q: She was skillful in applying his “humors.” Sir P. Sidney.

senses.d: To visit.
q: And he applied each place so fast. Chapman.

Apply.etym: [OF. aplier, F. appliquer, fr. L. applicare to join, fix, or attach to; ad + plicare to fold, to twist together. See Applicant, Ply.]

senses.d: To suit; to agree; to have some connection, agreement, or analogy; as, this argument applies well to the case.
To make request; to have recourse with a view to gain something; to make application. (to); to solicit; as, to apply to a friend for information.
To ply; to move.
q: I heard the sound of an oar applying swiftly through the water. T. Moore.

senses.d: To apply or address one's self; to give application; to attend closely (to).
To fix with power or firmness; to establish; to mark out.
q: When he appointed the foundations of the earth. Prov. viii. 29.

senses.d: To fix by a decree, order, command, resolve, decision, or mutual agreement; to constitute; to ordain; to prescribe; to fix the time and place of.
q: Thy servants are ready to do whatsoever my lord the king shall appoint. 2 Sam. xv. 15.
He hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness. Acts xvii. 31.
Say that the emperor request a parley . . . and appoint the meeting. Shak.

senses.d: To assign, designate, or set apart by authority.
q: Aaron and his shall go in, and appoint them every one to his service. Num. iv. 19.
These were cities appointed for all the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them. Josh. xx. 9.

senses.d: To furnish in all points; to provide with everything necessary by way of equipment; to equip; to fit out.
q: The English, being well appointed, did so entertain them that their ships departed terribly torn. Hayward.

senses.d: To point at by way, or for the purpose, of censure or commendation; to arraign.
q: Appoint not heavenly disposition. Milton.

senses.d: To direct, designate, or limit; to make or direct a new disposition of, by virtue of a power contained in a conveyance; — said of an estate already conveyed.

Appoint.etym: [OE. appointen, apointen, OF. apointier to prepare, arrange, lean, place, F. appointer to give a salary, refer a cause, fr. LL. appunctare to bring back to the point, restore, to fix the point in a controversy, or the points in an agreement; L. ad + punctum a point. See Point.]

senses.d: To ordain; to determine; to arrange.
q: For the Lord had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. 2 Sam. xvii. 14.

senses.d: The act of appointing; designation of a person to hold an office or discharge a trust; as, he erred by the appointment of unsuitable men.
The state of being appointed to som� service or office; an office to which one is appointed; station; position; an, the appointment of treasurer.
Stipulation; agreement; the act of fixing by mutual agreement. Hence:: Arrangement for a meeting; engagement; as, they made an appointment to meet at six.
Decree; direction; established order or constitution; as, to submit to the divine appointments.
q: According to the appointment of the priests. Ezra vi. 9.

senses.d: The exercise of the power of designating (under a “power of appointment”) a person to enjoy an estate or other specific property; also, the instrument by which the designation is made.
Equipment, furniture, as for a ship or an army; whatever is appointed for use and management; outfit; (pl.) the accouterments of military officers or soldiers, as belts, sashes, swords.
q: The cavaliers emulated their chief in the richness of their appointments. Prescott.
I'll prove it in my shackles, with these hands Void of appointment, that thou liest. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: An allowance to a person, esp. to a public officer; a perquisite; — properly only in the plural.
q: An expense proportioned to his appointments and fortune is necessary. Chesterfield.

senses.d: A honorary part or exercise, as an oration, etc., at a public exhibition of a college; as, to have an appointment.

Appointment.syn: Designation; command; order; direction; establishment; equipment.

senses.d: To take or seize; to take hold of.
q: We have two hands to apprehend it. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: Hence: To take or seize (a person) by legal process; to arrest; as, to apprehend a criminal.
To take hold of with the understanding, that is, to conceive in the mind; to become cognizant of; to understand; to recognize; to consider.
q: This suspicion of Earl Reimund, though at first but a buzz, soon got a sting in the king's head, and he violently apprehended it. Fuller.
The eternal laws, such as the heroic age apprehended them. Gladstone.

senses.d: To know or learn with certainty.
q: G. You are too much distrustful of my truth. E. Then you must give me leave to apprehend The means and manner how. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: To anticipate; esp., to anticipate with anxiety, dread, or fear; to fear.
q: The opposition had more reason than the king to apprehend violence. Macaulay.

Apprehend.syn: To catch; seize; arrest; detain; capture; conceive; understand; imagine; believe; fear; dread.
Apprehend.etym: [L. apprehendere; ad + prehendere to lay hold of, seize; prae before + -hendere (used only in comp.); akin to Gr. χανδάνειν to hold, contain, and E. get: cf. F. appréhender. See Prehensile, Get.]

senses.d: To think, believe, or be of opinion; to understand; to suppose.
To be apprehensive; to fear.
q: It is worse to apprehend than to suffer. Rowe.

senses.d: To come or go near, in place or time; to draw nigh; to advance nearer.
q: Wherefore approached ye so nigh unto the city? 2 Sam. xi. 20.
But exhorting one another; and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching. Heb. x. 25.

senses.d: To draw near, in a figurative sense; to make advances; to approximate; as, he approaches to the character of the ablest statesman.

Approach.etym: [OE. approchen, aprochen, OF. approcher, LL. appropriare, fr. L. ad + propiare to draw near, prope near.]

senses.d: To bring near; to cause to draw near; to advance.
To come near to in place, time, or character; to draw nearer to; as, to approach the city; to approach my cabin; he approached the age of manhood.
q: He was an admirable poet, and thought even to have approached Homer. Temple.

senses.d: To take approaches to.
The act of drawing near; a coming or advancing near.
q: A nearer approach to the human type. Owen.

senses.d: A access, or opportunity of drawing near.
