q: The approach to kings and principal persons. Bacon.

senses.d: Movements to gain favor; advances.
A way, passage, or avenue by which a place or buildings can be approached; an access.
The advanced works, trenches, or covered roads made by besiegers in their advances toward a fortress or military post.

Approach.etym: [Cf. F. approche. See Approach, v. i.]

senses.d: A stroke whose object is to land the ball on the putting green. It is made with an iron club.
The act of ingrafting a sprig or shoot of one tree into another, without cutting it from the parent stock; — called, also, inarching and grafting by approach.
To show to be real or true; to prove.
q: Wouldst thou approve thy constancy? Approve First thy obedience. Milton.

senses.d: To make proof of; to demonstrate; to prove or show practically.
q: Opportunities to approve . . . worth. Emerson.
He had approved himself a great warrior. Macaulay.
'T is an old lesson; Time approves it true. Byron.
His account . . . approves him a man of thought. Parkman.

senses.d: To sanction officially; to ratify; to confirm; as, to approve the decision of a court-martial.
To regard as good; to commend; to be pleased with; to think well of; as, we approve the measured of the administration.
To make or show to be worthy of approbation or acceptance.
q: The first care and concern must be to approve himself to God. Rogers.
They had not approved of the deposition of James. Macaulay.
They approved of the political institutions. W. Black.

Approve.etym: [OE. aproven, appreven, to prove, OF. aprover, F. approuver, to approve, fr. L. approbare; ad + probare to esteem as good, approve, prove. See Prove, and cf. Approbate.]

senses.d: To make profit of; to convert to one's own profit; — said esp. of waste or common land appropriated by the lord of the manor.

Approve.etym: [OF. aprouer; a (L. ad) + a form apparently derived fr. the pro, prod, in L. prodest it is useful or profitable, properly the preposition pro for. Cf. Improve.]

senses.d: Expressing approbation; commending; as, an approving smile.

An article of dress, of cloth, leather, or other stuff, worn on the fore part of the body, to keep the clothes clean, to defend them from injury, or as a covering. It is commonly tied at the waist by strings.
Something which by its shape or use suggests an apron;

Apron.etym: [OE. napron, OF. naperon, F. napperon, dim. of OF. nape, F. nappe, cloth, tablecloth, LL. napa, fr. L. mappa, napkin, table napkin. See Map.]

senses.d: Fit or fitted; suited; suitable; appropriate.
q: They have always apt instruments. Burke.
A river . . . apt to be forded by a lamb. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: Having an habitual tendency; habitually liable or likely; — used of things.
q: My vines and peaches . . . were apt to have a soot or smuttiness upon their leaves and fruit. Temple.
This tree, if unprotected, is apt to be stripped of the leaves by a leaf-cutting ant. Lubbock.

senses.d: Inclined; disposed customarily; given; ready; — used of persons.
q: Apter to give than thou wit be to ask. Beau. & Fl.
That lofty pity with which prosperous folk are apt to remember their grandfathers. F. Harrison.

senses.d: Ready; especially fitted or qualified (to do something); quick to learn; prompt; expert; as, a pupil apt to learn; an apt scholar.
q: Live a thousand years, I shall not find myself so apt to die. Shak.
I find thee apt . . . Now, Hamlet, hear. Shak.

Apt.syn: Fit; meet; suitable; qualified; inclined; disposed; liable; ready; quick; prompt.
Apt.etym: [F. apte, L. aptus, fr. obsolete apere to fasten, to join, to fit, akin to apisci to reach, attain: cf. Gr. � to fasten, Skr. āpta fit, fr. āp to reach attain.]

senses.d: To fit; to suit; to adapt.
q: That our speech be apted to edification. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: A genus of eagles.
A northern constellation southerly from Lyra and Cygnus and preceding the Dolphin; the Eagle.
Ere; before.
The Altar; a southern constellation, south of the tail of the Scorpion.
A name of the great blue and yellow macaw (Ara ararauna), native of South America.
One of a swarthy race occupying Arabia, and numerous in Syria, Northern Africa, etc.

Arab.etym: [Prob. ultimately fr. Heb. arabah a desert, the name employed, in the Old Testament, to denote the valley of the Jordan and Dead Sea. Ar. Arab, Heb. arabi, arbi, arbim: cf. F. Arabe, L. Arabs, Gr. �.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Arabia or its inhabitants.
A native of Arabia; an Arab.
Any part of a curved line.

Usually a curved member made up of separate wedge-shaped solids, with the joints between them disposed in the direction of the radii of the curve; used to support the wall or other weight above an opening. In this sense arches are segmental, round (i.e., semicircular), or pointed.
Any place covered by an arch; an archway; as, to pass into the arch of a bridge.
Any curvature in the form of an arch; as, the arch of the aorta.

Arch.etym: [F. arche, fr. LL. arca, for arcus. See Arc.]

senses.d: To cover with an arch or arches.
To form or bend into the shape of an arch.
q: The horse arched his neck. Charlesworth.

senses.d: To form into an arch; to curve.
Chief; eminent; greatest; principal.
q: The most arch act of piteous massacre. Shak.

senses.d: Cunning or sly; sportively mischievous; roguish; as, an arch look, word, lad.
q: spoke his request with so arch a leer. Tatler.

senses.d: A chief.
q: My worthy arch and patron comes to-night. Shak.

senses.d: A chief angel; one high in the celestial hierarchy.
A term applied to several different species of plants (Angelica archangelica, Lamium album, etc.).

Archangel.etym: [L. archangelus, Gr. αρχἄγγελοσ: cf. OF. archangel, F. archange. See Arch-, pref., and Angel.]

senses.d: A bowman, one skilled in the use of the bow and arrow.

Archer.etym: [archier, F. archer, LL. arcarius, fr. L. arcus bow. See Arc, Arch, n.]

senses.d: pl. of Arch, n.
A fixed star of the first magnitude in the constellation Boötes.
q: Canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons . Job xxxviii. 32.

Arcturus.etym: [L. Arcturus, Gr. � bearward, equiv. to �; � bear + � ward, guard. See Arctic.]

senses.d: The present indicative plural of the substantive verb to be; but etymologically a different word from be, or was. Am, art, are, and is, all come from the root as.

Are.etym: [AS. (Northumbrian) aron, akin to the 1st pers. pl. forms, Icel. erum, Goth. sijum, L. sumus, Gr. �, Skr. smas; all from a root as. � See Am and Is, and cf. Be.]

senses.d: The unit of superficial measure, being a square of which each side is ten meters in length; 100 square meters, or about 119.6 square yards.
A member of the Areopagus.
The highest judicial court at Athens. Its sessions were held on Mars' Hill. Hence, any high court or tribunal
To invent and offer reasons to support or overthrow a proposition, opinion, or measure; to use arguments; to reason.
q: I argue not Against Heaven's hand or will. Milton.

senses.d: To contend in argument; to dispute; to reason; — followed by with; as, you may argue with your friend without convincing him.

Argue.etym: [OE. arguen, F. arguer, fr. L. argutare, freq. of arguere to make clear; from the same root as E. argent.]

senses.d: To debate or discuss; to treat by reasoning; as, the counsel argued the cause before a full court; the cause was well argued.
To prove or evince; too manifest or exhibit by inference, deduction, or reasoning.
q: So many laws argue so many sins. Milton.

senses.d: To persuade by reasons; as, to argue a man into a different opinion.
To blame; to accuse; to charge with.
q: Thoughts and expressions . . . which can be truly argued of obscenity, profaneness, or immorality. Dryden.

Men of many words sometimes argue for the sake of talking; men of ready tongues frequently dispute for the sake of victory; men in public life often debate for the sake of opposing the ruling party, or from any other motive than the love of truth. Crabb.
Unskilled to argue, in dispute yet loud, Bold without caution, without honors proud. Falconer.
Betwixt the dearest friends to raise debate. Dryden.

Argue.syn: to reason; evince; discuss; debate; expostulate; remonstrate; controvert.

senses.d: Proof; evidence.
q: There is.. no more palpable and convincing argument of the existence of a Deity. Ray.
Why, then, is it made a badge of wit and an argument of parts for a man to commence atheist, and to cast off all belief of providence, all awe and reverence for religion? South.

senses.d: A reason or reasons offered in proof, to induce belief, or convince the mind; reasoning expressed in words; as, an argument about, concerning, or regarding a proposition, for or in favor of it, or against it.
A process of reasoning, or a controversy made up of rational proofs; argumentation; discussion; disputation.
q: The argument is about things, but names. Locke.

senses.d: The subject matter of a discourse, writing, or artistic representation; theme or topic; also, an abstract or summary, as of the contents of a book, chapter, poem.
q: You and love are still my argument. Shak.
The abstract or argument of the piece. Jeffrey.
with boastful argument portrayed. Milton.

senses.d: Matter for question; business in hand.
q: Sheathed their swords for lack of argument. Shak.

senses.d: The quantity on which another quantity in a table depends; as, the altitude is the argument of the refraction.
The independent variable upon whose value that of a function depends.

Argument.etym: [F. argument, L. argumentum, fr. arguere to argue.]

senses.d: To make an argument; to argue.
A variety of the gazelle (Antilope, or Gazella, dorcas), found in Arabia and adjacent countries.
A squirrel-like Australian marsupial, a species of Petaurus.
A beautiful Brazilian toucan Ramphastos ariel).
In the Cabala, a water spirit; in later folklore, a light and graceful spirit of the air.

Ariel.etym: [Heb. ariël, perh. confused with E. aërial.]

senses.d: Rightly; correctly; in a right way or form; without mistake or crime; as, to worship God aright.

To come up from a lower to a higher position; to come above the horizon; to come up from one's bed or place of repose; to mount; to ascend; to rise; as, to arise from a kneeling posture; a cloud arose; the sun ariseth; he arose early in the morning.

To spring up; to come into action, being, or notice; to become operative, sensible, or visible; to begin to act a part; to present itself; as, the waves of the sea arose; a persecution arose; the wrath of the king shall arise.
q: There arose up a new king . . . which knew not Joseph. Ex. i. 8.
The doubts that in his heart arose. Milton.

senses.d: To proceed; to issue; to spring.
q: Whence haply mention may arise Of something not unseasonable to ask. Milton.

Arise.etym: [AS. ārīsan; ā (equiv. to Goth. us-, ur-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + rīsan to rise; cf. Goth. urreisan to arise. See Rise.]

senses.d: Rising.
A chest, or coffer.
q: Bearing that precious relic in an ark. Spenser.

senses.d: The oblong chest of acacia wood, overlaid with gold, which supported the mercy seat with its golden cherubs, and occupied the most sacred place in the sanctuary. In it Moses placed the two tables of stone containing the ten commandments. Called also the Ark of the Covenant.
The large, chestlike vessel in which Noah and his family were preserved during the Deluge. Gen. vi. Hence: Any place of refuge.
A large flatboat used on Western American rivers to transport produce to market.

Ark.etym: [OE. ark, arke, arche, AS. arc, earc, earce, fr. L. arca, fr. arcere to inclose, keep off; akin to Gr. � to keep off.]

senses.d: Belonging to the ark.
The limb of the human body which extends from the shoulder to the hand; also, the corresponding limb of a monkey.
Anything resembling an arm
Fig.: Power; might; strength; support; as, the secular arm; the arm of the law.
q: To whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? Isa. lii. 1.

Arm.etym: [AS. arm, earm; akin to OHG. aram, G., D., Dan., & Sw. arm, Icel. armr, Goth. arms, L. armus arm, shoulder, and prob. to Gr. � joining, joint, shoulder, fr. the root � to join, to fit together; cf. Slav. rame. �. See Art, Article.]

senses.d: A branch of the military service; as, the cavalry arm was made efficient.
A weapon of offense or defense; an instrument of warfare; — commonly in the pl.
To take by the arm; to take up in one's arms.
q: And make him with our pikes and partisans A grave: come, arm him. Shak.
Arm your prize; I know you will not lose him. Two N. Kins.

senses.d: To furnish with arms or limbs.
q: His shoulders broad and strong, Armed long and round. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: To furnish or equip with weapons of offense or defense; as, to arm soldiers; to arm the country.
q: Abram . . . armed his trained servants. Gen. xiv. 14.

senses.d: To cover or furnish with a plate, or with whatever will add strength, force, security, or efficiency; as, to arm the hit of a sword; to arm a hook in angling.
Fig.: To furnish with means of defense; to prepare for resistance; to fortify, in a moral sense.
q: Arm yourselves . . . with the same mind. 1 Pet. iv. 1.

Arm.etym: [OE. armen, F. armer, fr. L. armare, fr. arma, pl., arms. See arms.]

senses.d: To provide one's self with arms, weapons, or means of attack or resistance; to take arms.
Furnished with weapons of offense or defense; furnished with the means of security or protection.
Furnished with whatever serves to add strength, force, or efficiency.
q: A distemper eminently armed from heaven. De Foe.

senses.d: Having horns, beak, talons, etc; — said of beasts and birds of prey.
The cavity under the shoulder; the armpit.
A hole for the arm in a garment.
Instruments or weapons of offense or defense.
q: He lays down his arms, but not his wiles. Milton.
Three horses and three goodly suits of arms. Tennyson.

senses.d: The deeds or exploits of war; military service or science.
Anything which a man takes in his hand in anger, to strike or assault another with; an aggressive weapon.
The ensigns armorial of a family, consisting of figures and colors borne in shields, banners, etc., as marks of dignity and distinction, and descending from father to son.
The legs of a hawk from the thigh to the foot.

Arms.etym: [OE. armes, F. arme, pl. armes, fr. L. arma, pl., arms, orig. fittings, akin to armus shoulder, and E. arm. See Arm, n.]

senses.d: A collection or body of men armed for war, esp. one organized in companies, battalions, regiments, brigades, and divisions, under proper officers.
A body of persons organized for the advancement of a cause; as, the Blue Ribbon Army.
A great number; a vast multitude; a host.
q: An army of good words. Shak.

Army.etym: [F. armée, fr. L. armata, fem. of armatus, p. p. of armare to arm. Cf. Armada.]

senses.d: The past or preterit tense of Arise.
Order; a regular and imposing arrangement; disposition in regular lines; hence, order of battle; as, drawn up in battle array.
q: Wedged together in the closest array. Gibbon.

senses.d: The whole body of persons thus placed in order; an orderly collection; hence, a body of soldiers.
q: A gallant array of nobles and cavaliers. Prescott.

senses.d: An imposing series of things.
q: Their long array of sapphire and of gold. Byron.

senses.d: Dress; garments disposed in order upon the person; rich or beautiful apparel.
A ranking or setting forth in order, by the proper officer, of a jury as impaneled in a cause.

Array.etym: [OE. arai, arrai, OF. arrai, arrei, arroi, order, arrangement, dress, F. arroi; a (L. ad) + OF. rai, rei, roi, order, arrangement, fr. G. or Scand.; cf. Goth. raidjan, garaidjan, to arrange, MHG. gereiten, Icel. reiði rigging, harness; akin to E. ready. Cf. Ready, Greith, Curry.]

senses.d: To place or dispose in order, as troops for battle; to marshal.
q: By torch and trumpet fast arrayed, Each horseman drew his battle blade. Campbell.
These doubts will be arrayed before their minds. Farrar.

senses.d: To deck or dress; to adorn with dress; to cloth to envelop; — applied esp. to dress of a splendid kind.
q: Pharaoh . . . arrayed him in vestures of fine linen. Gen. xli.�.
In gelid caves with horrid gloom arrayed. Trumbull.

senses.d: To set in order, as a jury, for the trial of a cause; that is, to call them man by man.

Array.syn: To draw up; arrange; dispose; set in order.
Array.etym: [OE. araien, arraien, fr. OE. arraier, arreier, arreer, arroier, fr. arrai. See Array, n.]

senses.d: To come to the shore or bank. In present usage: To come in progress by water, or by traveling on land; to reach by water or by land; — followed by at (formerly sometimes by to), also by in and from.
q: sailing with a fleet from Sicily, arrived . . . and landed in the country of Laurentum. Holland.
There was no outbreak till the regiment arrived at Ipswich. Macaulay.

senses.d: To reach a point by progressive motion; to gain or compass an object by effort, practice, study, inquiry, reasoning, or experiment.
q: When he arrived at manhood. Rogers.
We arrive at knowledge of a law of nature by the generalization of facts. McCosh.
If at great things thou wouldst arrive. Milton.

senses.d: To come; said of time; as, the time arrived.
To happen or occur.
q: Happy! to whom this glorious death arrives. Waller.

Arrive.etym: [OE. ariven to arrive, land, OF. ariver, F. arriver, fr. LL. arripare, adripare, to come to shore; L. ad + ripa the shore or sloping bank of a river. Cf. Riparian.]

senses.d: To bring to shore.
q: And made the sea-trod ship arrive them. Chapman.

senses.d: To reach; to come to.
q: Ere he arrive the happy isle. Milton.
Ere we could arrive the point proposed. Shak.
Arrive at last the blessed goal. Tennyson.

senses.d: Arrival.
q: How should I joy of thy arrive to hear! Drayton.

senses.d: Arrogance.
A missile weapon of offense, slender, pointed, and usually feathered and barbed, to be shot from a bow.

Arrow.etym: [OE. arewe, AS. arewe, earh; akin to Icel. ör, örvar, Goth. arhwazna, and perh. L. arcus bow. Cf. Arc.]

senses.d: The second person singular, indicative mode, present tense, of the substantive verb Be; but formed after the analogy of the plural are, with the ending -t, as in thou shalt, wilt, orig. an ending of the second person sing. pret. Cf. Be. Now used only in solemn or poetical style.
The employment of means to accomplish some desired end; the adaptation of things in the natural world to the uses of life; the application of knowledge or power to practical purposes.
q: Blest with each grace of nature and of art. Pope.

senses.d: A system of rules serving to facilitate the performance of certain actions; a system of principles and rules for attaining a desired end; method of doing well some special work; — often contradistinguished from science or speculative principles; as, the art of building or engraving; the art of war; the art of navigation.
q: Science is systematized knowledge . . . Art is knowledge made efficient by skill. J. F. Genung.

senses.d: The systematic application of knowledge or skill in effecting a desired result. Also, an occupation or business requiring such knowledge or skill.
q: The fishermen can't employ their art with so much success in so troubled a sea. Addison.

senses.d: The application of skill to the production of the beautiful by imitation or design, or an occupation in which skill is so employed, as in painting and sculpture; one of the fine arts; as, he prefers art to literature.
Those branches of learning which are taught in the academical course of colleges; as, master of arts.
q: In fearless youth we tempt the heights of arts. Pope.
Four years spent in the arts (as they are called in colleges) is, perhaps, laying too laborious a foundation. Goldsmith.

senses.d: Learning; study; applied knowledge, science, or letters.
q: So vast is art, so narrow human wit. Pope.

senses.d: Skill, dexterity, or the power of performing certain actions, acquired by experience, study, or observation; knack; as, a man has the art of managing his business to advantage.
Skillful plan; device.
q: They employed every art to soothe . . . the discontented warriors. Macaulay.

senses.d: Cunning; artifice; craft.
q: Madam, I swear I use no art at all. Shak.
Animals practice art when opposed to their superiors in strength. Crabb.

senses.d: The black art; magic.
q: In America, literature and the elegant arts must grow up side by side with the coarser plants of daily necessity. Irving.

Art.syn: Science; literature; aptitude; readiness; skill; dexterity; adroitness; contrivance; profession; business; trade; calling; cunning; artifice; duplicity. See Science.
Art.etym: [F. art, L. ars, artis, orig., skill in joining or fitting; prob. akin to E. arm, aristocrat, article.]

senses.d: A handicraft; a trade; art of making.
Workmanship; a skillfully contrived work.
q: The material universe.. in the artifice of God, the artifice of the best Mechanist. Cudworth.

senses.d: Artful or skillful contrivance.
q: His plots were constructed without much artifice. Craik.

senses.d: Crafty device; an artful, ingenious, or elaborate trick.
q: Those who were conscious of guilt employed numerous artifices for the purpose of averting inquiry. Macaulay.

Artifice.etym: [L. artificium, fr. artifex artificer; ars, artis, art + facere to make: cf. F. artifice.]

senses.d: An artistic worker; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind, as a silversmith.
One who makes or contrives; a deviser, inventor, or framer.
q: The great Artificer of all that moves. Cowper.

senses.d: A cunning or artful fellow.
A military mechanic, as a blacksmith, carpenter, etc.; also, one who prepares the shells, fuses, grenades, etc., in a military laboratory.
Munitions of war; implements for warfare, as slings, bows, and arrows.
q: And Jonathan gave his artillery unto his lad. 1 Sam. xx. 40.

senses.d: Cannon; great guns; ordnance, including guns, mortars, howitzers, etc., with their equipment of carriages, balls, bombs, and shot of all kinds.
The men and officers of that branch of the army to which the care and management of artillery are confided.
The science of artillery or gunnery.

Artillery.etym: [OE. artilrie, OF. artillerie, arteillerie, fr. LL. artillaria, artilleria, machines and apparatus of all kinds used in war, vans laden with arms of any kind which follow camps; F. artillerie great guns, ordnance; OF. artillier to work artifice, to fortify, to arm, prob. from L. ars, artis, skill in

senses.d: Denoting equality or likeness in kind, degree, or manner; like; similar to; in the same manner with or in which; in accordance with; in proportion to; to the extent or degree in which or to which; equally; no less than; as, ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil; you will reap as you sow; do as you are bidden.
q: His spiritual attendants adjured him, as he loved his soul, to emancipate his brethren. Macaulay.

senses.d: In the idea, character, or condition of, — limiting the view to certain attributes or relations; as, virtue considered as virtue; this actor will appear as Hamlet.
q: The beggar is greater as a man, than is the man merely as a king. Dewey.

senses.d: While; during or at the same time that; when; as, he trembled as he spoke.
q: As I return I will fetch off these justices. Shak.

senses.d: Because; since; it being the case that.
q: As the population of Scotland had been generally trained to arms . . . they were not indifferently prepared. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: Expressing concession. (Often approaching though in meaning).
q: We wish, however, to avail ourselves of the interest, transient as it may be, which this work has excited. Macaulay.

senses.d: That, introducing or expressing a result or consequence, after the correlatives so and such.
q: I can place thee in such abject state, as help shall never find thee. Rowe.

senses.d: As if; as though.
q: He lies, as he his bliss did know. Waller.

senses.d: For instance; by way of example; thus; — used to introduce illustrative phrases, sentences, or citations.
Than.
q: The king was not more forward to bestow favors on them as they free to deal affronts to others their superiors. Fuller.

senses.d: Expressing a wish.

As.etym: [OE. as, als, alse, also, al swa, AS. eal swā, lit. all so; hence, quite so, quite as: cf. G. als as, than, also so, then. See Also.]

senses.d: An ace.
A Roman weight, answering to the libra or pound, equal to nearly eleven ounces Troy weight. It was divided into twelve ounces.
A Roman copper coin, originally of a pound weight (12 oz.); but reduced, after the first Punic war, to two ounces; in the second Punic war, to one ounce; and afterwards to half an ounce.
An ancient name of a gum.

Asa.etym: [NL. asa, of oriental origin; cf. Per. azā mastic, Ar. asā healing, isā remedy.]

senses.d: To move upward; to mount; to go up; to rise; — opposed to descend.
q: Higher yet that star ascends. Bowring.
I ascend unto my father and your father. John xx. 17.
The smoke of it ascended up to heaven. Addison.

senses.d: To rise, in a figurative sense; to proceed from an inferior to a superior degree, from mean to noble objects, from particulars to generals, from modern to ancient times, from one note to another more acute, etc.; as, our inquiries ascend to the remotest antiquity; to ascend to our first progenitor.

Ascend.syn: To rise; mount; climb; scale; soar; tower.
Ascend.etym: [L. ascendere; ad + scandere to climb, mount. See Scan.]

senses.d: To go or move upward upon or along; to climb; to mount; to go up the top of; as, to ascend a hill, a ladder, a tree, a river, a throne.
Rising; moving upward; as, an ascending kite.
The act of rising; motion upward; rise; a mounting upward; as, he made a tedious ascent; the ascent of vapors from the earth.
q: To him with swift ascent he up returned. Milton.

senses.d: The way or means by which one ascends.
An eminence, hill, or high place.
The degree of elevation of an object, or the angle it makes with a horizontal line; inclination; rising grade; as, a road has an ascent of five degrees.

Ascent.etym: [Formed like descent, as if from a F. ascente, fr. a verb ascendre, fr. L. ascendere. See Ascend, Descent.]

senses.d: To attribute, impute, or refer, as to a cause; as, his death was ascribed to a poison; to ascribe an effect to the right cause; to ascribe such a book to such an author.
q: The finest that is ascribed to Satan in the whole poem. Addison.

senses.d: To attribute, as a quality, or an appurtenance; to consider or allege to belong.
q: More than good-will to me attribute naught. Spenser.
Ascribes his gettings to his parts and merit. Pope.
And fairly quit him of the imputed blame. Spenser.

Ascribe.etym: [L. ascribere, adscribere, to ascribe; ad + scribere to write: cf. OF. ascrire. See Scribe.]

senses.d: A genus of trees of the Olive family, having opposite pinnate leaves, many of the species furnishing valuable timber, as the European ash (Fraxinus excelsior) and the white ash (F. Americana).
The tough, elastic wood of the ash tree.

Ash.etym: [OE. asch, esh, AS. æsc; akin to OHG. asc, Sw. & Dan. ask, Icel. askr, D. esch, G. esche.]

senses.d: sing. of Ashes.
To strew or sprinkle with ashes.
To shame.

Ashame.etym: [Pref. a- + shame: cf. AS. āscamian to shame (where ā- is the same as Goth. us-, G. er-, and orig. meant out), gescamian, gesceamian, to shame.]

senses.d: Affected by shame; abashed or confused by guilt, or a conviction or consciousness of some wrong action or impropriety.
q: All that forsake thee shall be ashamed. Jer. xvii. 13.
I began to be ashamed of sitting idle. Johnson.
Enough to make us ashamed of our species. Macaulay.
An ashamed person can hardly endure to meet the gaze of those present. Darwin.

Ashamed.etym: [Orig. a p. p. of ashame, v. t.]

senses.d: The earthy or mineral particles of combustible substances remaining after combustion, as of wood or coal.
Specifically: The remains of the human body when burnt, or when “returned to dust” by natural decay.
q: Their martyred blood and ashes sow. Milton.
The coffins were broken open. The ashes were scattered to the winds. Macaulay.

senses.d: The color of ashes; deathlike paleness.
q: The lip of ashes, and the cheek of flame. Byron.

Ashes.etym: [OE. asche, aske, AS. asce, æsce, axe; akin to OHG. asca, G. asche, D. asch, Icel. & Sw. aska, Dan. aske, Goth. azgo.]

senses.d: The principal female divinity of the Phœnicians, as Baal was the principal male divinity.
On, or to, one side; out of a straight line, course, or direction; at a little distance from the rest; out of the way; apart.
q: Thou shalt set aside that which is full. 2 Kings iv. 4.
But soft! but soft! aside: here comes the king. Shak.
The flames were blown aside. Dryden.

senses.d: Out of one's thoughts; off; away; as, to put aside gloomy thoughts.
So as to be heard by others; privately.
q: Then lords and ladies spake aside. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: Something spoken aside; as, a remark made by a stageplayer which the other players are not supposed to hear.
To request; to seek to obtain by words; to petition; to solicit; — often with of, in the sense of from, before the person addressed.
q: Ask counsel, we pray thee, of God. Judg. xviii. 5.
If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you. John xv. 7.

senses.d: To require, demand, claim, or expect, whether by way of remuneration or return, or as a matter of necessity; as, what price do you ask?
q: Ask me never so much dowry. Gen. xxxiv. 12.
To whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more. Luke xii. 48.
An exigence of state asks a much longer time to conduct a design to maturity. Addison.

senses.d: To interrogate or inquire of or concerning; to put a question to or about; to question.
q: He is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself. John ix. 21.
He asked the way to Chester. Shak.

senses.d: To invite; as, to ask one to an entertainment.
To publish in church for marriage; — said of both the banns and the persons.

Ask.syn: To beg; request; seek; petition; solicit; entreat; beseech; implore; crave; require; demand; claim; exhibit; inquire; interrogate. See Beg.
Ask.etym: [OE. asken, ashen, axien, AS. āscian, ācsian; akin to OS. ēscōn, OHG. eiscōn, Sw. āska, Dan. æske, D. eischen, G. heischen, Lith. jëskóti, OSlav. iskati to seek, Skr. ish to desire. √5.]

senses.d: To request or petition; — usually followed by for; as, to ask for bread.
q: Ask, and it shall be given you. Matt. vii. 7.

senses.d: To make inquiry, or seek by request; — sometimes followed by after.
q: Wherefore . . . dost ask after my name? Gen. xxxii. 29.

senses.d: A water newt.
The act of inquiring or requesting; a petition; solicitation.
The publishing of banns.
In a state of sleep; in sleep; dormant.
q: Fast asleep the giant lay supine. Dryden.
By whispering winds soon lulled asleep. Milton.

senses.d: In the sleep of the grave; dead.
q: Concerning them which are asleep . . . sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. 1 Thess. iv. 13.

senses.d: Numbed, and, usually, tingling.
q: Leaning long upon any part maketh it numb, and, as we call it, asleep. Bacon.

senses.d: Same as Aspen.

A small, hooded, poisonous serpent of Egypt and adjacent countries, whose bite is often fatal. It is the Naja haje. The name is also applied to other poisonous serpents, esp. to Vipera aspis of southern Europe. See Haje.

Asp.etym: [L. aspis, fr. Gr. ασπἴσ: cf. OF. aspe, F. aspic.]

senses.d: A quadruped of the genus Equus (E. asinus), smaller than the horse, and having a peculiarly harsh bray and long ears. The tame or domestic ass is patient, slow, and sure-footed, and has become the type of obstinacy and stupidity. There are several species of wild asses which are swift-footed.
A dull, heavy, stupid fellow; a dolt.

Ass.etym: [OE. asse, AS. assa; akin to Icel. asni, W. asen, asyn, L. asinus, dim. aselus, Gr. �; also to AS. esol, OHG. esil, G. esel, Goth. asilus, Dan. æsel, Lith. asilas, Bohem. osel, Pol. osiel. The word is prob. of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. ath�n she ass. Cf. Ease.]

senses.d: A violent onset or attack with physical means, as blows, weapons, etc.; an onslaught; the rush or charge of an attacking force; onset; as, to make assault upon a man, a house, or a town.
q: The Spanish general prepared to renew the assault. Prescott.
Unshaken bears the assault Of their most dreaded foe, the strong southwest. Wordsworth.

senses.d: A violent onset or attack with moral weapons, as words, arguments, appeals, and the like; as, to make an assault on the prerogatives of a prince, or on the constitution of a government.

An apparently violent attempt, or willful offer with force or violence, to do hurt to another; an attempt or offer to beat another, accompanied by a degree of violence, but without touching his person, as by lifting the fist, or a cane, in a threatening manner, or by striking at him, and missing him. If the blow aimed takes effect, it is a battery.
q: Practically, however, the word assault is used to include the battery. Mozley & W.

Assault.syn: Attack; invasion; incursion; descent; onset; onslaught; charge; storm.
Assault.etym: [OE. asaut, assaut, OF. assaut, asalt, F. assaut, LL. assaltus; L. ad + saltus a leaping, a springing, salire to leap. See Assail.]

senses.d: To make an assault upon, as by a sudden rush of armed men; to attack with unlawful or insulting physical violence or menaces.
q: Insnared, assaulted, overcome, led bound. Milton.

senses.d: To attack with moral means, or with a view of producing moral effects; to attack by words, arguments, or unfriendly measures; to assail; as, to assault a reputation or an administration.
q: Before the gates, the cries of babes newborn, . . . Assault his ears. Dryden.

Assault.syn: To attack; assail; invade; encounter; storm; charge. See Attack.
Assault.etym: [From Assault, n.: cf. OF. assaulter, LL. assaltare.]

senses.d: Trial; attempt; essay.
q: I am withal persuaded that it may prove much more easy in the assay than it now seems at distance. Milton.

senses.d: Examination and determination; test; as, an assay of bread or wine.
q: This can not be, by no assay of reason. Shak.

senses.d: Trial by danger or by affliction; adventure; risk; hardship; state of being tried.
q: Through many hard assays which did betide. Spenser.

senses.d: Tested purity or value.
q: With gold and pearl of rich assay. Spenser.

senses.d: The act or process of ascertaining the proportion of a particular metal in an ore or alloy; especially, the determination of the proportion of gold or silver in bullion or coin.
The alloy or metal to be assayed.

Assay.etym: [OF. asai, essai, trial, F. essa. See Essay, n.]

senses.d: To try; to attempt; to apply.
q: To-night let us assay our plot. Shak.
Soft words to his fierce passion she assayed. Milton.

senses.d: To affect.
q: When the heart is ill assayed. Spenser.

senses.d: To try tasting, as food or drink.

To subject, as an ore, alloy, or other metallic compound, to chemical or metallurgical examination, in order to determine the amount of a particular metal contained in it, or to ascertain its composition.

Assay.etym: [OF. asaier, essaier, F. essayer, fr. essai. See Assay, n., Essay, v.]

senses.d: To attempt, try, or endeavor.
q: She thrice assayed to speak. Dryden.

senses.d: The act or process of testing, esp. of analyzing or examining metals and ores, to determine the proportion of pure metal.
A small foxlike animal (Vulpes cama) of South Africa, valued for its fur.
To collect into one place or body; to bring or call together; to convene; to congregate.
q: Thither he assembled all his train. Milton.
All the men of Israel assembled themselves. 1 Kings viii. 2.

Assemble.etym: [F. assembler, fr. LL. assimulare to bring together to collect; L. ad + simul together; akin to similis like, Gr. � at the same time, and E. same. Cf. Assimilate, Same.]

senses.d: To meet or come together, as a number of individuals; to convene; to congregate.
q: The Parliament assembled in November. W. Massey.

senses.d: To liken; to compare.
q: Bribes may be assembled to pitch. Latimer.

senses.d: To collect and put together the parts of; as, to assemble a bicycle, watch, gun, or other manufactured article.
A company of persons collected together in one place, and usually for some common purpose, esp. for deliberation and legislation, for worship, or for social entertainment.
A collection of inanimate objects.
A beat of the drum or sound of the bugle as a signal to troops to assemble.
To admit a thing as true; to express one's agreement, acquiescence, concurrence, or concession.
q: Who informed the governor . . . And the Jews also assented, saying that these things were so. Acts xxiv. 9.
The princess assented to all that was suggested. Macaulay.

Assent.syn: To yield; agree; acquiesce; concede; concur.
Assent.etym: [F. assentir, L. assentire, assentiri; ad + sentire to feel, think. See Sense.]

senses.d: The act of assenting; the act of the mind in admitting or agreeing to anything; concurrence with approval; consent; agreement; acquiescence.
q: Faith is the assent to any proposition, on the credit of the proposer. Locke.
The assent, if not the approbation, of the prince. Prescott.
Too many people read this ribaldry with assent and admiration. Macaulay.

Assent.etym: [OE. assent, fr. assentir. See Assent, v.]

senses.d: To appoint; to allot; to apportion; to make over.
q: In the order I assign to them. Loudon.
The man who could feel thus was worthy of a better station than that in which his lot had been assigned. Southey.
He assigned to his men their several posts. Prescott.

senses.d: To fix, specify, select, or designate; to point out authoritatively or exactly; as, to assign a limit; to assign counsel for a prisoner; to assign a day for trial.
q: All as the dwarf the way to her assigned. Spenser.
It is not easy to assign a period more eventful. De Quincey.

senses.d: To transfer, or make over to another, esp. to transfer to, and vest in, certain persons, called assignees, for the benefit of creditors.

Assign.etym: [OE. assignen, asignen, F. assigner, fr. L. assignare; ad + signare to mark, mark out, designate, signum mark, sign. See Sign.]

senses.d: A thing pertaining or belonging to something else; an appurtenance.
q: Six French rapiers and poniards, with their assigns, as girdles, hangers, and so. Shak.

senses.d: A person to whom property or an interest is transferred; as, a deed to a man and his heirs and assigns.
To give support to in some undertaking or effort, or in time of distress; to help; to aid; to succor.
q: Assist me, knight. I am undone! Shak.

Assist.syn: To help; aid; second; back; support; relieve; succor; befriend; sustain; favor. See Help.
Assist.etym: [L. assistere; ad + sistere to cause to stand, to stand, from stare to stand: cf. F. assister. See Stand.]

senses.d: To lend aid; to help.
q: With God not parted from him, as was feared, But favoring and assisting to the end. Milton.

senses.d: To be present as a spectator; as, to assist at a public meeting.
To join with one, as a friend, companion, partner, or confederate; as, to associate others with us in business, or in an enterprise.
To join or connect; to combine in acting; as, particles of gold associated with other substances.
To connect or place together in thought.
q: He succeeded in associating his name inseparably with some names which will last as long as our language. Macaulay.

senses.d: To accompany; to keep company with.
q: Friends should associate friends in grief and woe. Shak.

Associate.etym: [L. associatus, p. p. of associare; ad + sociare to join or unite, socius companion. See Social.]

senses.d: To unite in company; to keep company, implying intimacy; as, congenial minds are disposed to associate.
To unite in action, or to be affected by the action of a different part of the body.
Closely connected or joined with some other, as in interest, purpose, employment, or office; sharing responsibility or authority; as, an associate judge.
q: While I descend . . . to my associate powers. Milton.

senses.d: Admitted to some, but not to all, rights and privileges; as, an associate member.
Connected by habit or sympathy; as, associate motions, such as occur sympathetically, in consequence of preceding motions.
A companion; one frequently in company with another, implying intimacy or equality; a mate; a fellow.
A partner in interest, as in business; or a confederate in a league.
One connected with an association or institution without the full rights or privileges of a regular member; as, an associate of the Royal Academy.
Anything closely or usually connected with another; an concomitant.
q: The one no sooner comes into the understanding, than its associate appears with it. Locke.

Associate.syn: Companion; mate; fellow; friend; ally; partner; coadjutor; comrade; accomplice.

senses.d: The act of assuring; a declaration tending to inspire full confidence; that which is designed to give confidence.
q: Whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead. Acts xvii. 31.
Assurances of support came pouring in daily. Macaulay.

senses.d: The state of being assured; firm persuasion; full confidence or trust; freedom from doubt; certainty.
q: Let us draw with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience. Heb. x. 22.

senses.d: Firmness of mind; undoubting, steadiness; intrepidity; courage; confidence; self-reliance.
q: Brave men meet danger with assurance. Knolles.
Conversation with the world will give them knowledge and assurance. Locke.

senses.d: Excess of boldness; impudence; audacity; as, his assurance is intolerable.
Betrothal; affiance.
Insurance; a contract for the payment of a sum on occasion of a certain event, as loss or death.
Any written or other legal evidence of the conveyance of property; a conveyance; a deed.

Assurance.etym: [OE. assuraunce, F. assurance, fr. assurer. See Assure.]

senses.d: To make sure or certain; to render confident by a promise, declaration, or other evidence.
q: His promise that thy seed shall bruise our foe . . . Assures me that the bitterness of death Is past, and we shall live. Milton.

senses.d: To declare to, solemnly; to assert to (any one) with the design of inspiring belief or confidence.
q: I dare assure thee that no enemy Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus. Shak.

senses.d: To confirm; to make certain or secure.
q: And it shall be assured to him. Lev. xxvii. 19.
And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him. 1 John iii. 19.

senses.d: To affiance; to betroth.
To insure; to covenant to indemnify for loss, or to pay a specified sum at death. See Insure.

Assure.syn: To declare; aver; avouch; vouch; assert; asseverate; protest; persuade; convince.
Assure.etym: [OF. aseürer, F. assurer, LL. assecurare; L. ad + securus secure, sure, certain. See Secure, Sure, and cf. Insure.]

senses.d: Made sure; safe; insured; certain; indubitable; not doubting; bold to excess.
One whose life or property is insured.
Certainly; indubitably.
Of or pertaining to Assyria, or to its inhabitants.
A native or an inhabitant of Assyria; the language of Assyria.
Stunned; astonished. See Astony.
q: And I astonied fell and could not pray. Mrs. Browning.

senses.d: To stun; to render senseless, as by a blow.
q: Enough, captain; you have astonished him. . Shak.
The very cramp-fish [i.e., torpedo] . . . being herself not benumbed, is able to astonish others. Holland.

senses.d: To strike with sudden fear, terror, or wonder; to amaze; to surprise greatly, as with something unaccountable; to confound with some sudden emotion or passion.
q: Musidorus . . . had his wits astonished with sorrow. Sidney.
I, Daniel . . . was astonished at the vision. Dan. viii. 27.

Astonish.etym: [OE. astonien, astunian, astonen, OF. estoner, F. étonner, fr. L. ex out + tonare to thunder, but perhaps influenced by E. stun. See Thunder, Astound, Astony.]

senses.d: The condition of one who is stunned. Hence: Numbness; loss of sensation; stupor; loss of sense.
q: A coldness and astonishment in his loins, as folk say. Holland.

senses.d: Dismay; consternation.
The overpowering emotion excited when something unaccountable, wonderful, or dreadful is presented to the mind; an intense degree of surprise; amazement.
q: Lest the place And my quaint habits breed astonishment. Milton.

senses.d: The object causing such an emotion.
q: Thou shalt become an astonishment. Deut. xxviii. 37.

senses.d: To stun; to bewilder; to astonish; to dismay.
q: The captain of the Helots . . . strake Palladius upon the side of his head, that he reeled astonied. Sir P. Sidney.
This sodeyn cas this man astonied so, That reed he wex, abayst, and al quaking. Chaucer.

senses.d: Out of the right, either in a literal or in a figurative sense; wandering; as, to lead one astray.
q: Ye were as sheep going astray. 1 Pet. ii. 25.

senses.d: One who studies the stars; an astronomer.
One who practices astrology; one who professes to foretell events by the aspects and situation of the stars.
Apart; separate from each other; into parts; in two; separately; into or in different pieces or places.
q: I took my staff, even Beauty, and cut it asunder. Zech. xi. 10.
As wide asunder as pole and pole. Froude.

senses.d: Primarily, this word expresses the relations of presence, nearness in place or time, or direction toward; as, at the ninth hour; at the house; to aim at a mark. It is less definite than in or on; at the house may be in or near the house. From this original import are derived all the various uses of at.
A relation of proximity to, or of presence in or on, something; as, at the door; at your shop; at home; at school; at hand; at sea and on land.
The relation of some state or condition; as, at war; at peace; at ease; at your service; at fault; at liberty; at risk; at disadvantage.
The relation of some employment or action; occupied with; as, at engraving; at husbandry; at play; at work; at meat (eating); except at puns.

The relation of a point or position in a series, or of degree, rate, or value; as, with the thermometer at 80°; goods sold at a cheap price; a country estimated at 10,000 square miles; life is short at the longest.
The relations of time, age, or order; as, at ten o'clock; at twenty-one; at once; at first.

The relations of source, occasion, reason, consequence, or effect; as, at the sight; at this news; merry at anything; at this declaration; at his command; to demand, require, receive, deserve, endure at your hands.
Relation of direction toward an object or end; as, look at it; to point at one; to aim at a mark; to throw, strike, shoot, wink, mock, laugh at any one.

At.etym: [AS. æt; akin to OHG. az, Goth., OS., & Icel. at, Sw. åt, Dan. & L. ad.]

senses.d: the preterit of Eat.
The goddess of mischievous folly; also, in later poets, the goddess of vengeance.
Of or pertaining to Athens, the metropolis of Greece.
A native or citizen of Athens.
Wanting drink; thirsty.
Having a keen appetite or desire; eager; longing.

Athirst.etym: [OE. ofthurst, AS. ofpyrsted, p. p. of ofpyrstan; pref. of-, intensive + pyrstan to thirst. See Thirst.]

senses.d: Reconciliation; restoration of friendly relations; agreement; concord.
q: By whom we have now received the atonement. Rom. v. 11.
He desires to make atonement Betwixt the Duke of Gloucester and your brothers. Shak.

senses.d: Satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing of suffering that which will be received in satisfaction for an offense or injury; expiation; amends; — with for. Specifically, in theology: The expiation of sin made by the obedience, personal suffering, and death of Christ.
q: When a man has been guilty of any vice, the best atonement be can make for it is, to warn others. Spectator.
The Phocians behaved with, so much gallantry, that they were thought to have made a sufficient atonement for their former offense. Potter.

senses.d: To achieve or accomplish, that is, to reach by efforts; to gain; to compass; as, to attain rest.
q: Is he wise who hopes to attain the end without the means? Abp. Tillotson.

senses.d: To gain or obtain possession of; to acquire.
To get at the knowledge of; to ascertain.
q: Not well attaining his meaning. Fuller.

senses.d: To reach or come to, by progression or motion; to arrive at.
To overtake.
To reach in excellence or degree; to equal.

Attain.etym: [Of. atteinen, atteignen, atainen, OF. ateindre, ataindre, F. atteindre, fr. L. attingere; ad + tangere to touch, reach. See Tangent, and cf. Attinge, Attaint.]

senses.d: To come or arrive, by motion, growth, bodily exertion, or efforts toward a place, object, state, etc.; to reach.
q: If by any means they might attain to Phenice. Acts xxvii. 12.
Nor nearer might the dogs attain. Sir W. Scott.
To see your trees attain to the dignity of timber. Cowper.
Few boroughs had as yet attained to power such as this. J. R. Green.

senses.d: To come or arrive, by an effort of mind.
q: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I can not attain unto it. Ps. cxxxix. 6.

senses.d: Attainment.
To direct the attention to; to fix the mind upon; to give heed to; to regard.
q: The diligent pilot in a dangerous tempest doth not attend the unskillful words of the passenger. Sir P. Sidney.

senses.d: To care for; to look after; to take charge of; to watch over.
To go or stay with, as a companion, nurse, or servant; to visit professionally, as a physician; to accompany or follow in order to do service; to escort; to wait on; to serve.
q: The fifth had charge sick persons to attend. Spenser.
Attends the emperor in his royal court. Shak.
With a sore heart and a gloomy brow, he prepared to attend William thither. Macaulay.

senses.d: To be present with; to accompany; to be united or consequent to; as, a measure attended with ill effects.
q: What cares must then attend the toiling swain. Dryden.

senses.d: To be present at; as, to attend church, school, a concert, a business meeting.
To wait for; to await; to remain, abide, or be in store for.
q: The state that attends all men after this. Locke.
Three days I promised to attend my doom. Dryden.

Attend.syn: To Attend, Mind, Regard, Heed, Notice.
Attend.etym: [OE. atenden, OF. atendre, F. attendre, to expect, to wait, fr. L. attendre to stretch, (sc. animum), to apply the mind to; ad + tendere to stretch. See Tend.]

senses.d: To apply the mind, or pay attention, with a view to perceive, understand, or comply; to pay regard; to heed; to listen; — usually followed by to.
q: Attend to the voice of my supplications. Ps. lxxxvi. 6.
Man can not at the same time attend to two objects. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: To accompany or be present or near at hand, in pursuance of duty; to be ready for service; to wait or be in waiting; — often followed by on or upon.
q: He was required to attend upon the committee. Clarendon.

senses.d: (with to) To take charge of; to look after; as, to attend to a matter of business.
To wait; to stay; to delay.
q: For this perfection she must yet attend, Till to her Maker she espoused be. Sir J. Davies.

senses.d: Attention; regard; careful application.
q: Till I come, give attendance to reading. 1 Tim. iv. 13.

senses.d: The act of attending; state of being in waiting; service; ministry; the fact of being present; presence.
q: Constant attendance at church three times a day. Fielding.

senses.d: Waiting for; expectation.
q: Languishing attendance and expectation of death. Hooker.

senses.d: The persons attending; a retinue; attendants.
q: If your stray attendance by yet lodged. Milton.

Attendance.etym: [OE. attendance, OF. atendance, fr. atendre, F. attendre. See Attend, v. t.]

senses.d: Attentive; heedful.
q: Let thine ears be attent unto the prayer. 2 Chron. vi. 40.

Attent.etym: [L. attentus, p. p. of attendere. See Attend, v. t.]

senses.d: Attention; heed.
Heedful; intent; observant; regarding with care or attention.
Heedful of the comfort of others; courteous.

Attentive.syn: Heedful; intent; observant; mindful; regardful; circumspect; watchful.

senses.d: To dress; to array; to adorn; esp., to clothe with elegant or splendid garments.
q: Finely attired in a robe of white. Shak.
With the linen miter shall he be attired. Lev. xvi. 4.

Attire.etym: [OE. atiren to array, dispose, arrange, OF. atirier; à (L. ad) + F. tire rank, order, row; of Ger. origin: cf. As. tier row, OHG. ziarī, G. zier, ornament, zieren to adorn. Cf. Tire a headdress.]

senses.d: Dress; clothes; headdress; anything which dresses or adorns; esp., ornamental clothing.
q: Earth in her rich attire. Milton.
I 'll put myself in poor and mean attire. Shak.
Can a maid forget her ornament, or a bride her attire? Jer. ii. 32.

senses.d: The antlers, or antlers and scalp, of a stag or buck.
The internal parts of a flower, included within the calyx and the corolla.
Provided with antlers, as a stag.
The act of hearing; attention to sounds.
q: Thou, therefore, give due audience, and attend. Milton.

senses.d: Admittance to a hearing; a formal interview, esp. with a sovereign or the head of a government, for conference or the transaction of business.
q: According to the fair play of the world, Let me have audience: I am sent to speak. Shak.

senses.d: An auditory; an assembly of hearers. Also applied by authors to their readers.
q: Fit audience find, though few. Milton.
He drew his audience upward to the sky. Dryden.

Audience.etym: [F. audience, L. audientia, fr. audire to hear. See Audible, a.]

senses.d: To enlarge or increase in size, amount, or degree; to swell; to make bigger; as, to augment an army by reëforcements; rain augments a stream; impatience augments an evil.
q: But their spite still serves His glory to augment. Milton.

senses.d: To add an augment to.

Augment.etym: [L. augmentare, fr. augmentum an increase, fr. augere to increase; perh. akin to Gr. �, �, E. wax, v., and eke, v.: cf. F. augmenter.]

senses.d: To increase; to grow larger, stronger, or more intense; as, a stream augments by rain.
Enlargement by addition; increase.
A vowel prefixed, or a lengthening of the initial vowel, to mark past time, as in Greek and Sanskrit verbs.
The sister of one's father or mother; — correlative to nephew or niece. Also applied to an uncle's wife.
An old woman; and old gossip.
A bawd, or a prostitute.

Aunt.etym: [OF. ante, F. tante, L. amita father's sister. Cf. Amma.]

senses.d: Sour and astringent; rough to the state; having acerbity; as, an austere crab apple; austere wine.
Severe in modes of judging, or living, or acting; rigid; rigorous; stern; as, an austere man, look, life.
q: From whom the austere Etrurian virtue rose. Dryden.

senses.d: Unadorned; unembellished; severely simple.

Austere.syn: Harsh; sour; rough; rigid; stern; severe; rigorous; strict.
Austere.etym: [F. austère, L. austerus, fr. Gr. �, fr. � to parch, dry. Cf. Sear.]

senses.d: The beginner, former, or first mover of anything; hence, the efficient cause of a thing; a creator; an originator.
q: Eternal King; thee, Author of all being. Milton.

senses.d: One who composes or writes a book; a composer, as distinguished from an editor, translator, or compiler.
q: The chief glory of every people arises from its authors. Johnson.

senses.d: The editor of a periodical.
An informant.

Author.etym: [OE. authour, autour, OF. autor, F. auteur, fr. L. auctor, sometimes, but erroneously, written autor or author, fr. augere to increase, to produce. See Auction, n.]

senses.d: To occasion; to originate.
q: Such an overthrow . . . I have authored. Chapman.

senses.d: To tell; to say; to declare.
q: More of him I dare not author. Massinger.

senses.d: Legal or rightful power; a right to command or to act; power exercised buy a person in virtue of his office or trust; dominion; jurisdiction; authorization; as, the authority of a prince over subjects, and of parents over children; the authority of a court.
q: Thus can the demigod, Authority, Make us pay down for our offense. Shak.
By what authority doest thou these things ? Matt. xxi. 23.

senses.d: Government; the persons or the body exercising power or command; as, the local authorities of the States; the military authorities.

The power derived from opinion, respect, or esteem; influence of character, office, or station, or mental or moral superiority, and the like; claim to be believed or obeyed; as, an historian of no authority; a magistrate of great authority.
That which, or one who, is claimed or appealed to in support of opinions, actions, measures, etc.
q: Wilt thou be glass wherein it shall discern Authority for sin, warrant for blame. Shak.

Authority.etym: [OE. autorite, auctorite, F. autorité, fr. L. auctoritas, fr. auctor. See Author, n.]

senses.d: Same as Kava.
To turn to the advantage of; to be of service to; to profit; to benefit; to help; as, artifices will not avail the sinner in the day of judgment.
q: O, what avails me now that honor high ! Milton.

senses.d: To promote; to assist.
q: Then shall they seek to avail themselves of names. Milton.
I have availed myself of the very first opportunity. Dickens.

Avail.etym: [OE. availen, fr. F. � (L. ad) + valoir to be worth, fr. L. valere to be strong, to be worth. See Valiant.]

senses.d: To be of use or advantage; to answer the purpose; to have strength, force, or efficacy sufficient to accomplish the object; as, the plea in bar must avail, that is, be sufficient to defeat the suit; this scheme will not avail; medicines will not avail to check the disease.
q: Words avail very little with me, young man. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: Profit; advantage toward success; benefit; value; as, labor, without economy, is of little avail.
q: The avail of a deathbed repentance. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: Proceeds; as, the avails of a sale by auction.
q: The avails of their own industry. Stoddard.

senses.d: To take vengeance for; to exact satisfaction for by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain or evil on a wrongdoer.
q: He will avenge the blood of his servants. Deut. xxxii. 43.
Avenge, O Lord, thy slaughtered saints, whose bones Lie scattered on the Alpine mountains cold. Milton.
He had avenged himself on them by havoc such as England had never before seen. Macaulay.

senses.d: To treat revengefully; to wreak vengeance on.
q: Thy judgment in avenging thine enemies. Bp. Hall.
I avenge myself upon another, or I avenge another, or I avenge a wrong. I revenge only myself, and that upon another. C. J. Smith.

Avenge.etym: [OF. avengier; L. ad + vindicare to lay claim to, to avenge, revenge. See Vengeance.]

senses.d: To take vengeance.
Vengeance; revenge.
One who avenges or vindicates; as, an avenger of blood.
One who takes vengeance.
Turned away or backward.
q: The tracks averse a lying notice gave, And led the searcher backward from the cave. Dryden.

senses.d: Having a repugnance or opposition of mind; disliking; disinclined; unwilling; reluctant.
q: Averse alike to flatter, or offend. Pope.
Men who were averse to the life of camps. Macaulay.
Pass by securely as men averse from war. Micah ii. 8.

Averse.etym: [L. aversus, p. p. of avertere. See Avert.]

senses.d: To turn away.
To empty.
To emit or throw out; to void; as, to avoid excretions.
To quit or evacuate; to withdraw from.
q: Six of us only stayed, and the rest avoided the room. Bacon.

senses.d: To make void; to annul or vacate; to refute.
q: How can these grants of the king's be avoided? Spenser.

senses.d: To keep away from; to keep clear of; to endeavor no to meet; to shun; to abstain from; as, to avoid the company of gamesters.
q: What need a man forestall his date of grief. And run to meet what he would most avoid ? Milton.
He carefully avoided every act which could goad them into open hostility. Macaulay.

senses.d: To get rid of.
To defeat or evade; to invalidate. Thus, in a replication, the plaintiff may deny the defendant's plea, or confess it, and avoid it by stating new matter.
q: No man can pray from his heart to be kept from temptation, if the take no care of himself to avoid it. Mason.
So Chanticleer, who never saw a fox, Yet shunned him as a sailor shuns the rocks. Dryden.

Avoid.etym: [OF. esvuidier, es (L. ex) + vuidier, voidier, to empty. See Void, a.]

senses.d: To retire; to withdraw.
q: David avoided out of his presence. 1 Sam. xviii. 11.

senses.d: To become void or vacant.
To appeal to; to cite or claim as authority.
q: They avouch many successions of authorities. Coke.

senses.d: To maintain a just or true; to vouch for.
q: We might be disposed to question its authenticity, it if were not avouched by the full evidence. Milman.

senses.d: To declare or assert positively and as matter of fact; to affirm openly.
q: If this which he avouches does appear. Shak.
Such antiquities could have been avouched for the Irish. Spenser.

senses.d: To acknowledge deliberately; to admit; to confess; to sanction.
q: Thou hast avouched the Lord this day to be thy God. Deut. xxvi. 17.

Avouch.etym: [OF. avochier, LL. advocare to recognize the existence of a thing, to advocate, fr. L. advocare to call to; ad + vocare to call. Cf. Avow to declare, Advocate, and see Vouch, v. t.]

senses.d: Evidence; declaration.
q: The sensible and true avouch Of mine own eyes. Shak.

senses.d: To watch for; to look out for.
To wait on, serve, or attend.
To wait for; to stay for; to expect. See Expect.
q: Betwixt these rocky pillars Gabriel sat, Chief of the angelic guards, awaiting night. Milton.

senses.d: To be in store for; to be ready or in waiting for; as, a glorious reward awaits the good.
q: O Eve, some farther change awaits us night. Milton.

Await.etym: [OF. awaitier, agaitier; � (L. ad) + waitier, gaitier to watch, F. guetter. See Wait.]

senses.d: To watch.
To wait (on or upon).
To wait; to stay in waiting.
A waiting for; ambush; watch; watching; heed.
To rouse from sleep; to wake; to awaken.
q: Where morning's earliest ray . . . awake her. Tennyson.
And his disciples came to him, and awoke him, saying, Lord, save us; we perish. Matt. viii. 25.

senses.d: To rouse from a state resembling sleep, as from death, stupidity., or inaction; to put into action; to give new life to; to stir up; as, to awake the dead; to awake the dormant faculties.
q: I was soon awaked from this disagreeable reverie. Goldsmith.
It way awake my bounty further. Shak.
No sunny gleam awakes the trees. Keble.

Awake.etym: [AS. āwæcnan, v. i. (imp. awōc), and āwacian, v. i. (imp. awacode). See Awaken, Wake.]

senses.d: To cease to sleep; to come out of a state of natural sleep; and, figuratively, out of a state resembling sleep, as inaction or death.
q: The national spirit again awoke. Freeman.
Awake to righteousness, and sin not. 1 Cor. xv. 34.

senses.d: Not sleeping or lethargic; roused from sleep; in a state of vigilance or action.
q: Before whom awake I stood. Milton.
She still beheld, Now wide awake, the vision of her sleep. Keats.
He was awake to the danger. Froude.

Awake.etym: [From awaken, old p. p. of awake.]

senses.d: Watchful; vigilant or on one's guard against danger or difficulty.
Apprised; informed; cognizant; conscious; as, he was aware of the enemy's designs.
q: Aware of nothing arduous in a task They never undertook. Cowper.

Aware.etym: [OE. iwar, AS. gewær, fr. wær wary. The pref. ge- orig. meant together, completely. �. See Wary.]

senses.d: From a place; hence.
q: The sound is going away. Shak.
Have me away, for I am sore wounded. 2 Chron. xxxv. 23.

senses.d: Absent; gone; at a distance; as, the master is away from home.
Aside; off; in another direction.
q: The axis of rotation is inclined away from the sun. Lockyer.

senses.d: From a state or condition of being; out of existence.
q: Be near me when I fade away. Tennyson.

senses.d: By ellipsis of the verb, equivalent to an imperative: Go or come away; begone; take away.
q: And the Lord said . . . Away, get thee down. Exod. xix. 24.

senses.d: On; in continuance; without intermission or delay; as, sing away.

Away.etym: [AS. aweg, anweg, onweg; on on + weg way.]

senses.d: Dread; great fear mingled with respect.
q: His frown was full of terror, and his voice Shook the delinquent with such fits of awe. Cowper.

senses.d: The emotion inspired by something dreadful and sublime; an undefined sense of the dreadful and the sublime; reverential fear, or solemn wonder; profound reverence.
q: There is an awe in mortals' joy, A deep mysterious fear. Keble.
To tame the pride of that power which held the Continent in awe. Macaulay.
The solitude of the desert, or the loftiness of the mountain, may fill the mind with awe — the sense of our own littleness in some greater presence or power. C. J. Smith.

Awe.etym: [OE. a”e, aghe, fr. Icel. agi; akin to AS. ege, ōga, Goth. agis, Dan. ave chastisement, fear, Gr. ἄχοσ pain, distress, from the same root as E. ail. √3. Cf. Ugly.]

senses.d: To strike with fear and reverence; to inspire with awe; to control by inspiring dread.
q: That same eye whose bend doth awe the world. Shak.
His solemn and pathetic exhortation awed and melted the bystanders. Macaulay.

senses.d: A tool or instrument of steel, or of iron with a steel edge or blade, for felling trees, chopping and splitting wood, hewing timber, etc. It is wielded by a wooden helve or handle, so fixed in a socket or eye as to be in the same plane with the blade. The broadax, or carpenter's ax, is an ax for hewing timber, made heavier than the chopping ax, and with a broader and thinner blade and a shorter handle.

Ax.etym: [OE. ax, axe, AS. eax, æx, acas; akin to D. akse, OS. accus, OHG. acchus, G. axt, Icel. öx, öxi, Sw. yxe, Dan. ökse, Goth. aqizi, Gr. �, L. ascia; not akin to E. acute.]

senses.d: To ask; to inquire or inquire of.
A bar or beam of wood or iron, connecting the opposite wheels of a carriage, on the ends of which the wheels revolve.
A spindle or axle of a wheel.
The imperial standard of the Turkish Empire.
To transfer or pass over property to another, whether for the benefit of the assignee or of the assignor's creditors, or in furtherance of some trust.
